EXPOSÉ XXII
REDUCTIVE GROUPS: SPLITTINGS, SUBGROUPS, QUOTIENT GROUPSby M. Demazure

This exposé consists of two parts. The first (1 to 5.5) collects the technical results needed for the proof of the uniqueness and existence theorems. The second (5.6 to the end) will not be used in that proof; the end of no. 5 will be used in particular in Exposé XXVI, devoted to parabolic subgroups; no. 6 establishes, in the setting of schemes, the classical results on the derived group of a reductive group.

pages.title: 1. Roots and coroots. Split groups and root data

blocks.html: 1. Roots and coroots. Split groups and root data

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 1.1

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\), \(\alpha\) a root of \(G\) with respect to \(T\).

  1. (i)

    There exists a unique morphism of groups with group of operators \(T\) \[ \exp_\alpha : \mathbf{W}(\mathfrak{g}^\alpha) \longrightarrow G \] which induces on the Lie Algebras the canonical morphism \(\mathfrak{g}^\alpha \to \mathfrak{g}\). This morphism is a closed immersion. The corresponding morphism \[ T \cdot_\alpha \mathbf{W}(\mathfrak{g}^\alpha) \longrightarrow G \] is likewise a closed immersion. If \(p_\alpha : \mathbf{G}_{a, S} \to G\) is a monomorphism normalised by \(T\) with multiplier \(\alpha\), there exists a unique \(X_\alpha \in \Gamma(S, \mathfrak{g}^\alpha)^*\) such that \(p_\alpha(x) = \exp_\alpha(x X_\alpha)\); one has \(\mathrm{Lie}(p_\alpha)(1) = X_\alpha\), and the two preceding formulas establish a bijective correspondence between \(\Gamma(S, \mathfrak{g}^\alpha)^*\) and the set of monomorphisms \(\mathbf{G}_{a, S} \to G\) normalised by \(T\) with multiplier \(\alpha\).

  2. (ii)

    There exist a unique duality (written \((X, Y) \mapsto XY\)) \[ \mathfrak{g}^\alpha \otimes_{\mathscr{O}_S} \mathfrak{g}^{-\alpha} \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \mathscr{O}_S, \] and a unique morphism of groups \[ \alpha^* : \mathbf{G}_{m, S} \longrightarrow T, \] such that formula (F) of Exp. XX 2.1 holds. One has \[ \alpha \circ \alpha^* = 2, \qquad (-\alpha)^* = -\alpha^*, \] and \(\alpha^*\) is given by the formula of Exp. XX 2.7.

Indeed, a morphism normalised by \(T\) with multiplier \(\alpha\) necessarily factors through the closed subgroup \(Z_\alpha = \underline{\mathrm{Centr}}_G(T_\alpha)\) of \(G\) (cf. Exp. XIX 3.9). Now \((Z_\alpha, T, \alpha)\) is an elementary \(S\)-system (Exp. XX 1.4), and one is reduced to the results of Exposé XX (1.5, 2.1 and 5.9).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 1.2

Part (i) of theorem 1.1 remains valid if one assumes only that \(\alpha\) is a character of \(T\), non-trivial on each fibre. Indeed, one then has a decomposition \(S = S' \amalg S''\) such that \(\alpha|_{S'}\) is a root of \(G_{S'}\) with respect to \(T_{S'}\) and \(\mathfrak{g}^\alpha|_{S''} = 0\). If \(S = S'\), one is reduced to 1.1; if \(S = S''\) the result is trivial; the general case follows at once.
Notations 1.3.

As in Exposé XX, one denotes by \(U_\alpha\) the image of \(\mathbf{W}(\mathfrak{g}^\alpha)\); it is a closed subgroup of \(G\), canonically endowed with a vector structure. We shall say that it is the vector group associated with the root \(\alpha\). One says that \(\alpha^*\) is the coroot associated with \(\alpha\). Sections \(X_\alpha \in \Gamma(S, \mathfrak{g}^\alpha)\) and \(X_{-\alpha} \in \Gamma(S, \mathfrak{g}^{-\alpha})\) are said to be paired if \(X_\alpha X_{-\alpha} = 1\). Then \(X_\alpha \in \Gamma(S, \mathfrak{g}^\alpha)^*\), and similarly for \(X_{-\alpha}\). The corresponding morphisms \(p_\alpha\) and \(p_{-\alpha}\) are contragredient to one another in the sense of XX, 1.5, and one has \[ p_\alpha(x) \, p_{-\alpha}(y) = p_{-\alpha}\!\left(\frac{y}{1+xy}\right) \, \alpha^*(1+xy) \, p_\alpha\!\left(\frac{x}{1+xy}\right). \]

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.4

Under the conditions of 1.1, let \(w \in \mathrm{Norm}_G(T)(S)\). Then \(\beta = \alpha \circ \mathrm{int}(w)^{-1} : T \to \mathbf{G}_{m,S}\) is a root of \(G\) with respect to \(T\), \(\beta^* = \mathrm{int}(w) \circ \alpha^*\) is the corresponding coroot, and the following diagram is commutative: \[ \xymatrix{ \mathbf{W}(\mathfrak{g}^\alpha) \ar[r]^{\exp_\alpha} \ar[d]_{\mathrm{Ad}(w)} & G \ar[d]^{\mathrm{int}(w)} \\ \mathbf{W}(\mathfrak{g}^\beta) \ar[r]^{\exp_\beta} & G. } \]
Trivial: transport of structure.

blocks.title: Definitions
blocks.html:
Definitions 1.5

(a) Under the conditions of 1.1, one denotes by \(s_\alpha\) the automorphism of \(T\) defined by \[ s_\alpha(t) = t \cdot \alpha^*(\alpha(t))^{-1}. \] Then \(s_\alpha\) operates on \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(T, \mathbf{G}_{m,S})\), resp. \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(\mathbf{G}_{m,S}, T)\), by the formulas \[ s_\alpha(m) = m - (\alpha^*, m)\, \alpha, \] \[ s_\alpha(u) = u - (u, \alpha)\, \alpha^*, \] where \(m\) and \(u\) are arbitrary sections of \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(T, \mathbf{G}_{m,S})\) and \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(\mathbf{G}_{m,S}, T)\) respectively, and \((\;,\;)\) denotes the canonical pairing \[ \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(\mathbf{G}_{m,S}, T) \times \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(T, \mathbf{G}_{m,S}) \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(\mathbf{G}_{m,S}, \mathbf{G}_{m,S}) = \mathbf{Z}_S. \] One has \(s_\alpha \circ s_\alpha = \mathrm{id}\), \(s_{-\alpha} = s_\alpha\).

(b) If \(X \in \Gamma(S, \mathfrak{g}^\alpha)^*\), then the inner automorphism of \(T\) defined by \[ w_\alpha(X) = \exp_\alpha(X)\, \exp_{-\alpha}(-X^{-1})\, \exp_\alpha(X) \] (cf. Exp. XX 3.1) coincides with \(s_\alpha\) (loc. cit.). One then concludes from 1.4:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.6

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\), \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) two roots of \(G\) with respect to \(T\). Then \[ s_\alpha(\beta) = \beta - (\alpha^*, \beta)\, \alpha \] is a root of \(G\) with respect to \(T\), the corresponding coroot being \[ s_\alpha(\beta)^* = s_\alpha(\beta^*) = \beta^* - (\beta^*, \alpha)\, \alpha^*. \]

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.7

Under the preceding conditions, \(\alpha^* = \beta^*\) implies \(\alpha = \beta\).

Indeed, if \(\alpha^* = \beta^*\), one has \[ s_\beta(\alpha) = \alpha - 2\beta, \qquad s_\alpha(\beta) = \beta - 2\alpha, \] and one deduces at once \[ (s_\beta s_\alpha)^n(\alpha) = \alpha + 2n(\beta - \alpha). \]

If \(\beta \ne \alpha\), there exists an \(s \in S\) with \(\alpha_s \ne \beta_s\). But then the preceding formula shows that there exist infinitely many distinct roots of \(G_s\) with respect to \(T_s\), which is impossible.

If \(u : \mathbf{G}_{m,S} \to T\) is a morphism of groups, one says that \(u\) is a coroot of \(G\) with respect to \(T\) if there exists a root \(\alpha\) of \(G\) with respect to \(T\) such that \(\alpha^* = u\). Consider the functor \(R^*\) of coroots of \(G\) with respect to \(T\), defined as follows: \[ R^*(S') = \text{set of coroots of } G_{S'} \text{ with respect to } T_{S'}. \] If \(R\) is the functor of roots of \(G\) with respect to \(T\) (Exp. XIX 3.8), one has a canonical morphism \(R \to R^*\). By 1.7 and Exp. XIX 3.8, one has:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.8

The canonical morphism \(R \to R^*\) is an isomorphism. In particular, \(R^*\) is representable by a finite twisted constant \(S\)-prescheme which is an open and closed subprescheme of \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{S\text{-gr}}(\mathbf{G}_{m,S}, T)\).
This leads one to lay down the following definition:

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 1.9

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(T\) an \(S\)-torus. One calls a twisted root datum in \(T\) the datum:

  1. (i)

    of a finite subscheme \(R\) of \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(T, \mathbf{G}_{m,S})\),

  2. (ii)

    of a finite subscheme \(R^*\) of \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(\mathbf{G}_{m,S}, T)\),

  3. (iii)

    of an isomorphism \(R \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} R^*\) written \(\alpha \mapsto \alpha^*\),

satisfying the following conditions:

(DR 1) For every \(S' \to S\) and every \(\alpha \in R(S')\), one has \(\alpha \circ \alpha^* = 2\).

(DR 2) For every \(S' \to S\) and all \(\alpha, \beta \in R(S')\), one has \[ \alpha - (\beta^*, \alpha)\, \beta \in R(S'), \qquad \alpha^* - (\alpha^*, \beta)\, \beta^* \in R(S'). \]

Moreover, if \(\alpha \in R(S')\) (\(S' \ne \varnothing\)) implies \(2\alpha \notin R(S')\), one says that the root datum is reduced.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.10

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\), \(R\) (resp. \(R^*\)) the scheme of roots (resp. of coroots) of \(G\) with respect to \(T\). Then \((R, R^*)\) is a reduced twisted root datum in \(T\).
The only fact that remains to be checked is that this twisted root datum is reduced. That was done in Exp. XIX 3.10.

Let \(T = D_S(M)\) be a trivialised torus. If one denotes by \(M^*\) the abelian group dual to \(M\), one has canonical isomorphisms (cf. Exp. VIII 1.5): \[ \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(T, \mathbf{G}_{m,S}) \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} M_S \] \[ \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(\mathbf{G}_{m,S}, T) \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} M^*_S, \] hence isomorphisms of groups: \[ \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(T, \mathbf{G}_{m,S}) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Hom}_{\text{loc.const.}}(S, M), \] \[ \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(\mathbf{G}_{m,S}, T) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Hom}_{\text{loc.const.}}(S, M^*). \]

A character of \(T\) (resp. a morphism of groups \(\mathbf{G}_{m,S} \to T\)) will be said to be constant (relatively to the given trivialisation) if the preceding isomorphism transforms it into a constant map from \(S\) to \(M\) (resp. \(M^*\)).

With the same notations, let \((M, M^*, R, R^*)\) be a root datum (Exp. XXI). Then \((R_S, R^*_S)\) is a twisted root datum in \(T\). Conversely, if \((R, R^*)\) is a twisted root datum in a torus \(T\), one will call a splitting of this root datum the datum of an ordinary root datum \((M, M^*, R, R^*)\) together with an isomorphism \(T \simeq D_S(M)\) which transforms \((R, R^*)\) into \((R_S, R^*_S)\).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 1.13

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\). One calls a splitting of \(G\) relative to \(T\) the datum

  1. (i)

    of an abelian group \(M\) and of an isomorphism \(T \simeq D_S(M)\),

  2. (ii)

    of a root system \(R\) of \(G\) with respect to \(T\) (Exp. XIX 3.6),

satisfying the two following conditions:

(D1) \(S\) is non-empty and the roots \(\alpha \in R\) (resp. the corresponding coroots) are identified with constant functions from \(S\) to \(M\) (resp. \(M^*\)).

(D2) The \(\mathfrak{g}^\alpha\) (\(\alpha \in R\)) are free \(\mathscr{O}_S\)-Modules.

One says that \(G\) is splittable relative to \(T\) if there exists a splitting of \(G\) relative to \(T\). One calls a splitting of \(G\) the datum of a maximal torus \(T\) of \(G\) and of a splitting of \(G\) with respect to \(T\). One says that \(G\) is splittable if there exists a splitting of \(G\). One calls a split \(S\)-group a reductive \(S\)-group endowed with a splitting; it will be denoted by a symbol of the type \((G, T, M, R)\), or simply \(G\) if no confusion is possible.
Condition (D 1) entails that \(R\) (resp. \(R^*\)) is canonically identified with a subset of \(M\) (resp. \(M^*\)).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.14

Let \(S\) be a (non-empty) prescheme, \((G, T, M, R)\) a split \(S\)-group; then \[ \mathscr{R}(G, T, M, R) = (M, M^*, R, R^*) \] is a reduced root datum (Exp. XXI 1.1 and 2.1.3); it is a splitting of the twisted root datum of 1.10.
This is a trivial consequence of 1.10 and of Exp. XIX 3.7.
We shall sometimes write, for simplicity, \(\mathscr{R}(G, T, M, R) = \mathscr{R}(G)\). We shall systematically use the notations \(V\), \(V(R)\), \(W\), \(\ldots\) of Exp. XXI.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 1.15

a) If \(S\) is connected and non-empty (resp. if \(\mathrm{Pic}(S) = 0\)) condition (D 1) (resp. (D 2)) is automatically satisfied.

b) If \((G, T, M, R)\) is a split \(S\)-group, then for every \(S' \to S\), \(S' \ne \varnothing\), \((G_{S'}, T_{S'}, M, R)\) is a split \(S'\)-group and \(\mathscr{R}(G, T, M, R) = \mathscr{R}(G_{S'}, T_{S'}, M, R)\).

Let \(T = D_S(M)\) be a trivialised torus. The Lie Algebra \(\mathfrak{t}\) of \(T\) is canonically identified (Exp. II 5.1, cor.) with \[ \mathfrak{t} \simeq M^* \otimes \mathscr{O}_S. \] For every morphism of groups \(u : T \to \mathbf{G}_{m,S}\), \(\mathrm{Lie}(u)\) is a linear form \[ \mathrm{Lie}(u) : \mathfrak{t} \longrightarrow \mathscr{O}_S = \mathrm{Lie}(\mathbf{G}_{m,S}/S). \] In particular, if \(u\) is defined by an element \(\alpha \in M\), then \(\mathrm{Lie}(u)\) is the linear form \(\alpha\) on \(M^* \otimes \mathscr{O}_S\) defined by \(\alpha\): \[ \alpha(m \otimes x) = (m, \alpha)\, x. \] Symmetrically, for every morphism of groups \(h : \mathbf{G}_{m,S} \to T\), \(\mathrm{Lie}(h)\) is an \(\mathscr{O}_S\)-morphism \(\mathscr{O}_S = \mathrm{Lie}(\mathbf{G}_{m,S}/S) \to \mathfrak{t}\), canonically defined by the section \[ H = \mathrm{Lie}(h)(1) \in \Gamma(S, \mathfrak{t}). \] In particular, if \(h\) is defined by an element \(m \in M^*\), one has \[ H = \mathrm{Lie}(h)(1) = m \otimes 1. \] Comparing the two definitions, one finds in particular \[ \alpha(H) = (h, \alpha) \cdot 1 \in \Gamma(S, \mathscr{O}_S). \]

These definitions apply in particular to the case where \(T\) is the maximal torus of a split group. Every root \(\alpha \in R\) defines an infinitesimal root \(\alpha \in \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathscr{O}_S}(\mathfrak{t}, \mathscr{O}_S)\) with \[ \alpha(m \otimes x) = (m, \alpha)\, x. \] Each coroot \(\alpha \in R\) defines an infinitesimal coroot \[ H_\alpha \in \Gamma(S, \mathfrak{t}), \qquad H_\alpha = \alpha^* \otimes 1. \] One has, for \(\alpha, \beta \in R\), the relation \[ \alpha(H_\beta) = (\beta^*, \alpha) \cdot 1, \] and in particular \[ \alpha(H_\alpha) = 2. \] In particular, if \(2\) is invertible on \(S\), \(\alpha\) and \(H_\alpha\) are non-zero on each fibre.

pages.title: 2. Existence of a splitting. Type of a reductive group

blocks.html: 2. Existence of a splitting. Type of a reductive group

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.1

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\). Suppose \(T\) trivial. Then \(G\) is locally splittable with respect to \(T\): for every \(s_0 \in S\), there exists an open neighbourhood \(U\) of \(s_0\) such that the \(U\)-group \(G_U\) is splittable relative to \(T_U\).

Indeed, write \(T \simeq D_S(M)\) and \[ \mathfrak{g} = \bigoplus_{m \in M} \mathfrak{g}^m. \] Let \(R = \{m \in M \mid m \ne 0, \mathfrak{g}^m(s_0) \ne 0\}\). After possibly shrinking \(S\) and replacing it by an open neighbourhood of \(s_0\), one may assume the \(\mathfrak{g}^\alpha\), \(\alpha \in R\), free, and the \(\mathfrak{g}^m\), \(m \ne 0\), \(m \notin R\), zero. One then has \[ \mathfrak{g} = \mathfrak{t} \oplus \bigoplus_{\alpha \in R} \mathfrak{g}^\alpha, \] the \(\mathfrak{g}^\alpha\) being free of rank 1. It follows that \(R\) is a root system of \(G\) with respect to \(T\) (Exp. XIX 3.6). The coroots \(\alpha^*\) corresponding to the \(\alpha \in R\) are then identified with locally constant functions on \(S\) with values in \(M^*\). By shrinking \(S\) further, one may assume them constant, and we are done.
Note that the proof gives at once:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.2

Let \(S\) be a connected non-empty prescheme such that \(\mathrm{Pic}(S) = 0\), for example \(\mathrm{Spec}(\mathbf{Z})\) or a local scheme (in particular the spectrum of a field). If \(G\) is a reductive \(S\)-group possessing a trivial maximal torus \(T\), then \(G\) is splittable relative to \(T\).
One deduces at once from 2.1 and from the fact that a reductive group possesses maximal tori locally for the étale topology (Exp. XIX 2.5):

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.3

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group (resp. and \(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\)). Then \(G\) is locally splittable (resp. locally splittable relative to \(T\)) for the étale topology on \(S\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.4

Let \(k\) be a field, \(G\) a reductive \(k\)-group. There exists a finite separable extension \(K/k\) such that \(G_K\) is splittable.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 2.5

Using 2.1 and Exp. XIX 2.9, one proves at once the following result: let \(\mathscr{G} = (G, T, M, R)\) be a split \(S\)-group; there exists a covering of \(S\) by open sets \(U_i\) such that each split group \(G_{U_i}\) arises by base change from a split group over a noetherian ring (and in fact a \(\mathbf{Z}\)-algebra of finite type). We shall in fact prove that every split group over \(S\) already arises from a split \(\mathbf{Z}\)-group (Exp. XXV).

Let \(k\) be an algebraically closed field and \(G\) a reductive \(k\)-group. It is known (2.4, for example) that there exist splittings of \(G\). Let \((G, T, M, R)\) and \((G, T', M', R')\) be two splittings of \(G\); then the two root data \(\mathscr{R}(G, T, M, R)\) and \(\mathscr{R}(G, T', M', R')\) are isomorphic.

Indeed, one sees first that one may reduce to the case where \(T = T'\) (for there exists \(g \in G(k)\) with \(T' = \mathrm{int}(g) T\), and one checks easily that if one transports a splitting by an automorphism of \(G\), one finds a root datum isomorphic to the initial one); but \(S = \mathrm{Spec}(k)\) being connected, the isomorphism \(D_k(M) \xrightarrow{\sim} T \xrightarrow{\sim} D_k(M')\) arises from a unique isomorphism \(M \simeq M'\); for the same reason, there is at most one root system of \(G\) with respect to \(T\).

One will call the type of \(G\) the isomorphism class of the root datum defined by an arbitrary splitting of \(G\); if \(G\) is a torus, of type \(M\) in the sense of Exp. IX 1.4, then the type of \(G\) as a reductive group is given by the trivial root datum \((M, M^*, \varnothing, \varnothing)\). By 1.17, the type is invariant under (algebraically closed) extension of the base field.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 2.7

If \(G\) is a reductive \(S\)-group and if \(s \in S\), one calls the type of \(G\) at \(s\) the type of the reductive \(s\)-group \(G_s\).
For every \(S' \to S\) and every \(s' \in S'\) projecting to \(s \in S\), the type of \(G_{S'}\) at \(s'\) is equal to the type of \(G\) at \(s\).

If \(G\) is splittable, and if \((G, T, M, R)\) is a splitting of \(G\), then the type of \(G\) at \(s\) is the isomorphism class of \(\mathscr{R}(G, T, M, R)\), by 1.17. There then follows at once from 2.3 the

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.8

Let \(G\) be a reductive \(S\)-group. The function \[ s \mapsto \text{type of } G \text{ at } s \] is locally constant on \(S\). In particular, there exists a partition of \(S\) into non-empty open subpreschemes such that on each of them \(G\) is of constant type. More precisely, let \(E\) be the set of types of the fibres of \(G\); for every \(t \in E\), let \(S_t\) be the set of points \(s \in S\) at which \(G\) is of type \(t\); then \((S_t)_{t \in E}\) is a partition of \(S\) and each \(S_t\) is open and closed (and non-empty).
3. The Weyl group

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\). Then \[ W_G(T) = \mathrm{Norm}_G(T)/T \] is a finite étale \(S\)-group (Exp. XIX 2.5). By passage to the quotient starting from \(n \mapsto \mathrm{int}(n)\), one has a canonical monomorphism (which is moreover an open immersion) \[ W_G(T) \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(T). \]

Suppose now that \(G\) is splittable relative to \(T\). Choose a splitting, say \((G, T, M, R)\). One then has a canonical isomorphism (Exp. VIII 1.5) \[ \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(T) \simeq (\mathrm{Aut}_{\text{gr.}}(M))_S. \] In particular, if \(W\) is the Weyl group of the root datum \(\mathscr{R}(G)\) (Exp. XXI 1.1.8), one has a monomorphism \[ W_S \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(T). \]

For each root \(\alpha \in R\), the symmetry \(s_\alpha \in W\) operates on \(M\) by \[ s_\alpha(x) = x - (\alpha^*, x)\, \alpha, \] hence on \(T\) (by the preceding morphism), by \[ s_\alpha(t) = t \cdot \alpha^*(\alpha(t))^{-1}. \] On the other hand, since \(\mathfrak{g}^\alpha\) is assumed free, there exists an \(X \in \Gamma(S, \mathfrak{g}^\alpha)^*\). Consider then \(w_\alpha(X) \in \mathrm{Norm}_G(T)(S)\) (Exp. XX 3.1). One has (loc. cit.) \[ \mathrm{int}(w_\alpha(X))(t) = s_\alpha(t). \] Since \(W\) is generated by the \(s_\alpha\), \(\alpha \in R\), it follows from the preceding remarks that if one regards \(W\) and \(\mathrm{Norm}_G(T)(S)/T(S)\) as groups of automorphisms of \(T\), one has \[ W \subset \mathrm{Norm}_G(T)(S)/T(S) \subset W_G(T)(S). \] By definition of the constant group \(W_S\) associated with \(W\), one thus has a commutative diagram \[ \xymatrix{ W_S \ar[rd] \ar[r] & W_G(T) \ar[d] \\ & \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(T). } \]

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.4

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \((G, T, M, R)\) a split \(S\)-group, \(W\) the Weyl group of the root datum \(\mathscr{R}(G)\). Then the canonical monomorphism \[ W_S \longrightarrow W_G(T) = \mathrm{Norm}_G(T)/T \] is an isomorphism.

These are indeed groups étale over \(S\); it therefore suffices to check that for every \(s \in S\), \(W_S(s) \to W_G(T)(s)\) is an isomorphism. Now this last assertion follows, for example, from BIBLE, 11-07, th. 2.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 3.5

Using 2.3, 3.4 gives a new proof of the fact that the Weyl group of a maximal torus of a reductive group is finite (Exp. XIX 2.5 (ii)).

Under the conditions of 3.1, for every \(w \in W_G(T)(S)\), we denote by \(Q_w\) the fibre product of the diagram \[ \xymatrix{ Q_w \ar[r] \ar[d] & \mathrm{Norm}_G(T) \ar[d] \\ S \ar[r]^{w} & W_G(T). } \] It is an open and closed sub-prescheme of \(\mathrm{Norm}_G(T)\), which is a principal homogeneous bundle under \(T\) on the left (resp. on the right) by the law \((t, q) \mapsto tq\) (resp. \((q, t) \mapsto qt\)). If \(n \in Q_w(S)\), one has \[ Q_{ww'} = n \cdot Q_{w'}, \qquad Q_{w'w} = Q_{w'} \cdot n. \]

In particular, if \(\alpha\) is a root of \(G\) with respect to \(T\), \(Q_{s_\alpha}\) is nothing but what was denoted by \(Q\) in Exp. XX no. 3. If \(\mathfrak{g}^\alpha\) is free over \(S\), one therefore has \(Q_{s_\alpha}(S) \ne \varnothing\).
From 3.4 and condition (D 2) of the splitting, one deduces the

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.8

Under the conditions of 3.4, \[ \mathrm{Norm}_G(T)(S) \longrightarrow W_G(T)(S) = \mathrm{Hom}_{\text{loc.cons.}}(S, W) \] is surjective. In particular, for every \(w \in W\), there exists an \(n_w \in \mathrm{Norm}_G(T)(S)\) such that \(\mathrm{int}(n_w)|_T = w\).
4. Homomorphisms of split groups
4.1. The "big cell"
Let \((G, T, M, R)\) be a split \(S\)-group. Let us choose a system of positive roots (Exp. XXI 3.2.1) \(R^+\) of the root datum \(\mathscr{R}(G)\). We set \(R^- = -R^+\).

Let us choose a total order on \(R^+\) (resp. \(R^-\)) and consider the morphism induced by the product in \(G\) \[ u : \prod_{\alpha \in R^-} U_\alpha \times_S T \times_S \prod_{\alpha \in R^+} U_\alpha \longrightarrow G. \]

It is an open immersion. Indeed, since both sides are flat and of finite presentation over \(S\), it suffices to verify this on each geometric fibre (SGA 1, I 5.7 and VIII 5.4); one is thus reduced to the case where \(S\) is the spectrum of an algebraically closed field; but, by BIBLE, 13-11, cor. 2 to th. 3, \(u\) is radicial and dominant; since the tangent map to \(u\) at the origin is an isomorphism (definition of a root system), \(u\) is birational; but \(G\) being normal, one may apply the Main Theorem (EGA III1, 4.4.9) and \(u\) is an open immersion. Let us show that the image \(\Omega\) of this open immersion is independent of the order chosen on \(R^+\) (resp. \(R^-\)). Since it is a question of comparing open subsets of \(G\), one is reduced to proving that they have the same geometric points, so one may again assume that \(S\) is the spectrum of an algebraically closed field. But then the assertion is nothing but BIBLE, 13-05, th. 1, and 13-02, prop. 1.
We have thus proved:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.1.2

Let \((G, T, M, R)\) be a split \(S\)-group. Let \(R^+\) be a system of positive roots of \(R\). There exists an open subset \(\Omega_{R^+}\) of \(G\) such that for every total order on \(R^+\) (resp. \(R^-\)), the morphism induced by the product in \(G\) \[ \prod_{\alpha \in R^-} U_\alpha \times_S T \times_S \prod_{\alpha \in R^+} U_\alpha \longrightarrow G \] is an open immersion with image \(\Omega_{R^+}\).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 4.1.3

One can translate 4.1.2 as follows: let us choose for every \(\alpha \in R\) an isomorphism of vector groups \(p_\alpha : \mathbf{G}_{a,S} \xrightarrow{\sim} U_\alpha\) (cf. 1.19); then the morphism (we set \(N = \mathrm{Card}(R^+) = \mathrm{Card}(R^-)\)) \[ \mathbf{G}_{a,S}^N \times_S T \times_S \mathbf{G}_{a,S}^N \longrightarrow G \] defined set-theoretically by \[ ((x_\alpha)_{\alpha \in R^-}, t, (x_\alpha)_{\alpha \in R^+}) \longmapsto \prod_{\alpha \in R^-} p_\alpha(x_\alpha) \cdot t \cdot \prod_{\alpha \in R^+} p_\alpha(x_\alpha) \] is an open immersion, whose image depends only on \(R^+\) (and not on the choice of the \(p_\alpha\) and of the orders on \(R^+\) and \(R^-\)).
Notation 4.1.4.
We write \(\Omega_{R^+} = \prod_{\alpha \in R^-} U_\alpha \cdot T \cdot \prod_{\alpha \in R^+} U_\alpha\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.1.5

The prescheme \(\Omega_{R^+}\) is of finite presentation over \(S\) (hence retrocompact in \(G\)) and relatively schematically dense in \(G\) (Exp. XVIII 1).
The first assertion is trivial, the second follows from the fact that \(\Omega_{R^+}\) contains the unit section, hence meets each fibre of \(G\), and from Exp. XVIII 1.3.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 4.1.6

Under the conditions of 4.1.2, one has \[ \mathrm{Centr}(G) = \bigcap_{\alpha \in R} \mathrm{Ker}(\alpha). \]

One may invoke Exp. XII 4.8 and 4.11; one may also prove it directly as follows. It obviously suffices to prove that \(\mathrm{Centr}(G)(S) = \bigcap_\alpha \mathrm{Ker}(\alpha)(S)\). If \(t \in T(S)\) and if \(\alpha(t) = 1\) for every \(\alpha \in R\), then \(\mathrm{int}(t)\) induces the identity on \(T\) and on each \(U_\alpha\), \(\alpha \in R\), hence also on \(\Omega_{R^+}\), hence on \(G\) by schematic density. Conversely, if \(g \in G(S)\) centralises \(T\) and the \(U_\alpha\), it is a section of \(T\) (Exp. XIX 2.8) which annihilates the \(\alpha \in R\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 4.1.7

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group. Then the centre of \(G\) is representable by a closed subgroup of \(G\), of multiplicative type; it is also "the intersection of the maximal tori of \(G\)" in the following sense: For every \(S' \to S\), \(\mathrm{Centr}(G)(S')\) is the set of \(g \in G(S')\) whose inverse image in \(G(S'')\), for every \(S'' \to S'\), is contained in all the \(T(S'')\), where \(T\) runs through the set of maximal tori of \(G_{S''}\).

The first assertion is trivial by descent. Let us prove the second. Let \(H\) be "the intersection of the maximal tori of \(G\)" in the above sense. One obviously has \(\mathrm{Centr}(G) \subset H\). To prove \(\mathrm{Centr}(G) = H\), it suffices to prove that if \(G\) is split, \(\mathrm{Centr}(G)\) is the intersection of the maximal tori of \(G\) (in the usual sense); this then follows from the following remark: if \(X \in \Gamma(S, \mathfrak{g}^\alpha)^*\), then \(\mathrm{int}(\exp_\alpha(X))(T) \cap T = \mathrm{Ker}(\alpha)\), as a trivial computation shows. (Cf. also Exp. XII 8.6 and 8.8 for a more general statement).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 4.1.8

In what follows, in the split case we shall systematically identify \(T\) with \(D_S(M)\). Then \(\mathrm{Centr}(G)\) is nothing but \(D_S(M/\Gamma_0(R))\), where (Exp. XXI) \(\Gamma_0(R)\) is the subgroup of \(M\) generated by \(R\). If \(\{\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_n\}\) is a system of simple roots of \(R\), one has at once (cf. Exp. XX 1.19): \[ \mathrm{Centr}(G) = \bigcap \mathrm{Ker}(\alpha_i) = \bigcap \mathrm{Centr}(Z_{\alpha_i}). \]

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.1.9

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \((G, T, M, R)\) a split \(S\)-group, \(Q\) an \(S\)-torus, \(\alpha_0\) a character of \(Q\), \(\mathscr{L}\) an invertible \(\mathscr{O}_S\)-Module, \[ f : Q \longrightarrow T, \qquad p : \mathbf{W}(\mathscr{L}) \longrightarrow G \] group morphisms satisfying the set-theoretic relation \[ p(\alpha_0(q)\, x) = \mathrm{int}(f(q)) \cdot p(x), \] for all \(q \in Q(S')\), \(x \in \mathbf{W}(\mathscr{L})(S')\), \(S' \to S\). Suppose that \(f\) separates the elements of \(R\) in the following sense: if \(\alpha, \alpha' \in R\) and if \(m, m' \in \mathbf{Z}\) then \(m\, \alpha \circ f = m'\, \alpha' \circ f\) implies \(m\, \alpha = m'\, \alpha'\). Finally, let \(s \in S\) be such that \((\alpha_0)_s \ne e\) and \(p_s \ne e\).

Then there exist an open subset \(U\) of \(S\) containing \(s\), an integer \(q > 0\) such that \(x \mapsto x^q\) is an endomorphism of \(\mathbf{G}_{a,U}\), a root \(\alpha \in R\) and an isomorphism of \(\mathscr{O}_U\)-Modules \[ h : (\mathscr{L}|_U)^{\otimes q} \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \mathfrak{g}^\alpha|_U \] such that

  1. (i)

    \((\alpha \circ f)_U = (q\, \alpha_0)_U\),

  2. (ii)

    \(p(X) = \exp_\alpha(h(X^q))\) for every \(X \in \mathbf{W}(\mathscr{L})(S')\), \(S' \to U\).

Moreover, once \(U\) has been chosen, \(q\), \(\alpha\) and \(h\) are uniquely determined.

After possibly shrinking \(S\), we may assume that \(\alpha_0\) is non-zero on each fibre of \(S\). Let us choose a system of positive roots \(R^+\) of \(R\) and let \(U = p^{-1}(\Omega_{R^+})\). It is an open subset of \(\mathbf{W}(\mathscr{L})\) containing the zero section and stable under multiplication by any \(\alpha_0(q)\), \(q \in Q(S')\), \(S' \to S\). Since \(\alpha_0\) is non-trivial on each fibre, it follows immediately that \(U = \mathbf{W}(\mathscr{L})\), hence that \(p\) factors through \(\Omega_{R^+}\). Let us choose an arbitrary order on \(R^+\) and \(R^-\); all products will be understood to be taken in this order. One thus has unique morphisms \[ a_\alpha : \mathbf{W}(\mathscr{L}) \longrightarrow U_\alpha, \quad \alpha \in R, \qquad b : \mathbf{W}(\mathscr{L}) \longrightarrow T \] such that \[ p(x) = \prod_{\alpha \in R^-} a_\alpha(x) \cdot b(x) \cdot \prod_{\alpha \in R^+} a_\alpha(x). \]

Writing out the covariance condition under \(Q\), one obtains at once \[ a_\alpha(\alpha_0(q)\, x) = \alpha(f(q))\, a_\alpha(x), \quad \alpha \in R \] \[ b(\alpha_0(q)\, x) = b(x) \] for all \(x \in \mathbf{W}(\mathscr{L})(S')\), \(q \in Q(S')\), \(S' \to S\). The second condition gives at once \(b = e\).

Now let \(\alpha \in R\) be such that \((a_\alpha)_s e e\) (we know that such an \(\alpha\) exists, since \(p_s\) is assumed \( e e\)). Applying Exp. XIX 4.12 (a), one deduces that there exists an integer \(n > 0\) such that \((\alpha \circ f)_s = (n\, \alpha_0)_s\). After possibly shrinking \(S\), one may assume \(\alpha \circ f = n\, \alpha_0\) (Exp. IX 5.3). But then, for every \(\alpha' \in R\), \(\alpha' e \alpha\), one has \((\alpha' \circ f)_s e n\, \alpha_0\) for every integer \(m > 0\) in virtue of the hypothesis made on \(f\) (and of the fact that the only roots proportional to \(\alpha\) are \(\alpha\) and \(-\alpha\)). Applying Exp. XIX 4.12 (a) again, this time to \(a_{\alpha'}\), one deduces that \(a_{\alpha'}\) is zero in a neighbourhood of \(S\); \(R\) being finite, one may, after possibly shrinking \(S\) further, assume the \(a_{\alpha'}\) zero for \(\alpha' \in R\), \(\alpha' e \alpha\). One then has \(p = a_\alpha\), and one may apply to it Exp. XIX 4.12 (b), then (c), which gives the announced result (the uniqueness assertions are obvious).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 4.1.10

The condition imposed on \(f\) in 4.1.9 is satisfied in particular if \(f\) is surjective (= faithfully flat).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.1.11

Let \((G, T, M, R)\) be a split \(S\)-group, \(R^+\) a system of positive roots of \(R\), \(\Omega_{R^+}\) the corresponding "big cell".

  1. (i)

    Let \(H\) be an \(S\)-group functor, separated for (fppf). If \(f, g : G \rightrightarrows H\) are two group morphisms which coincide on \(\Omega_{R^+}\), then \(f = g\).

  2. (ii)

    Let \(H\) be an \(S\)-group sheaf for (fppf) and \(f : \Omega_{R^+} \to H\) an \(S\)-morphism satisfying the following condition: for every \(S' \to S\) and all \(x, y \in \Omega_{R^+}(S')\) such that \(xy \in \Omega_{R^+}(S')\), one has \(f(xy) = f(x) f(y)\). Then there exists a (unique, by (i)) group morphism \(f : G \to H\) which extends \(f\).
Indeed, by 4.1.5, (i) (resp. (ii)) follows at once from Exp. XVIII 2.2 (resp. 2.3 and 2.4).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 4.1.12

If \(\alpha \in R^+\), one has \[ \Omega_{R^+} \cap Z_\alpha = U_{-\alpha} \cdot T \cdot U_\alpha. \] In particular, if \(X \in \Gamma(S, \mathfrak{g}^\alpha)\) and \(Y \in \Gamma(S, \mathfrak{g}^{-\alpha})\), one has \[ (\exp_\alpha(X)\, \exp_{-\alpha}(Y) \in \Omega(S)) \iff (1 + XY \text{ invertible}). \]
Indeed \(Z_\alpha = \mathrm{Centr}(T_\alpha)\), and \(\alpha\) and \(-\alpha\) are the only two elements of \(R\) vanishing on \(T_\alpha\).
4.2. Morphisms of split groups

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 4.2.1

Let \(S\) be a (non-empty) prescheme, \((G, T, M, R)\) and \((G', T', M', R')\) two split \(S\)-groups. One says that the morphism of \(S\)-groups \(f : G \to G'\) is compatible with the splittings, or defines a morphism of split groups, if the restriction of \(f\) to \(T\) factors through a morphism \(f_T : T \to T'\) which is of the form \(f_T = D_S(h)\), where \(h : M' \to M\) is a group homomorphism satisfying the following condition:

there exist a bijection \(u : R \xrightarrow{\sim} R'\) and, for each \(\alpha \in R\), an integer \(q(\alpha) > 0\) such that \(x \mapsto x^{q(\alpha)}\) is an endomorphism of \(\mathbf{G}_{a,S}\) and such that \[ h(u(\alpha)) = q(\alpha)\, \alpha, \qquad {}^t h(\alpha^*) = q(\alpha)\, u(\alpha)^*. \]

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 4.2.2

It is immediate that \(h\), \(u\), \(q(\alpha)\) for \(\alpha \in R\), are uniquely determined by \(f\). One writes \(h = \mathscr{R}(f)\). The \(q(\alpha)\) are the root exponents of \(f\) (or of \(h\)).

Let \(p\) be the prime number (if it exists) which is zero on \(S\); we set \(p = 1\) if there is no prime number zero on \(S\). Then \(\mathscr{R}(f)\) is a \(p\)-morphism of reduced root data in the sense of Exp. XXI 6.8. We have thus defined a functor \(\mathscr{R}\) from the category of split \(S\)-groups into that of reduced root data [for the notion of \(p\)-morphism].

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.2.3

Under the conditions of 4.2.1, one has the following properties:

  1. (i)

    For every \(\alpha \in R\), there exists a unique isomorphism of \(\mathscr{O}_S\)-Modules \[ f_\alpha : (\mathfrak{g}^\alpha)^{\otimes q(\alpha)} \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \mathfrak{g}'^{u(\alpha)} \] such that \[ f(\exp_\alpha(X)) = \exp_{u(\alpha)}(f_\alpha(X^{q(\alpha)})) \] for every \(X \in \mathbf{W}(\mathfrak{g}^\alpha)(S')\), \(S' \to S\).

  2. (ii)

    For every \(\alpha \in R\), one has \(q(-\alpha) = q(\alpha)\) and \(f_\alpha\) and \(f_{-\alpha}\) are contragredient to one another.

  3. (iii)

    For every \(\alpha \in R\), every \(Z \in \mathbf{W}(\mathfrak{g}^\alpha)^*(S')\), \(S' \to S\), one has \[ f(w_\alpha(Z)) = w_{u(\alpha)}(Z^{q(\alpha)}). \]

By hypothesis the diagram \[ \xymatrix{ \mathbf{G}_{m,S} \ar[r]^{\alpha^*} \ar[d]_{q(\alpha)} & T \ar[r]^{\alpha} \ar[d]^{f_T} & \mathbf{G}_{m,S} \ar[d]^{q(\alpha)} \\ \mathbf{G}_{m,S} \ar[r]^{u(\alpha)^*} & T' \ar[r]^{u(\alpha)} & \mathbf{G}_{m,S} } \] is commutative. It follows that \(f\) maps \(\mathrm{Ker}(\alpha)\) into \(\mathrm{Ker}(u(\alpha))\), hence \(T_\alpha\) into \(T'_{u(\alpha)}\), hence \(Z_\alpha\) into \(Z'_{u(\alpha)}\). It then only remains to apply Exp. XX 3.10 and 3.11 to the groups \(Z_\alpha\) and \(Z'_{u(\alpha)}\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.2.4

The morphism \(f\) induces a morphism \(f_N\) from \(\mathrm{Norm}(T)\) into \(\mathrm{Norm}_{G'}(T')\), hence a morphism \(f_w\) from \(W_G(T)\) into \(W_{G'}(T')\); the latter is an isomorphism. More precisely, if one denotes by \(u : W(\mathscr{R}(G)) = W \to W' = W(\mathscr{R}(G'))\) the isomorphism which extends \(s_\alpha \mapsto s_{u(\alpha)}\) (Exp. XXI 6.8.4), one has a commutative diagram of isomorphisms: \[ \xymatrix{ W_G(T) \ar[r]^{f_w}_{\sim} & W_{G'}(T') \\ W_S \ar[u]^{\wr} \ar[r]^{u_S}_{\sim} & W'_S. \ar[u]_{\wr} } \]
This follows at once from 3.4, Exp. XXI 6.8.4, and (iii) above.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 4.2.5

With the notations of 4.2.3, the restriction of \(f\) to \(\Omega_{R^+}\) (for a system of positive roots \(R^+\)) can be written explicitly: it maps \(\Omega_{R^+}\) into \(\Omega'_{u(R^+)}\) (\(u(R^+)\) is a system of positive roots of \(R'\) by Exp. XXI 6.8.7) and is given by the set-theoretic formula: \[ f\!\left(\prod_{\alpha \in R^-} \exp_\alpha(X_\alpha) \cdot t \cdot \prod_{\alpha \in R^+} \exp_\alpha(X_\alpha)\right) = \prod_{\alpha \in R^-} \exp_{u(\alpha)}(f_\alpha(X_\alpha^{q(\alpha)})) \cdot f_T(t) \cdot \prod_{\alpha \in R^+} \exp_{u(\alpha)}(f_\alpha(X_\alpha^{q(\alpha)})). \]

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.2.6
  1. (i)

    \(f\) is surjective (= faithfully flat in the present case, cf. Exp. VIB) if and only if \(f_T\) is.

  2. (ii)

    One has \(\mathrm{Ker}(f) \subset \Omega_{R^+}\).

Let us prove (i): if \(f\) is surjective, then \(f(T) = f_T(T)\) is a maximal torus of \(G'\) (indeed \(f_T(T)\) is a subtorus of \(T'\), Exp. IX 6.8; to check that it is maximal, one is reduced to the case of an algebraically closed field, where this is BIBLE, 7.05, th. 3 (a)), hence equal to \(T'\). If \(f_T\) is surjective, then the preceding formula shows that \(f|_\Omega\) is surjective, which implies that \(f\) is surjective (Exp. VI).

Let us prove (ii), and for this let us admit a result which will be proved below (5.7.4): let us choose for each \(w \in W\) an \(n_w \in \mathrm{Norm}_G(T)(S)\) representing it; then the open subsets \(n_w \Omega\) (\(w \in W\)) form a covering of \(G\). It suffices to prove that \(\mathrm{Ker}(f) \cap n_w \Omega \ne \varnothing\) implies \(w = 1\). If \(x \in \Omega(S')\), \(S' \to S\) and \(f(n_w x) = e\), one has \(f(x) = f(n_w)^{-1}\); now \(f(x) \in \Omega'(S')\) and \(f(n_w)^{-1} \in \mathrm{Norm}_{G'}(T')(S')\). In virtue of 4.2.4, one is reduced to proving:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 4.2.7

Under the conditions of 4.1.2, one has \[ \Omega \cap \mathrm{Norm}_G(T) = T. \]

Let \[ x = \prod_{\alpha \in R^-} p_\alpha(x_\alpha) \cdot t \cdot \prod_{\alpha \in R^+} p_\alpha(x_\alpha) = v\, t\, u \in \Omega(S'). \] If \(x\) normalises \(T_{S'}\), one has for every \(t' \in T(S')\), \[ x t' x^{-1} = t'' \in T(S'), \] that is to say \(x t' = t'' x\), which can be written \[ v\, (tt') \, (t'^{-1} u t') = (t'' v t''^{-1})\, (t'' t)\, u, \] which gives \(t'^{-1} u t' = u\), hence \(u \in \mathrm{Centr}_G(T)(S') = T(S')\), that is \(u = e\). Likewise \(v = e\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 4.2.8

One has \[ \mathrm{Ker}(f) = \prod_{\alpha \in R^-} K_\alpha \cdot \mathrm{Ker}(f_T) \cdot \prod_{\alpha \in R^+} K_\alpha, \] where for each \(\alpha \in R\), \(K_\alpha\) denotes the finite \(S\)-group \[ K_\alpha = \mathrm{Ker}(U_\alpha \xrightarrow{\otimes q(\alpha)} U_\alpha) \simeq \alpha_{q(\alpha), S}. \]
In order to apply this lemma, let us set:

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 4.2.9

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) and \(G'\) two reductive \(S\)-groups. A morphism of \(S\)-groups \(f : G \to G'\) which is faithfully flat and finite (i.e. surjective and with finite kernel over \(S\)) is called an isogeny. If \(\mathrm{Ker}(f)\) is a central subgroup of \(G\), one says that \(f\) is a central isogeny.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.2.10

Let \(f : G \to G'\) be a morphism of split groups. For \(f\) to be an isogeny (resp. a central isogeny) it is necessary and sufficient that \(f_T\) be an isogeny, i.e. that \(\mathscr{R}(f)\) be injective with finite cokernel (resp. and that for every \(\alpha \in R\), one have \(q(\alpha) = 1\)).

Indeed, by 4.2.8, \(\mathrm{Ker}(f)\) is finite over \(S\) if and only if \(\mathrm{Ker}(f_T)\) is finite over \(S\), and \(\mathrm{Ker}(f) \subset T\) if and only if each \(q(\alpha) = 1\) (\(\mathrm{Ker}(f)\) is then central, being of multiplicative type and invariant, cf. Exp. IX 5.5).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 4.2.11

a) One thus sees that \(f : G \to G'\) is a central isogeny if and only if \(\mathscr{R}(f) : \mathscr{R}(G') \to \mathscr{R}(G)\) is an isogeny in the sense of Exp. XXI 6.2; moreover one has in this case (with the notations of loc. cit.): \[ \mathrm{Ker}(f) = D_S(K(\mathscr{R}(f))), \qquad K(\mathscr{R}(f)) = \mathrm{Coker}(\mathscr{R}(f)). \]

b) If \(G\) and \(G'\) are semi-simple, every morphism of split groups \(f : G \to G'\) is an isogeny.

c) If \(f : G \to G'\) is faithfully flat and finite and if \(G\) is reductive (resp. semi-simple), then so is \(G'\). It is indeed of finite presentation over \(S\) (Exp. V 9.1), affine over \(S\) (EGA II 6.7.1), smooth over \(S\) (Exp. VI 9.2), with connected and reductive (resp. semi-simple) geometric fibres by Exp. XIX 1.7.
Definition 4.2.1 may seem arbitrary. It is justified by the proposition which follows (which we shall state, for simplicity, for semi-simple groups).
Let us say that a morphism \(f : G \to G'\) of reductive \(S\)-groups is splittable if there exist splittings of \(G\) and \(G'\) with which \(f\) is compatible. One then has the

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.2.12

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) and \(G'\) two semi-simple \(S\)-groups, \(f : G \to G'\) a group morphism. Let \(s \in S\). The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    \(\mathrm{Ker}\, f_s\) is finite (\(\Leftrightarrow\) \(e\) is isolated in \(\mathrm{Ker}\, f(s)\)) and \(f_s\) is surjective, i.e. \(f_s\) is an isogeny.

  2. (ii)

    \(f_s\) is splittable.

  3. (iii)

    There exists an étale morphism \(S' \to S\) covering \(s\) such that \(f_{S'} : G_{S'} \to G'_{S'}\) is splittable.

One obviously has (iii) \(\Leftrightarrow\) (ii); (ii) \(\Leftrightarrow\) (i) follows from 4.2.11 (b) (it is here that the hypothesis that \(G\) and \(G'\) are semi-simple comes in – the other implications are valid for reductive groups).

Let us now prove (i) \(\Rightarrow\) (iii). One may assume \(G\) and \(G'\) split in such a way that \(f\) induces a morphism \(f_T : T \to T'\) (2.3 and Exp. XIX 2.8); after possibly shrinking \(S\), one may assume that \(f_T = D_S(h)\), where \(h\) is a group morphism \(M' \to M\). Let \(\alpha \in R\), and consider the composite morphism \[ p : \mathbf{W}(\mathfrak{g}^\alpha) \xrightarrow{\exp_\alpha} G \xrightarrow{f} G'. \] Since \(\mathrm{Ker}(p_s)\) is finite, \(p_s \ne e\). On the other hand \(f_{T_s}\) is surjective; one may therefore apply 4.1.9 and there exist an open subset \(V_\alpha\) of \(S\) containing \(s\), a root \(\alpha' \in R'\), an integer \(q(\alpha)\) such that \(x \mapsto x^{q(\alpha)}\) is an endomorphism of \(\mathbf{G}_{a, V_\alpha}\), and an isomorphism of \(\mathscr{O}_{V_\alpha}\)-Modules \[ f_\alpha : (\mathfrak{g}^\alpha)^{\otimes q(\alpha)}|_{V_\alpha} \longrightarrow \mathfrak{g}^{\alpha'}|_{V_\alpha} \] such that \(f(\exp_\alpha(X_\alpha)) = \exp_{u(\alpha)}(f_\alpha(X_\alpha^{q(\alpha)}))\) and \(\alpha' \circ f_T = h(\alpha') = q(\alpha)\, \alpha\). One may replace \(S\) by the intersection of the \(V_\alpha\), for \(\alpha \in R\). Let us set \(\alpha' = u(\alpha)\). It is clear that \(u : R \to R'\) is a bijection, since the kernel of \(h\) is finite (\(f_{T_s}\) being surjective). It only remains to prove that \(f_T \circ \alpha^* = q(\alpha)\, \alpha'^*\), which is done by a trivial modification of the argument used in Exp. XX 3.11.
In any case, as was seen in the course of the proof, one has (i) \(\Rightarrow\) (iii). One therefore has:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 4.2.13

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(f : G \to G'\) an isogeny of reductive groups. Then \(f\) is locally splittable for the étale topology.
4.3. Central quotients of reductive groups
Let us first consider a special case.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.3.1

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \((G, T, M, R)\) a split \(S\)-group, \(N\) a subgroup of \(M\) containing \(R\), \(Q = D_S(M/N) \subset \mathrm{Centr}(G)\). Then \(G' = G/Q\) is a reductive \(S\)-group, \(T' = T/Q\) is a maximal torus of it; if one identifies \(T'\) with \(D_S(N)\), then \(R \subset N\) is a root system of \(G'\) with respect to \(T'\), \((G', T', N, R)\) is a splitting of \(G\), \(\mathscr{R}(G')\) is canonically identified with the induced root datum (Exp. XXI 6.5) \(\mathscr{R}(G)_N\); the canonical morphism \[ G \longrightarrow G' \] is compatible with the splittings and has root exponents \(1\), and yields by functoriality the canonical morphism (loc. cit.) \(\mathscr{R}(G)_N \to \mathscr{R}(G)\).

We know that \(G' = G/Q\) is representable by a prescheme affine over \(S\) (Exp. VIII 5.7), smooth over \(S\) (Exp. VI), with connected reductive geometric fibres (as quotients of reductive groups (Exp. XIX 1.7); hence \(G'\) is a reductive \(S\)-group. It is clear that \(T' = T/Q \simeq D_S(N)\) is a maximal torus of it. Let us next remark that, on choosing a system of positive roots \(R^+\) of \(R\), the open set \(\Omega_{R^+}\) of 4.2 is stable under \(Q\) and that one has a canonical isomorphism \[ \Omega_{R^+}/Q \simeq \prod_{\alpha \in R^-} U_\alpha \times_S T/Q \times_S \prod_{\alpha \in R^+} U_\alpha, \] \(\Omega_{R^+}/Q\) being an open subset of \(G'\) containing the unit section (Exp. IV 4.7.2 and 6.4.1). It follows that, if we denote by \(\mathfrak{g}'\) the Lie Algebra of \(G'\) and by \(\alpha\) the character of \(T/Q\) induced by \(\alpha\) (or, what amounts to the same, defined by \(\alpha \in N\) under the identification \(T/Q = D_S(N)\)), the canonical morphism \(\mathfrak{g} \to \mathfrak{g}'\) induces for each \(\alpha \in R\) an isomorphism \[ \mathfrak{g}^\alpha \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \mathfrak{g}'^{\alpha}. \] We have thus proved that \(R\) is a root system of \(G'\) with respect to \(T'\), and the proof is completed without difficulty.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 4.3.2

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(Q\) an invariant subgroup of multiplicative type of \(G\). Then \(Q\) is central in \(G\), and the quotient \(G/Q\) is representable by a reductive \(S\)-group. The canonical morphism \(G \to G/Q\) is locally splittable for the étale topology (with root exponents equal to \(1\)).
The first assertion follows from Exp. IX 5.5; the others are local for the étale topology and one is reduced to 4.3.1.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 4.3.3

Let \(G\) be a reductive \(S\)-group. We say that \(G\) is adjoint (resp. simply connected) if for every \(s \in S\) the type of \(G\) at \(s\) is given by an adjoint (resp. simply connected) root datum, i.e. (Exp. XXI 6.2.6) one such that \(M\) is generated by \(R\) (resp. \(M^*\) is generated by \(R^*\)).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.3.4
  1. (i)

    An adjoint (resp. simply connected) reductive group is semi-simple.

  2. (ii)

    If \(T\) is a maximal torus of the adjoint (resp. simply connected) reductive group \(G\) and if \(\alpha\) is a root of \(G\) with respect to \(T\), then the infinitesimal root \(\alpha\) is nonzero on each fibre (resp. \(\alpha^*\) is a monomorphism and the infinitesimal coroot \(H_\alpha\) is nonzero on each fibre).
Indeed, (i) is trivial; (ii) may be verified on the geometric fibres and follows at once from Exp. XXI 6.2.8.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.3.5
  1. (i)

    In order that the reductive group \(G\) be adjoint, it is necessary and sufficient that \(\mathrm{Centr}(G) = e\).

  2. (ii)

    For every reductive group \(G\), the quotient group \(G/\mathrm{Centr}(G)\) is an adjoint reductive group.
Indeed, one may assume \(G\) split; (i) is trivial (since \(\mathrm{Centr}(G) = D_S(M/\Gamma_0(R))\)), and (ii) follows from 4.3.1.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 4.3.6

Let \(G\) be a reductive \(S\)-group. The adjoint group of \(G\), denoted \(\mathrm{ad}(G)\), is by definition the group \(G/\mathrm{Centr}(G)\). The radical of \(G\), denoted \(\mathrm{rad}(G)\), is by definition the maximal torus (unique, Exp. XII 1.12) of \(\mathrm{Centr}(G)\). The semi-simple group associated with \(G\) is by definition the quotient \(G/\mathrm{rad}(G)\).
The preceding definitions are compatible with base change. If \(s \in S\), then \(\mathrm{rad}(G)_s\) is indeed the radical of \(G_s\) in the usual sense (Exp. XIX 1.6).

If \((G, T, M, R)\) is a split group, then \(\mathrm{rad}(G) = D_S(M/N)\), where \(N = M \cap V(R)\), so that the semi-simple group associated with \(G\) (as indeed the adjoint group of \(G\)) is endowed with a canonical splitting (4.3.1), and one has a diagram of split groups \[ G \longrightarrow \mathrm{ss}(G) \longrightarrow \mathrm{ad}(G) \] corresponding to the canonical diagram of root data (Exp. XXI 6.5.5) \[ \mathrm{ad}(\mathscr{R}(G)) \longrightarrow \mathrm{ss}(\mathscr{R}(G)) \longrightarrow \mathscr{R}(G). \]

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 4.3.8

Let \((G, T, M, R)\) be an adjoint (resp. simply connected) split \(S\)-group, \(R_0\) a system of simple roots of \(R\). Then the family \(\{\alpha\}_{\alpha \in R_0}\), resp. \(\{\alpha^*\}_{\alpha \in R_0}\), induces an isomorphism \[ T \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} (\mathbf{G}_{m,S})^{R_0}, \qquad \text{resp.}\; (\mathbf{G}_{m,S})^{R_0} \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} T. \]

Indeed, \(M = \Gamma_0(R)\) (resp. \(\ldots\)) and \(R_0\) is a basis of the free group \(\Gamma_0(R)\) (Exp. XXI 3.1.8).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 4.3.9

The radical of a reductive group is a characteristic subgroup (i.e. stable under \(\underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G)\)), in view of its definition.
5. Subgroups of type (R)
We are especially interested in reductive groups, but some of the results we are going to establish are valid more generally for a wider class of groups: the groups of type (RR).
5.1. Groups of type (RR)

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 5.1.1

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) an \(S\)-group prescheme. We say that \(G\) is of type (RR) if it satisfies the following conditions:

  1. (i)

    \(G\) is smooth and of finite presentation over \(S\), with connected fibres.

  2. (ii)

    \(G\) possesses maximal tori locally for the (fpqc) topology.

  3. (iii)

    For every \(s \in S\), every maximal torus \(T\) of \(G_s\) and every root of \(G_s\) with respect to \(T_s\) (Exp. XIX 1.10), \(\mathrm{Lie}(G_s)^\alpha\) is of rank \(1\) (as a vector space over \(k(s)\)).

  4. (iv)

    For every \(s \in S\) and every maximal torus \(T\) of \(G_s\), let us denote by \(R\) the set of roots of \(G_s\) with respect to \(T\) and by \(\Gamma_0(R)\) the subgroup of \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{s\text{-gr.}}(T, \mathbf{G}_{m,s})\) generated by \(R\); then the content of every root \(\alpha \in R\) in the free abelian group \(\Gamma_0(R)\) (which is therefore an integer \(> 0\)) is invertible on \(S\).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 5.1.2

a) By virtue of Exp. XII 7.1 (where the hypothesis that \(G\) be separated is superfluous, being automatically satisfied, Exp. VI), (i) and (ii) imply that \(G\) possesses maximal tori (resp. Cartan groups) locally for the étale topology, conjugate locally for the étale topology.

b) The Cartan groups of \(G\) have connected fibres (Exp. XII 6.6).

c) If \(G\) is affine over \(S\), (i) and (ii) are respectively equivalent to

(i') \(G\) is smooth over \(S\) and has connected fibres.

(ii') The reductive rank of the fibres of \(G\) is locally constant (Exp. XII 1.7).

d) By Exp. XII 8.8 (c), \(G\) possesses a reductive centre \(Z\); under the conditions of (iv), one has \(Z_s = \bigcap_{\alpha \in R} \mathrm{Ker}(\alpha)\) (loc. cit. (d)), hence \[ \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{s\text{-gr.}}((T/Z)_s, \mathbf{G}_{m,s}) \simeq \Gamma_0(R). \]

e) Condition (iv) is satisfied in particular in the following two cases: 1°) \(S\) is of characteristic \(0\); 2°) every root is an indivisible element of the group generated by the roots.

f) The property of being of type (RR) is stable under base change and local for (fpqc).
From remarks (c) and (e) there follows at once the following:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.1.3

A reductive group is of type (RR).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.1.4

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) an \(S\)-group of type (RR), \(Q\) a central subgroup of \(G\) of finite presentation over \(S\) such that the quotient \(G/Q\) is representable (for example \(G\) affine over \(S\) and \(Q\) of multiplicative type, or else \(S\) artinian); then \(G/Q\) is an \(S\)-group of type (RR).

Indeed (i) is clear (\(G/Q\) is smooth over \(S\) (Exp. VIB), of finite presentation over \(S\) (Exp. V 9.1), with connected fibres); (ii) follows from Exp. XII 7.6; it remains to verify (iii) and (iv). Let us first prove:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 5.1.5

Under the conditions of 5.1.4, let \(T = D_S(M)\) be a trivial maximal torus of \(G\), and assume that the decomposition of \(\mathfrak{g}\) under \(\mathrm{Ad}(T)\) is of the form \[ \mathfrak{g} = \mathfrak{g}^0 \oplus \bigoplus_{\alpha \in R} \mathfrak{g}^\alpha, \quad R \subset M - \{0\}, \] where for every \(s \in S\) one has \(\mathfrak{g}^\alpha(s) \ne 0\) for \(\alpha \in R\) (so that \(\mathfrak{g}^\alpha\) is an invertible \(\mathscr{O}_S\)-Module for every \(\alpha \in R\), and \(R\) is the set of roots of \(G_s\) with respect to \(T_s\) for every \(s \in S\)). Let us write \(G' = G/Q\), let \(u : G \to G'\) be the canonical morphism and \(T' = u(T)\) the maximal torus of \(G'\) image of \(T\) (Exp. XII 7.1 e)); for each \(\alpha \in R\), let us likewise denote by \(\alpha\) the character of \(T'\) defined by \(\alpha\) (indeed \(Q \cap T \subset Z = \bigcap_{\alpha \in R} \mathrm{Ker}\, \alpha\)). Then the Lie Algebra \(\mathfrak{g}'\) of \(G'\) decomposes under \(\mathrm{Ad}(T')\) in the following way: \[ \mathfrak{g}' = \mathfrak{g}'^0 \oplus \bigoplus_{\alpha \in R} \mathfrak{g}'^{\alpha} \] and \(\mathrm{Lie}(u)\) induces an isomorphism of \(\mathfrak{g}^\alpha\) onto \(\mathfrak{g}'^{\alpha}\).

Indeed, let \(p = \mathrm{Lie}(u) : \mathfrak{g} \to \mathfrak{g}'\). One has at once \(p(\mathfrak{g}^\alpha) \subset \mathfrak{g}'^{\alpha}\) for every \(\alpha \in R\), and \(p(\mathfrak{g}^0) \subset \mathfrak{g}'^0\). Since \[ \mathrm{Ker}(p) = \mathrm{Lie}(Q) \subset \mathrm{Lie}(\mathrm{Centr}_G(T)) = \mathfrak{g}^0, \] \(p\) induces a monomorphism of \(\mathfrak{g}^\alpha\) into \(\mathfrak{g}'^{\alpha}\), for every \(\alpha \in R\).

To prove the lemma, it suffices to do so when \(S\) is the spectrum of an algebraically closed field, and by virtue of the preceding remarks it then suffices to prove that \(\mathrm{rg}(\mathfrak{g}') = \mathrm{rg}(\mathfrak{g}'^0) + \mathrm{Card}(R)\). Now let us put \(C = \mathrm{Centr}_G(T)\), \(C' = \mathrm{Centr}_{G'}(T')\); by Exp. XII 7.1 (e), \(u\) induces a faithfully flat morphism \(C \to C'\) with kernel \(Q\). One has therefore \[ \dim C' + \dim Q = \dim C. \] But \(G\), \(G'\), \(C\) and \(C'\) are smooth, whence \[ \dim G = \mathrm{rg}(\mathfrak{g}) = \mathrm{rg}(\mathfrak{g}^0) + \mathrm{Card}(R) = \dim C + \mathrm{Card}(R) \] \[ = \dim Q + \dim C' + \mathrm{Card}(R) = \dim Q + \mathrm{rg}(\mathfrak{g}'^0) + \mathrm{Card}(R) \] \[ \mathrm{rg}(\mathfrak{g}') = \dim G' = \dim G - \dim Q \] which yields \[ \mathrm{rg}(\mathfrak{g}') = \mathrm{rg}(\mathfrak{g}'^0) + \mathrm{Card}(R), \] that is to say the desired relation.

Let us return to the proof of 5.1.4; one may assume that \(S\) is the spectrum of an algebraically closed field. Let \(T\) be a maximal torus of \(G\); applying 5.1.5, one obtains at once (iii) and (iv) for \(G/Q\).
In order to make use of the preceding proposition, let us introduce a definition:

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 5.1.6

We say that the \(S\)-group prescheme \(G\) is of type (RA) if it is of type (RR) and if it satisfies moreover the condition (iv') (stronger than (iv)):

(iv') For every \(s \in S\) and every maximal torus \(T\) of \(G_s\), every root of \(G_s\) with respect to \(T\) has a content in \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{s\text{-gr.}}(T, \mathbf{G}_{m,s})\) which is invertible on \(S\).

blocks.title: Remarks
blocks.html:
Remarks 5.1.7

a) An adjoint reductive \(S\)-group is of type (RA).

b) If \(S\) is of characteristic \(0\), every group of type (RR) is of type (RA).

c) The property of being of type (RA) is stable under base change and local for (fpqc).
The preceding remark (a) is generalized by:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.1.8

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) an \(S\)-group of type (RR), \(Z\) its reductive centre; assume the quotient \(G/Z\) representable (for example \(G\) affine over \(S\), or \(S\) artinian); then \(G/Z\) is of type (RA).
Indeed, this follows at once from 5.1.4, 5.1.5 and 5.1.2 (d).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 5.1.9

If \(G\) is of type (RR) and if \(T\) is a maximal torus of \(G\), one may apply Exp. XIX 6.3. In particular \(W_G(T)\) is étale, quasi-finite and separated over \(S\).
5.2. Subgroups of type (R)

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 5.2.1

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) an \(S\)-group prescheme which is smooth, of finite presentation and with connected fibres, \(H\) a group subprescheme of \(G\). We say that \(H\) is of type (R) if:

  1. (i)

    \(H\) is smooth, of finite presentation over \(S\) (= retrocompact in \(G\)) and with connected fibres.

  2. (ii)

    For every \(s \in S\), \(H_s\) contains a Cartan subgroup of \(G_s\).

This notion is stable under base change and local for (fpqc).
Reminder 5.2.2.
(cf. Exp. XII 7.9) Under the preceding conditions:
a) \(H = \mathrm{Norm}_G(H)^0\).

b) If \(G\) contains Cartan subgroups (resp. maximal tori) locally for the étale topology, the same holds for \(H\), and the Cartan subgroups (resp. the maximal tori) of \(H\) are Cartan subgroups (resp. maximal tori) of \(G\).

blocks.title: Examples
blocks.html:
Examples 5.2.3

a) Borel groups: a Borel group of \(G\) is a subgroup of type (R) whose fibres are Borel groups of the fibres of \(G\).

b) Parabolic groups: a parabolic subgroup of \(G\) is a subgroup of type (R) whose geometric fibres contain Borel groups.

Further examples are given by the following propositions.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.2.4

Let \(G\) be as in 5.2.1, \(K \subset H\) two group subpreschemes of \(G\), \(H\) being assumed of type (R). Then \(K\) is a subgroup of type (R) of \(H\) if and only if it is a subgroup of type (R) of \(G\).
Trivial.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.2.5

Let \(G\) be as in 5.2.1, \(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\), \(Q\) a subtorus of \(T\), \(Z = \mathrm{Centr}_G(Q)\). If \(H\) is a subgroup of type (R) of \(G\) containing \(T\), then \(H \cap Z\) is a subgroup of type (R) of \(Z\).

Let us first recall that \(Z\) is a closed group subprescheme of \(G\), of finite presentation (Exp. XI 6.11), with connected fibres (Exp. XII 6.6), smooth over \(S\) (Exp. IX 3.3), so that it satisfies the conditions imposed in definition 5.2.1. Likewise, \(H \cap Z\) is of finite presentation, smooth and with connected fibres (since \(H \cap Z = \mathrm{Centr}_H(Q)\)); moreover \(H \cap Z \supset \mathrm{Centr}_G(T)\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.2.6

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) an \(S\)-group of type (RR) (resp. (RA)), \(H\) a subgroup of type (R) of \(G\). Then \(H\) is an \(S\)-group of type (RR) (resp. (RA)).

Indeed (i) is clear, (ii) follows from 5.2.2 (b), and (iii) and (iv) (resp. (iv')) are to be verified when \(S\) is the spectrum of an algebraically closed field. Then \(H\) contains a maximal torus \(T\) of \(G\) (and hence also \(C = \mathrm{Centr}_G(T)\)) and the assertions to be proved follow at once from:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 5.2.7

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) an \(S\)-group of type (RR), \(T = D_S(M)\) a trivial maximal torus of \(G\); assume that \[ \mathfrak{g} = \mathfrak{g}^0 \oplus \bigoplus_{\alpha \in R} \mathfrak{g}^\alpha, \] the \(\mathfrak{g}^\alpha\) being invertible. Let \(H\) be a subgroup of type (R) containing \(C = \mathrm{Centr}_G(T)\) (i.e. containing \(T\)). Then \(\mathfrak{h} = \mathrm{Lie}(H/S)\) is locally on \(S\) of the form \[ \mathfrak{g}_{R'} = \mathfrak{g}^0 + \bigoplus_{\alpha \in R'} \mathfrak{g}^\alpha\;; \] more precisely, for each \(s \in S\) let \(R'(s) = \{\alpha \in R \mid \mathfrak{g}^\alpha(s) \subset \mathfrak{h}(s)\}\). Then \(R'(s)\) is a locally constant function of \(s\); if \(U\) is an open subset of \(S\) on which \(R'(s) = R'\), one has \[ \mathfrak{h}_U = \mathfrak{g}^0_U \oplus \bigoplus_{\alpha \in R'} \mathfrak{g}^\alpha_U. \]
Indeed, \(\mathfrak{h}\) is a sub-Module of \(\mathfrak{g}\), locally a direct summand, containing \(\mathfrak{g}^0\) and stable under \(T\).
5.3. Strict transporter of two subgroups of type (R). Applications

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.3.1

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) an \(S\)-group of type (RA) (5.1.6), \(H\) a subgroup of type (R) of \(G\), \(\mathfrak{g} \supset \mathfrak{h}\) their Lie Algebras.

Then \(\mathrm{Norm}_G(\mathfrak{h})\) (which is in any case representable by a closed subprescheme of \(G\) of finite presentation over \(S\)) is smooth over \(S\) along the unit section, and one has \[ H = \mathrm{Norm}_G(\mathfrak{h})^0. \]

Since \(H\) is smooth and of finite presentation over \(S\), the proposition is equivalent (Exp. VI) to the following fact: for every \(s \in S\) \[ \mathrm{Norm}_{\mathfrak{g}(s)}(\mathfrak{h}(s)) = \mathfrak{h}(s). \] One is thus reduced by 5.2.7 to proving:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 5.3.2

Under the conditions of 5.2.7, if \(G\) is of type (RA), one has, for every \(s \in S\), \[ \mathrm{Norm}_{\mathfrak{g}(s)}(\mathfrak{h}(s)) = \mathfrak{h}(s). \]

Indeed, one is reduced to the case where \(S\) is the spectrum of a field, hence where \(\mathfrak{h} = \mathfrak{g}_{R'}\) for a certain \(R' \subset R\). But one already has \[ \mathrm{Transp}_\mathfrak{g}(\mathfrak{t}, \mathfrak{h}) = \mathfrak{h}. \] Indeed, if \(H \in \mathfrak{t}\) and \(X \in \mathfrak{g}^\alpha\), one has \([H, X] = \alpha(H)\, X\), where \(\alpha : \mathfrak{t} \to \mathscr{O}_S\) is the morphism derived from \(\alpha\). Now condition (iv') says precisely that \(\alpha \ne 0\) for every \(\alpha \in R\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.3.3

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) an \(S\)-group of type (RA), \(H\) and \(H'\) two subgroups of type (R) of \(G\), \(\mathfrak{h}\) and \(\mathfrak{h}'\) their Lie Algebras. Then \[ H = H' \iff \mathfrak{h} = \mathfrak{h}'. \]

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.3.4

Under the conditions of 5.2.7, \(G\) being of type (RA), the maps \[ H \mapsto \mathrm{Lie}(H/S), \qquad \mathfrak{h} \mapsto \mathrm{Norm}_G(\mathfrak{h})^0 \] set up a bijective correspondence between the set of subgroups of type (R) of \(G\) containing \(T\), and the set of Lie sub-Algebras of \(\mathfrak{g}\) containing \(\mathfrak{g}^0\), stable under \(T\), and whose normalizer in \(G\) is smooth along the unit section.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.3.5

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) an \(S\)-group of type (RR) (5.1.1), \(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\), \(H\) and \(H'\) two subgroups of type (R) of \(G\) containing \(T\). Then \[ H = H' \iff \mathfrak{h} = \mathfrak{h}'. \]

By virtue of the finite presentation hypotheses, one reduces as usual (cf. EGA IV3, § 8 and Exp. VIB § 10) to the case where \(S\) is noetherian; it then suffices to verify that \((\mathfrak{h} = \mathfrak{h}') \Rightarrow H_{S'} = H'_{S'}\) for every \(S'\) the spectrum of an artinian quotient of a local ring of \(S\); one is thus reduced to the case where \(S\) is artinian and where one may apply 5.1.8. Let us put \(G' = G/Z\) and let \(T' = T/Z\) be the maximal torus of \(G'\) corresponding to \(T\). By virtue of Exp. XII 7.12, there exist subgroups of type (R) \(H_1\) and \(H'_1\) of \(G'\), containing \(T'\), such that \(H = u^{-1}(H_1)\) and \(H' = u^{-1}(H'_1)\), where \(u : G \to G'\) is the canonical morphism. It suffices to prove that \(H_1 = H'_1\). But by 5.2.7 and 5.1.5, one has \[ \mathrm{Lie}(H_1) = \mathrm{Lie}(H'_1), \] and one is reduced to 5.3.3.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 5.3.6

The fact that \(H\) and \(H'\) contain the same maximal torus is essential for the validity of 5.3.5 when \(G\) is not of type (RA). Example: maximal tori of \(\mathrm{SL}_{2,k}\), for \(k\) of characteristic \(2\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.3.7

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) an \(S\)-group of type (RR), \(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\), \(H\) and \(H'\) two subgroups of type (R) of \(G\) containing \(T\). The set \(U\) of \(s \in S\) such that \(H_s = H'_s\) is open and closed in \(S\), and \(H_U = H'_U\).
Indeed, this follows at once from 5.3.5 and 5.2.7.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.3.8

The "functor of subgroups of type (R) containing \(T\)", where \(T\) is a given maximal torus in a group \(G\) of type (RR), is formally unramified (Exp. XI 1.1).

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 5.3.9

Let \(G\) be an \(S\)-group of type (RR) (5.1.1), \(H\) and \(H'\) two subgroups of type (R) (5.2.1). Let \(\mathrm{Transt}_G(H, H')\) be the strict transporter of \(H\) into \(H'\), defined by \[ \mathrm{Transt}_G(H, H')(S') = \{g \in G(S') \mid \mathrm{int}(g) H_{S'} = H'_{S'}\}. \] Then \(\mathrm{Transt}_G(H, H')\) is representable by a closed subprescheme of \(G\), which is smooth and of finite presentation over \(S\).

The fact that \(\mathrm{Transt}_G(H, H')\) is representable by a closed subprescheme of \(G\), of finite presentation over \(S\), follows from Exp. XI 6.11 (a). To prove that it is smooth over \(S\), one must show that if \(S\) is affine and if \(S_0\) is the closed subprescheme defined by a nilpotent ideal \(J\), and if \(g_0 \in G(S_0)\) and \(\mathrm{int}(g_0) H_0 = H'_0\), then there exists a \(g \in G(S)\) projecting onto \(g_0\) and such that \(\mathrm{int}(g) H = H'\). Since the question of smoothness is local for (ét), one may assume that \(H\) contains a maximal torus \(T\) of \(G\).

Then \(T_0\) is a maximal torus of \(H_0\), so that \(\mathrm{int}(g_0) T_0\) is a maximal torus of \(H'_0\). By Exp. IX 3.6 bis, there exists a torus \(T'\) of \(H'\) such that \(T'_0 = \mathrm{int}(g_0) T_0\); by Exp. IX 3.3 bis, there exists therefore a \(g \in G(S)\), projecting onto \(g_0\) and such that \(\mathrm{int}(g) T = T'\). After possibly replacing \(H\) by \(\mathrm{int}(g) H\), one may therefore assume that \(H\) and \(H'\) contain the same maximal torus \(T\) and that \(H_0 = H'_0\). But then \(H = H'\) by 5.3.7. Q.E.D.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.3.10

Let \(G\) be an \(S\)-group of type (RR), \(H\) a subgroup of type (R) of \(G\). Then \(\mathrm{Norm}_G(H)\) is representable by a closed group subprescheme of \(G\), of finite presentation and smooth over \(S\).
Reasoning now as in Exp. XI 5.2 bis \(\Rightarrow\) 5.4 bis, one obtains:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.3.11

Under the hypotheses of 5.3.9, the following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    \(H\) and \(H'\) are conjugate locally in \(G\) for the étale topology.

  2. (i bis)

    likewise for the (fpqc) topology.

  3. (ii)

    For every \(s \in S\), \(H_s\) and \(H'_s\) are conjugate by an element of \(G(s)\).

  4. (ii bis)

    The structural morphism \(\mathrm{Transt}_G(H, H') \to S\) is surjective.

  5. (iii)

    \(\mathrm{Transt}_G(H, H')\) is a principal homogeneous bundle under the action of the smooth \(S\)-group prescheme of finite presentation \(\mathrm{Norm}_G(H)\).
Let us merely remark that the non-trivial assertion (iii) \(\Rightarrow\) (i) is Hensel's lemma.
Using now BIBLE, 6-09, th. 4 and 9-03, th. 1, one obtains by 5.3.10 and 5.3.11:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.3.12

Let \(G\) be an \(S\)-group of type (RR). The Borel subgroups of \(G\) are closed in \(G\), are their own normalizer, and are conjugate locally for the étale topology.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 5.3.13

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) an \(S\)-group prescheme which is smooth, of finite presentation and with connected fibres. By a Killing couple of \(G\) we mean a couple \(T \subset B\), where \(T\) is a maximal torus of \(G\) and \(B\) a Borel group of \(G\) containing \(T\).
Using now the conjugacy of maximal tori in \(B\) (cf. 5.1.2 (a) and 5.2.6, for example), one has:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.3.14

Let \(G\) be an \(S\)-group of type (RR). The Killing couples of \(G\) are conjugate locally for the étale topology.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.3.15

Let \(G\) be an \(S\)-group of type (RR). Let \(T\) be a maximal torus of \(G\), \(W_G(T) = \mathrm{Norm}_G(T)/\mathrm{Centr}_G(T)\) the corresponding Weyl group (Exp. XIX 6.3). The "functor of Borel groups of \(G\) containing \(T\)" is formally principal homogeneous under \(W_G(T)\).
This follows at once from 5.3.14 and from the fact that if \(B\) is a Borel group of \(G\) containing \(T\), one has \[ \mathrm{Norm}_G(T) \cap B = \mathrm{Centr}_G(T), \] cf. Exp. XIV 4.4.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.3.16

Let \(G\) be an \(S\)-group of type (RR), \(H\) an \(S\)-group of type (R), \(N = \mathrm{Norm}_G(H)\) its normalizer (5.3.10). Let \(T\) be a maximal torus of \(H\), and \(W_H(T)\) and \(W_N(T)\) the corresponding Weyl groups (étale, quasi-finite and separated by Exp. XIX 6.3). One has the following exact sequence of (ét) sheaves (the morphisms are induced by the obvious morphisms): \[ 1 \longrightarrow W_H(T) \longrightarrow W_N(T) \longrightarrow N/H \longrightarrow 1. \]

The only non-trivial point is the fact that the last arrow is an epimorphism. So let \(n \in N(S')\), \(S' \to S\). The two maximal tori \(T\) and \(\mathrm{int}(n) T\) of \(H\) are conjugate in \(H\) locally for the étale topology. There exists therefore a covering family \(\{S'_i \to S'\}\) and for each \(i\) an \(h_i \in H(S'_i)\) with \(\mathrm{int}(h_i) T = \mathrm{int}(n) T\). One has therefore \(n h_i^{-1} \in \mathrm{Norm}_N(T)\), which yields the desired result.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 5.3.17

One may describe \(W_N(T)\) in the following way: suppose we are reduced to the situation of 5.2.7, with \(\mathfrak{h} = \mathfrak{g}_{R'}\). Then \(W_N(T) = \mathrm{Norm}_W(R')\), the sheaf of sections of \(W = W_G(T)\) which, operating on \(R\), normalize \(R'\). Indeed, by 5.3.5, one has \[ \mathrm{Norm}_N(T) = \mathrm{Norm}_G(H) \cap \mathrm{Norm}_G(T) = \mathrm{Norm}_G(\mathfrak{h}) \cap \mathrm{Norm}_G(T). \]

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.3.18

Let \(G\) be an \(S\)-group of type (RR), and \(H\) a subgroup of type (R). Suppose that "the Weyl groups of \(G\) are finite", i.e. that for every \(S' \to S\) and every maximal torus \(T\) of \(G_{S'}\), the étale \(S'\)-prescheme \(\mathrm{Norm}_{G_{S'}}(T)/\mathrm{Centr}_{G_{S'}}(T)\) is finite (cf. Exp. XIX 6.3 (iii)). The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    \(H\) is closed in \(G\).

  2. (ii)

    \(\mathrm{Norm}_G(H)/H\) is representable by a finite étale \(S\)-prescheme.

  3. (iii)

    "the Weyl groups of \(H\) are finite".

Indeed, we may suppose that \(H\) possesses a maximal torus \(T\). Since \(W_N(T)\) is closed in \(W_G(T)\), \(W_N(T)\) is finite over \(S\). One evidently has (i) \(\Rightarrow\) (iii), (iii) \(\Rightarrow\) (ii) by the exact sequence of 5.3.16, and (ii) \(\Rightarrow\) (i), for if \(N/H\) is finite it is separated, hence \(H\) is closed in \(N\).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 5.3.19

When \(G\) is reductive, the preceding conditions on \(H\) seem always to be satisfied. We prove them below in most cases.
5.4. Subgroups of type (R) of a split reductive group (generalities)

If \(H\) is a subgroup of type (R) of the reductive group \(G\), then \(H\) contains, locally for the étale topology, a maximal torus of \(G\) (5.2.2). By 2.3, we may, locally for the étale topology, suppose \(G\) split with respect to that torus. Let then \((G, T, M, R)\) be a split \(S\)-group, and \(H\) a subgroup of type (R) of \(G\) containing \(T\). By 5.3.5 such a subgroup is characterised by its Lie Algebra, which (5.2.7) is locally on \(S\) of the form \(\mathfrak{g}_{R'}\): \[ \mathfrak{g}_{R'} = \mathfrak{t} \oplus \bigoplus_{\alpha \in R'} \mathfrak{g}^\alpha. \]

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 5.4.2

Let \((G, T, M, R)\) be a split \(S\)-group. We shall say that the subset \(R'\) of \(R\) is of type (R) if \(\mathfrak{g}_{R'}\) is the Lie algebra of a subgroup of type (R) of \(G\) containing \(T\). This subgroup, uniquely determined by \(R'\), is denoted \(H_{R'}\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 5.4.3

Under the preceding conditions, one has the following equivalences: \[ H \cap Z_\alpha = T \iff \alpha \notin R',\; -\alpha \notin R', \] \[ H \supset U_\alpha \iff \alpha \in R', \] \[ H \cap U_\alpha = e \iff \alpha \notin R', \] \[ H \supset Z_\alpha \iff \alpha \in R',\; -\alpha \in R'. \]

Indeed, \(H \cap Z_\alpha\) is a subgroup of type (R) of \(Z_\alpha\), by 5.2.5; but a subgroup of type (R) of \(Z_\alpha\) containing \(T\) is locally equal to one of the following subgroups: \(T\), \(T \cdot U_\alpha\), \(T \cdot U_{-\alpha}\), \(Z_\alpha\), by 5.3.5.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 5.4.4

Under the conditions of 5.4.2, let \(R^+\) be a system of positive roots; let us choose orderings on \(R' \cap R^+\) and \(R' \cap -R^+\). The morphism \[ \Omega_{R^+, R'} = \prod_{\alpha \in R' \cap -R^+} U_\alpha \times_S T \times_S \prod_{\alpha \in R' \cap R^+} U_\alpha \longrightarrow G \] induced by the product in \(G\) induces an open immersion \[ \Omega_{R^+, R'} \longrightarrow H_{R'}. \]
By 5.4.3, this morphism factors through \(H_{R'}\) and hence induces an immersion \(\Omega_{R^+, R'} \to H_{R'}\). One then argues as in 4.1.1.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.4.5

Let \((G, T, M, R)\) be a split \(S\)-group. Let \(R'\) and \(R''\) be two subsets of \(R\), of type (R).

  1. (i)

    \(H_{R'} \cap H_{R''}\) is smooth along the unit section, \(R' \cap R''\) is of type (R), and one has \[ (H_{R'} \cap H_{R''})^0 = H_{R' \cap R''}. \]

  2. (ii)

    One has the equivalence \[ H_{R'} \subset H_{R''} \iff R' \subset R''. \]

Indeed, (ii) follows immediately from (i). To prove (i), it suffices to prove that \(H_{R'} \cap H_{R''}\) is smooth along the unit section: its identity component will then be a subgroup of type (R) containing \(T\), hence equal to \(H_{R' \cap R''}\); but \(\Omega_{R^+, R'} \cap \Omega_{R^+, R''} = \Omega_{R^+, R' \cap R''}\) is an open subset of \(H_{R'} \cap H_{R''}\) containing the unit section and smooth over \(S\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.4.6

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\), and \(s\) a point of \(S\). If \(H\) and \(H'\) are two subgroups of type (R) of \(G\) containing \(T\) such that \(H_s \subset H'_s\), there exists an open subset \(U\) of \(S\) containing \(s\) such that \(H_U \subset H'_U\).
We may indeed suppose \(G\) split with respect to \(T\). The assertion then follows immediately from 5.4.5 (ii).

One is led to ask which subsets \(R'\) of \(R\) are of type (R). We may suppose the group adjoint; it must then be checked that \(\mathfrak{g}_{R'}\) is a Lie Algebra and that its normalizer is smooth along the unit section. The most important case is given by the

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 5.4.7

Every closed subset \(R'\) of \(R\) is of type (R). (We recall, cf. Exp. XXI 3.1.4, that \(R' \subset R\) is said to be closed if \(\alpha, \beta \in R'\), \(\alpha + \beta \in R\) implies \(\alpha + \beta \in R'\)).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 5.4.8

We shall see later (Exp. XXIII 6.6) that if \(S\) has residue characteristics distinct from \(2\) and \(3\) (i.e. if \(6\) is not zero on \(S\)), the fact that \(\mathfrak{g}_{R'}\) is a Lie Algebra already implies that \(R'\) is closed, so that \(R'\) is of type (R) if and only if it is closed. The theorem 5.4.7 thus gives all the subsets of type (R) that are "independent of the characteristic".
Let us first prove:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 5.4.9

Let us choose, for each \(\alpha \in R\), an \(X_\alpha \in \Gamma(S, \mathfrak{g}^\alpha)^*\). Let \(\alpha, \beta \in R\), with \(\alpha + \beta \ne 0\), and let \(q\) be the largest integer \(i\) such that \(\alpha + i\beta \in R\). There exist sections \(M_{\alpha,\beta,i} \in \Gamma(S, \mathscr{O}_S)\), uniquely determined, such that \[ \mathrm{Ad}(\exp_\alpha(x X_\alpha))(X_\beta) = X_\beta + \sum_{i=1}^{q} M_{\alpha,\beta,i}\, x^i\, X_{\beta + i\alpha}, \] for every \(x \in \mathbf{G}_a(S')\), \(S' \to S\).

Indeed, \(x \mapsto \mathrm{Ad}(\exp_\alpha(x X_\alpha))(X_\beta)\) defines a morphism \(\mathbf{G}_{a,S} \to \mathbf{W}(\mathfrak{g}) \simeq \mathbf{G}_{a,S}^m\). There exist therefore sections \(Y_n \in \Gamma(S, \mathfrak{g})\), uniquely determined, such that \[ \mathrm{Ad}(\exp_\alpha(x X_\alpha))(X_\beta) = \sum_{n \geqslant 0} x^n\, Y_n. \] Letting the inner automorphism defined by a section \(t\) of \(T\) act, one finds at once \[ \mathrm{Ad}(t)(Y_n) = \beta(t)\, \alpha(t)^n\, Y_n, \] which implies \(Y_n \in \Gamma(S, \mathfrak{g}^{\beta + n\alpha})\). Since \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are not proportional, none of the \(\beta + n\alpha\) is zero; one therefore has \(Y_n = 0\) for \(n > q\), \(Y_n = M_{\alpha,\beta,n}\, X_{\beta + n\alpha}\) for \(0 \leqslant n \leqslant q\), where \(M_{\alpha,\beta,n} \in \mathbf{G}_a(S)\) is uniquely determined. Setting \(x = 0\) in the formula obtained, one finds \(Y_0 = X_\beta\), which completes the proof.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 5.4.10

Differentiating the preceding formula at \(x = 0\), one finds \[ [X_\alpha, X_\beta] = N_{\alpha,\beta}\, X_{\alpha + \beta}, \quad \text{where}\; N_{\alpha,\beta} = M_{\alpha,\beta,1}, \quad \text{if}\; \alpha + \beta \in R, \] \[ [X_\alpha, X_\beta] = 0 \quad \text{if}\; \alpha + \beta \notin R,\; \alpha + \beta \ne 0. \]
