Let us now prove 5.4.7; if \(R'\) is a closed subset of \(R\), then \(\mathfrak{g}_{R'}\) is a Lie subalgebra of \(\mathfrak{g}\), by 5.4.10 and Exp. XX 2.10, formula (3). By 5.4.9 and Exp. XX 2.10, formula (2), \(U_\alpha\) normalizes \(\mathfrak{g}_{R'}\) for each \(\alpha \in R'\). Let us choose a system of positive roots \(R^+\) and consider the open subset \(\Omega_{R^+}\) of 4.1.2; let \(\Omega_{R^+, R'}\) be the closed subprescheme of \(\Omega_{R^+}\) defined as follows: \[ \Omega_{R^+, R'} = \left(\prod_{\alpha \in R' \cap -R^+} U_\alpha\right) \cdot T \cdot \left(\prod_{\alpha \in R' \cap R^+} U_\alpha\right). \] The canonical immersion \(\Omega_{R^+, R'} \to G\) factors through \(i : \Omega_{R^+, R'} \to \mathrm{Norm}_G(\mathfrak{g}_{R'})\). Suppose \(G\) adjoint; the tangent map to \(i\) at the points of the unit section is bijective by 5.3.2; in particular, the morphism \(i\) is smooth along the unit section (Exp. VI), hence is a local immersion along the unit section, and therefore \(\mathrm{Norm}_G(\mathfrak{g}_{R'})\) is smooth along the unit section, which is what we had to prove.
5.5. Borel subgroups of a split reductive group

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.5.1

Let \((G, T, M, R)\) be a split \(S\)-group. For every system of positive roots \(R^+\) of \(R\), \(H_{R^+}\) (which exists by 5.4.7) is a Borel subgroup of \(G\) and, for every ordering on \(R^+\), the morphism induced by the product in \(G\) \[ T \times_S \prod_{\alpha \in R^+} U_\alpha \longrightarrow G \] is a closed immersion with image \(H_{R^+}\). One writes \(B_{R^+} = H_{R^+}\).

By the definition of Borel groups, the first assertion may be checked after replacing \(S\) by the spectrum of an algebraically closed field. Let then \(B\) be the Borel subgroup of \(G\) containing \(T\) and corresponding to the system of positive roots \(R^+\) (BIBLE, 10-11, prop. 9); the Lie algebra of \(B\) is \(\mathfrak{g}_{R^+}\); one therefore has \(B = H_{R^+}\) by 5.3.5.

Let us prove the second assertion: the morphism of the statement induces an open immersion \(i : T \times_S \prod_{\alpha \in R^+} U_\alpha \to H_{R^+}\) (5.4.4). Now \(i\) is surjective (BIBLE, 15-03, cor. 1 to prop. 1).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.5.2

Let us choose an arbitrary ordering on \(R^+\) and, for each \(\alpha \in R^+\), an \(X_\alpha \in \Gamma(S, \mathfrak{g}^\alpha)^*\). Let \(\alpha, \beta \in R^+\). For each pair \((i, j) \in \mathbf{N} \times \mathbf{N}\), \(i \ne 0\), \(j \ne 0\), such that \(i\alpha + j\beta \in R\), there exists a unique section \[ C_{i,j,\alpha,\beta} \in \Gamma(S, \mathscr{O}_S) \] such that, for all \(x, y \in \mathbf{G}_a(S')\), \(S' \to S\), one has \[ \exp_\alpha(x X_\alpha) \exp_\beta(y X_\beta) \exp_\alpha(x X_\alpha)^{-1} = \exp_\beta(y X_\beta) \prod_{\substack{i,j \in \mathbf{N}^* \\ i\alpha + j\beta \in R}} \exp_{i\alpha + j\beta}(C_{i,j,\alpha,\beta}\, x^i y^j\, X_{i\alpha + j\beta}). \]

If \(\alpha = \beta\), the assertion is trivial. Suppose therefore \(\alpha \ne \beta\); then, by virtue of the proposition, there exist unique morphisms \[ F_0 : \mathbf{G}_{a,S}^2 \longrightarrow T, \qquad F_\gamma : \mathbf{G}_{a,S}^2 \longrightarrow \mathbf{G}_{a,S} \quad (\gamma \in R^+) \] such that one has \[ \exp(x X_\alpha) \exp(y X_\beta) \exp(x X_\alpha) = F_0(x, y) \prod_{\gamma \in R^+} \exp(F_\gamma(x, y) X_\gamma). \] Let \(t \in T(S')\), \(S' \to S\). Letting \(\mathrm{int}(t)\) act on this formula, one obtains at once the relations \[ F_0(\alpha(t)\, x, \beta(t)\, y) = F_0(x, y), \tag{1} \] \[ F_\gamma(\alpha(t)\, x, \beta(t)\, y) = \gamma(t)\, F_\gamma(x, y). \tag{2} \] Since \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are two linearly independent (over \(\mathbf{Q}\)) characters of \(T\), one concludes as usual from the first relation that \(F_0\) is constant, hence \(F_0(x, y) = e\). Let us next write \[ F_\gamma(x, y) = \sum a_{ij} x^i y^j, \quad \text{with} \quad a_{ij} \in \Gamma(S, \mathscr{O}_S). \] Substituting into relation (2) and identifying the polynomials on the two sides, one finds \[ a_{ij}\big(\alpha(t)^i \beta(t)^j - \gamma(t)\big) = 0. \] If \(\gamma \ne i\alpha + j\beta\), one knows (Exp. XIX 4.13) that there exist a faithfully flat quasi-compact \(S' \to S\) and a \(t \in T(S')\) with \(\alpha(t)^i \beta(t)^j - \gamma(t) = 1\). One therefore has \(a_{ij} = 0\) on \(S'\), hence on \(S\). If \(\gamma = i\alpha + j\beta\), one puts \(a_{ij} = C_{i,j,\alpha,\beta}\). Setting successively \(x = 0\) and \(y = 0\), one finds \(C_{0,1} = 1\), \(C_{1,0} = 0\).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 5.5.3

Differentiating at \(y = 0\) and comparing with 5.4.9, one finds \[ C_{i,1,\alpha,\beta} = M_{\alpha,\beta,i}. \]

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.5.4

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\), and \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) two roots of \(G\) with respect to \(T\) such that \(\alpha + \beta\) is non-trivial on each fibre. Let us order the set of the \(i\alpha + j\beta\) (\(i, j \in \mathbf{N}\), \(i \ne 0\), \(j \ne 0\)) in an arbitrary manner. For all \(i, j \in \mathbf{N}\), \(i \ne 0\), \(j \ne 0\), there exists a unique morphism of \(\mathscr{O}_S\)-Modules \[ f_{\alpha,\beta,i,j} : (\mathfrak{g}^\alpha)^{\otimes i} \otimes (\mathfrak{g}^\beta)^{\otimes j} \longrightarrow \mathfrak{g}^{i\alpha+j\beta} \] such that for every \(S' \to S\) and all \(X \in \mathbf{W}(\mathfrak{g}^\alpha)(S')\), \(Y \in \mathbf{W}(\mathfrak{g}^\beta)(S')\) one has (the \(\exp\) on the right-hand side being taken in the sense of 1.2): \[ \exp_\alpha(X) \exp_\beta(Y) \exp_\alpha(-X) = \exp_\beta(Y) \prod_{(i,j)} \exp_{i\alpha+j\beta}(f_{ij}(X^i Y^j)). \]

The assertion is local for (fpqc). We may therefore suppose \(G\) split relative to \(T\), with \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) constant in the splitting. Since \(\alpha + \beta \ne 0\), there exists a system of positive roots \(R^+\) containing \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) (Exp. XXI 3.5.4), and one is reduced to 5.5.2.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.5.5

Let \(S\) be a prescheme and \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group.

  1. (i)

    \(G\) possesses Borel groups locally for the étale topology. If \(T\) is a maximal torus of \(G\), then \(G\) likewise possesses, locally for the étale topology, Borel groups containing \(T\).

  2. (ii)

    If \(T\) is a maximal torus of \(G\), the "functor of Borel groups of \(G\) containing \(T\)" is representable by a principal homogeneous bundle under \(W_G(T)\).

  3. (iii)

    If \((G, T, M, R)\) is split, every Borel group \(B\) of \(G\) containing \(T\) is locally on \(S\) of the form \(B_{R^+}\), where \(R^+\) is a system of positive roots of \(R\).

  4. (iv)

    If \(T \subset B\) is a Killing couple of \(G\), there exists a covering family \(\{S_i \to S\}\) for the étale topology, and for each \(i\) a splitting \((G_{S_i}, T_{S_i}, M_i, R_i)\) and a system of positive roots \(R_i^+\) of \(R_i\) such that \(B_{S_i} = B_{R_i^+}\).
Indeed, (i) follows from 2.3 and 5.5.1, (ii) from (i) and 5.3.15, (iii) from (ii) and from 5.5.1, (iv) from (iii) and 2.3.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 5.5.6

Let us choose on the group \(\Gamma_0(R)\) generated by the roots a structure of totally ordered group such that the roots \(> 0\) are the elements of \(R^+\) (cf. Exp. XXI 3.5.6). Let \(\alpha_1 < \cdots < \alpha_N\) be the elements of \(R^+\). Consider the isomorphism \[ f : T \times_S U_{\alpha_1} \times_S \cdots \times_S U_{\alpha_N} \longrightarrow B_{R^+} \] induced by the product in \(G\). Put, for \(i = 1, \ldots, N\), \[ U_{\geqslant i} = f(U_{\alpha_i} \times_S \cdots \times_S U_{\alpha_N}). \]

  1. (i)

    Each \(U_{\geqslant i}\) is an invariant subgroup of \(B_{R^+}\).

  2. (ii)

    For \(1 \leqslant i \leqslant N - 1\), \(U_{\geqslant i}\) is identified with the semi-direct product \[ U_{\geqslant i} = U_{\alpha_i} \cdot U_{\geqslant i+1}. \]

  3. (iii)

    \(B_{R^+}\) is identified with the semi-direct product \[ B_{R^+} = T \cdot U_{\geqslant 1}. \]

  4. (iv)

    For \(1 \leqslant i \leqslant N - 1\), the inner automorphisms of \(U_{\geqslant 1}\) operate trivially on \(U_{\geqslant i}/U_{\geqslant i+1}\) (which is identified with \(U_{\alpha_i}\) by (ii)).
Let us first prove by induction on \(i\) the following assertion:
\(U_{\geqslant i}\) is an invariant subgroup of \(B_{R^+}\), the semi-direct product of \(U_{\alpha_i}\) and \(U_{\geqslant i+1}\).

The assertion is true for \(i = N\); let us suppose it true for \(i + 1\) and prove it for \(i\). One has (as preschemes) \[ U_{\geqslant i} = U_{\alpha_i} \cdot U_{\geqslant i+1}; \] it is clear first of all that \(U_{\geqslant i}\) is stable under inner automorphisms of \(B_{R^+}\). This is clear for \(\mathrm{int}(t)\), \(t \in T(S)\), so it suffices to check it for \(\mathrm{int}(x)\), \(x \in U_\alpha(S)\), \(\alpha \in R^+\). Now \(U_{\geqslant i+1}\) is assumed invariant, so it suffices to see that \(\mathrm{int}(x) U_{\alpha_i} \subset U_{\geqslant i}\). By 5.5.2, if \(y \in U_{\alpha_i}(S')\), one has \(y^{-1} x y x^{-1} \in U_{\geqslant i+1}(S')\), which implies \(\mathrm{int}(x)(y) \in U_{\geqslant i}(S')\).

Let us now prove that \(U_{\geqslant i}\) is a subgroup of \(B_{R^+}\). If \(x, y \in U_{\geqslant i}(S)\), one may write \(x = p x'\), \(y = q y'\), with \(p, q \in U_{\alpha_i}(S)\) and \(x', y' \in U_{\geqslant i+1}(S)\). One has \[ x y = p x' q y' = p q (q^{-1} x' q) y' \in U_{\alpha_i}(S') U_{\geqslant i+1}(S'); \] similarly \(x^{-1} = p^{-1}(p x'^{-1} p^{-1})\). We have thus proved (i) and (ii), as well as (iv) along the way. As for (iii), it is a trivial consequence of 5.5.1.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 5.5.7

With the preceding notation, let us choose for each \(1 \leqslant i \leqslant N\) an \(X_i \in \Gamma(S, \mathfrak{g}^{\alpha_i})^*\) and consider the isomorphism \[ a : \mathbf{G}_{a,S}^N \longrightarrow U_{\geqslant 1} \] defined set-theoretically by \[ a(x_1, \ldots, x_N) = \exp_{\alpha_1}(x_1 X_1) \cdots \exp_{\alpha_N}(x_N X_N). \] There exists a unique family \((Q_i)\), \(i = 1, \ldots, N\), of polynomials \[ Q_i = Q_i(x_1, \ldots, x_N, y_1, \ldots, y_N) \] with coefficients in \(\Gamma(S, \mathscr{O}_S)\) such that one has set-theoretically \[ a(x_1, \ldots, x_N)\, a(y_1, \ldots, y_N) = a\big(Q_1(x_1, \ldots, y_N), \ldots, Q_N(x_1, \ldots, y_N)\big). \] Moreover, the \(Q_i\) have coefficients in the subring of \(\Gamma(S, \mathscr{O}_S)\) generated by the \(C_{i,j,\alpha,\beta}\) of 5.5.2 (\(\alpha, \beta \in R^+\), \(i, j \in \mathbf{N}^*\)) and each \(Q_i\) is of the form \[ Q_i(x_1, \ldots, y_N) = x_i + y_i + Q'_i(x_1, \ldots, x_{i-1}, y_1, \ldots, y_{i-1}). \]

The existence and uniqueness of the \(Q_i\) follow immediately from the fact that \(a\) is an isomorphism of preschemes. Denoting by \(z\), \(z'\), \(z''\) sections of \(U_{\geqslant i+1}\), one has \[ a(x_1, \ldots, x_N)\, a(y_1, \ldots, y_N) = a(x_1, \ldots, x_{i-1}, 0, \ldots 0) \exp(x_i X_i)\, z \cdot a(y_1, \ldots, y_{i-1}, 0, \ldots, 0) \exp(y_i X_i)\, z'; \] using 5.5.6 (i) and (iv), this may be written \[ a(x_1, \ldots, x_{i-1}, 0, \ldots, 0)\, a(y_1, \ldots, y_{i-1}, 0, \ldots, 0)\, \exp((x_i + y_i) X_i)\, z''; \] which gives, on again using 5.5.6, \[ Q_i(x_1, \ldots, x_N, y_1, \ldots, y_N) = x_i + y_i + Q'_i(x_1, \ldots, x_{i-1}, y_1, \ldots, y_{i-1}), \] with \[ Q'_i(x_1, \ldots, x_{i-1}, y_1, \ldots, y_{i-1}) = Q_i(x_1, \ldots, x_{i-1}, 0, \ldots, 0, y_1, \ldots, y_{i-1}, 0, \ldots, 0); \] that is, the precise form required.

Let us prove finally the assertion about the coefficients of the polynomials \(Q_i\). Let \(A\) be the subring of \(\Gamma(S, \mathscr{O}_S)\) generated by the \(C_{i,j,\alpha,\beta}\) (\(\alpha, \beta \in R^+\), \(i, j \in \mathbf{N}^*\)). Let us prove by induction on \(i\) that if \(x_1 = \cdots = x_{i-1} = 0\) and \(y_1 = \cdots = y_{i-1} = 0\), that is to say if \(a((x_i))\) and \(a((y_i))\) are sections of \(U_{\geqslant i}\), the polynomials \[ R_j(x_i, \ldots, x_N, y_i, \ldots, y_N) = Q_j((x_i), (y_i)), \] have coefficients in \(A\). This is trivial for \(i = N\), and also for \(j < i\) (since \(R_j = 0\)). Let \(i < N\); let us suppose the assertion verified for \(i + 1\) and prove it for \(i\) (and \(j \geqslant i\)). One has \[ a(0, \ldots, 0, x_i, \ldots, x_N) = \exp(x_i X_i)\, a(0, \ldots, 0, x_{i+1}, \ldots, x_N) = \exp(x_i X_i)\, Z_i. \] Let us write similarly \[ a(0, \ldots, y_i, \ldots, y_N) = \exp(y_i X_i)\, T_i. \] One has \[ a(0, \ldots, x_i, \ldots, x_N)\, a(0, \ldots, y_i, \ldots, y_N) = \exp((x_i + y_i) X_i)\, \mathrm{int}(\exp(-y_i X_i))(Z_i) \cdot T_i. \] Now \[ \mathrm{int}(\exp(-y_i X_i))(Z_i) = \mathrm{int}(\exp(-y_i X_i))\big(\exp(x_{i+1} X_{i+1}) \cdots \exp(x_N X_N)\big) \] is a product of \(N - i - 1\) sections of \(U_{\geqslant i+1}\) whose coefficients in the decomposition \(U_{\geqslant i+1} = U_{\alpha_{i+1}} \cdots U_{\alpha_N}\) are polynomials in \(y_i\) and the \(x_{i+1}, \ldots, x_N\) with coefficients in \(A\) (by 5.5.2). Applying the induction hypothesis, one deduces that the coefficients of \[ \mathrm{int}(\exp(-y_i X_i))(Z_i) \cdot T_i \] are likewise polynomials with coefficients in \(A\), which completes the proof.
Let us remark that the preceding induction gives at once a proof of the

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 5.5.8

With the notation of 5.5.6, let there be given for each \(i = 1, \ldots, N\) a morphism of groups \[ f_i : U_{\alpha_i} \longrightarrow H, \] where \(H\) is an \(S\)-group functor. In order that the morphism \[ f : U_{\geqslant 1} \longrightarrow H \] defined by \[ f\big(\exp(x_1 X_1) \cdots \exp(x_N X_N)\big) = f_1(\exp(x_1 X_1)) \cdots f_N(\exp(x_N X_N)) \] be a morphism of groups, it is necessary and sufficient that for every pair \(i < j\), one have \[ f_j(\exp(x_j X_j))\, f_i(\exp(x_i X_i))\, f_j(\exp(-x_j X_j)) = f\big(\exp(x_j X_j)\, \exp(x_i X_i)\, \exp(-x_j X_j)\big). \]
5.6. Subgroups of type (R) with solvable fibres

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.6.1

Let \((G, T, M, R)\) be a split \(S\)-group, \(R'\) a subset of \(R\) of type (R) (5.4.2), and \(H_{R'}\) the corresponding subgroup of \(G\). The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    \(H_{R'}\) has solvable geometric fibres.

  2. (ii)

    There exists a system of positive roots \(R^+\) such that \(R' \subset R^+\), hence \(H_{R'} \subset B_{R^+}\) (cf. 5.4.5).

  3. (iii)

    \(R' \cap -R' = \varnothing\).

  4. (iv)

    For every ordering on \(R'\), the morphism induced by the product in \(G\) \[ T \times_S \prod_{\alpha \in R'} U_\alpha \longrightarrow H_{R'} \] is an isomorphism.

  5. (v)

    \(H_{R'} \cap \mathrm{Norm}_G(T) = T\).

  6. (vi)

    For every subset \(R''\) of \(R\) of type (R), one has (cf. 5.4.5) \[ H_{R'} \cap \mathrm{Norm}_G(H_{R''}) = H_{R' \cap R''}. \]

We shall prove these equivalences according to the logical scheme \[ \xymatrix{ {(\text{iii})} \ar@{=>}[dd] & {(\text{ii})} \ar@{=>}[l] \ar@{=>}[r] \ar@{=>}[d] & {(\text{vi})} \ar@{=>}[dd] \\ & {(\text{iv})} \ar@{=>}[dr] & \\ {(\text{i})} \ar@{=>}[uur] & & {(\text{v})} \ar@{=>}[ll] } \] One evidently has (ii) \(\Rightarrow\) (iii) and (vi) \(\Rightarrow\) (v) (take \(R'' = \varnothing\)). By 5.4.6, (i) \(\Rightarrow\) (ii) is to be checked on the geometric fibres; now if \(S\) is the spectrum of an algebraically closed field, \(H_{R'}\) is contained in a Borel group containing \(T\), hence of the form \(H_{R^+}\) (5.5.5 (iii)).

Similarly (iii) \(\Rightarrow\) (i) is checked on the geometric fibres; suppose (iii) satisfied; if \(H_{R'}\) were not solvable, there would exist a subtorus \(Q\) of \(T\), of codimension 1 in \(T\), such that \(\mathrm{Centr}_{H_{R'}}(Q)\) is not solvable (BIBLE, 10-09, prop. 8); now \(\mathrm{Centr}_{H_{R'}}(Q)\) has as Lie Algebra \(\mathfrak{g}_{R''}\), where \(R''\) is the set of roots of \(R'\) vanishing on \(Q\), hence of the form \(R'' = \varnothing\), or \(R'' = \{r\}\) (by virtue of (iii)); therefore \(\mathrm{Centr}_{H_{R'}}(Q)\), which is a subgroup of type (R) of \(G\), is \(T\) or \(T \cdot U_\alpha\), hence solvable, contrary to the hypothesis.

Similarly (ii) \(\Rightarrow\) (iv) is checked on the geometric fibres (since we are dealing with flat \(S\)-preschemes of finite presentation); by BIBLE, 13-05, th. 1 d), the morphism in question is bijective; it induces an isomorphism on the tangent spaces at the origin, and one concludes as usual (cf. 4.1.1).

One has (iv) \(\Rightarrow\) (v) by 4.2.7. To prove (v) \(\Rightarrow\) (i), one is again reduced to the case where \(S\) is the spectrum of an algebraically closed field, and one concludes by BIBLE, 10-08, cor. to prop. 6 and 9-05, cor. 3 to th. 1.

It therefore remains only to prove the assertion (ii) \(\Rightarrow\) (vi). We may reduce to the case where \(G\) is adjoint. One then has, by 5.3.3 \[ \mathrm{Norm}_G(H_{R''}) = \mathrm{Norm}_G(\mathfrak{g}_{R''}) \subset \mathrm{Transp}_G(\mathfrak{t}, \mathfrak{g}_{R''}). \] By 5.4.5, it suffices to prove \[ H_{R'}(S) \cap \mathrm{Transp}_{G(S)}(\mathfrak{t}, \mathfrak{g}_{R''}) \subset H_{R' \cap R''}(S). \tag{x} \] Let us first prove a lemma.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 5.6.2

In the notation of 5.5.7, let \[ u = \exp(x_1 X_1) \cdots \exp(x_N X_N) \] where \(x_i \in \mathbf{G}_a(S)\). Let \(m\) be an integer, \(1 \leqslant m \leqslant N\), such that \(x_i = 0\) for \(i < m\).

  1. a)

    If \(X \in \Gamma(S, \mathfrak{t})\), the component of \(\mathrm{Ad}(u)X\) on \(\mathfrak{g}^{\alpha_m}\) is \[ -\overline{\alpha}_m(X)\, x_m\, X_m. \]

  2. b)

    If \(Y \in \Gamma(S, \mathfrak{g}^{-\alpha_m})\), the component of \(\mathrm{Ad}(u)Y\) on \(\mathfrak{t}\) is \[ x_m\, \langle X_m Y \rangle\, H_{\alpha_m}. \]

Let us indeed write \(\mathfrak{h} = \mathfrak{g}^{\alpha_{m+1}} + \cdots + \mathfrak{g}^{\alpha_N}\). By virtue of 5.4.9, one has \[ \mathrm{Ad}(\exp(x_i X_i))\mathfrak{h} \subset \mathfrak{h}, \qquad \text{for} \quad i > m. \] By Exp. XX 2.10, one has \[ \mathrm{Ad}(\exp(x_i X_i))X = X - \overline{\alpha}_i(X)\, x_i\, X_i. \] This gives at once, modulo \(\mathfrak{h}\), \[ \mathrm{Ad}(u)X = \mathrm{Ad}(\exp(x_m X_m))X, \] which yields the first result.

Similarly, let us write \(\mathfrak{u} = \mathfrak{g}^{\alpha_1} + \cdots + \mathfrak{g}^{\alpha_m}\). For \(i > m\), one has \(\alpha_i > \alpha_m\), hence (5.4.9) \[ \mathrm{Ad}(u)Y - Y \in \mathfrak{u}. \] Applying Exp. XX 2.10, one therefore has \[ \mathrm{Ad}(u)Y - Y - x_m\, (X_m Y)\, H_{\alpha_m} \in \mathfrak{u}, \qquad \text{qed}. \]

Let us return to the proof of formula (x). Suppose there exists an \(h \in H_{R'}(S)\), \(h \notin H_{R' \cap R''}(S)\), with \[ \mathrm{Ad}(h)\mathfrak{t} \subset \mathfrak{g}_{R''}. \] One may write \[ h = t \exp(x_1 X_1) \cdots \exp(x_N X_N). \] Since \(h \notin H_{R' \cap R''}(S)\), there exists a smallest \(m\) such that \[ t \exp(x_1 X_1) \cdots \exp(x_{m-1} X_{m-1}) \in H_{R' \cap R''}(S), \] \[ \alpha_m \notin R'', \qquad x_m \ne 0. \] Then \(h' = \exp(x_m X_m) \cdots \exp(x_N X_N)\) also satisfies the conditions imposed on \(h\) above. But by 5.6.2, the component of \(\mathrm{Ad}(h')X\) on \(\mathfrak{g}^{\alpha_m}\) is \(-\overline{\alpha}_m(X)\, x_m\, X_m\), if \(X \in \Gamma(S, \mathfrak{t})\). By virtue of the hypothesis on \(h\) and on \(m\), one therefore has \(\overline{\alpha}_m(X) = 0\), which is impossible (since \(G\) is assumed adjoint and \(\overline{\alpha}_m\) is therefore non-zero on each fibre).

blocks.label: 5.6.2 bis
blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 5.6.2 bis

Let us resume the notation of 5.6.2. If \(\mathrm{Ad}(u)\) is the identity on \(\mathfrak{t}\) and \(\mathfrak{g}^{-\alpha_m}\), one has \(x_m = 0\). Indeed, one has \(x_m \cdot \overline{\alpha}_m = 0\), \(x_m \cdot H_{\alpha_m} = 0\); if \(\alpha_m \notin 2M\), \(\overline{\alpha}_m\) is non-zero on each fibre; if \(\alpha_m \in 2M\), then \(\alpha_m^* \notin 2M^*\) and \(H_{\alpha_m}\) is non-zero on each fibre; in either case, this implies \(x_m = 0\). It follows that \(u = e\) if \(\mathrm{Ad}(u)\) operates trivially on \(\mathfrak{g}\).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 5.6.3

If \(H\) is a subgroup of type (R) of the reductive group \(G\), with solvable geometric fibres, then \(H\) is closed in \(G\) and \(\mathrm{Norm}_G(H)/H\) is representable by a finite étale \(S\)-scheme.
Trivial by 5.3.18.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.6.4

Let \((G, T, M, R)\) be a split reductive group. If \(R' \subset R\) is closed and if \(R' \cap -R' = \varnothing\), then \(R'\) is contained in a system of positive roots.
Indeed, \(R'\) is of type (R) by 5.4.7.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.6.5

Under the conditions of 5.6.1, the product in \(G\) induces an isomorphism \[ \prod_{\alpha \in R'} U_\alpha \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} U_{R'}, \] where \(U_{R'}\) is a closed group subprescheme of \(G\), smooth over \(S\), with connected unipotent geometric fibres, independent of the choice of the ordering on \(R'\). Moreover, \(H_{R'}\) is the semi-direct product \(T \cdot U_{R'}\) (\(U_{R'}\) invariant).

Indeed, if \(R' \subset R^+\), \(H_{R'} \cap U_1\) (notation of 5.5.6) is a closed subgroup of \(G\) of finite presentation, invariant in \(H_{R'}\). By 5.6.1 (iv), one has \(H_{R'} = T \cdot U_{R'}\), which implies the other assertions.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 5.6.6

In particular, \(U_{R^+}\) is the group \(U_{\geqslant 1}\) of 5.5.6.
Let us draw out some corollaries of the preceding results concerning the groups of type \(U_{R'}\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.6.7

Let \((G, T, M, R)\) be a split reductive group, and let \(R'\) and \(R''\) be two subsets of type (R), with \(R' \cap -R' = \varnothing\).

  1. (i)

    We have \[ U_{R'} \cap \mathrm{Norm}_G(H_{R''}) = U_{R' \cap R''}. \]

  2. (ii)

    Suppose \(R'\) closed. If, for \(\alpha \in R'\) and \(\beta \in R''\), the relation \(\alpha + \beta \in R\) implies \(\alpha + \beta \in R'\), then \(H_{R''}\) normalises \(U_{R'}\).

Indeed, (i) follows at once from 5.6.5 and 5.6.1 (vi). To prove (ii), it suffices, in view of 5.4.4, to show that \(T\) and each \(U_\beta\), \(\beta \in R''\), normalise \(U_{R'}\). For \(T\) this is trivial; for \(U_\beta\), it follows from 5.5.2 and Exp. XXI 2.3.5.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.6.8

Let \((G, T, M, R)\) be a split \(S\)-group, \(R^+\) a system of positive roots, and \(\alpha\) a simple root of \(R^+\) (i.e. an element of \(R^+\) such that \(R^+ - \{\alpha\}\) is closed). Write \[ U_{\widehat{\alpha}} = U_{R^+ - \{\alpha\}}. \] Then

  1. (i)

    \(U_{\widehat{\alpha}}\) is an invariant subgroup of \(B_{R^+}\).

  2. (ii)

    \(U_{R^+}\) is the semi-direct product of \(U_{\widehat{\alpha}}\) by \(U_\alpha\).

  3. (iii)

    \(U_{-\alpha}\) normalises \(U_{\widehat{\alpha}}\).

  4. (iv)

    \(Z_\alpha\) normalises \(U_{\widehat{\alpha}}\).

If one defines in the same way \(U_{-\widehat{\alpha}} = U_{R^- - \{-\alpha\}}\) (where \(R^- = -R^+\)), one has \[ \Omega_{R^+} = U_{-\widehat{\alpha}} \cdot U_{-\alpha} \cdot T \cdot U_\alpha \cdot U_{\widehat{\alpha}}. \]

Indeed, (i) is trivial by 5.6.7 (ii), (ii) is clear by 5.6.5, (iii) follows from 5.5.2 (indeed, if \(\beta \in R^+\), \(\beta \ne \alpha\), no combination \(i(-\alpha) + j\beta\), with \(i, j > 0\), can be negative, since \(\beta\) contains at least one simple root \(\ne \alpha\)), (iv) follows at once from (i) and (iii), since \(U_{-\alpha} \cdot T \cdot U_\alpha\) is schematically dense in \(Z_\alpha\). The last assertion is trivial by (ii).
Let us return to the general situation.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.6.9

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, and \(H\) a subgroup of type (R) with solvable geometric fibres.

  1. (i)

    \(\mathrm{D}_S(H) = \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(H, \mathbf{G}_{m,S})\) is representable by a twisted constant \(S\)-group, whose type at \(s \in S\) is \(\mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{rgred}(G_s)}\). The biduality morphism (Exp. VIII § 1) \[ f : H \longrightarrow \mathrm{D}_S(\mathrm{D}_S(H)) \] is smooth and surjective.

  2. (ii)

    The kernel \(H^u\) of \(f\) is the largest closed invariant subgroup-prescheme of \(H\) that is smooth over \(S\) with connected unipotent geometric fibres. It is called the unipotent part of \(H\). One also writes \(H^u = \mathrm{rad}^u(H)\). It is also the sheaf of commutators of \(H\): every group morphism from \(H\) into a commutative \(S\)-group-presheaf, separated for (fppf), vanishes on \(H^u\) and hence factors through \(H/H^u = \mathrm{D}_S(\mathrm{D}_S(H))\).

  3. (iii)

    If \(T\) is a maximal torus of \(H\), the morphism \(T \to H\) induces isomorphisms \(\mathrm{D}_S(H) \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \mathrm{D}_S(T)\) and \(T \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \mathrm{D}_S(\mathrm{D}_S(H))\). Moreover, \(H\) is identified with the semi-direct product of \(H^u\) by \(T\).

  4. (iv)

    In the situation of 5.6.1, if \(H = H_{R'}\), then \(H^u = U_{R'}\).

The assertions of the proposition are local for the étale topology (Exp. X 5.5). We may therefore reduce to the case of 5.6.1. We know (5.6.5) that \(H_{R'}\) is the semi-direct product of \(U_{R'}\) by \(T\). Let us show that \(U_{R'}\) is the sheaf of commutators of \(H_{R'}\): since \(H_{R'}/U_{R'} = T\) is commutative, it suffices to prove that every group morphism \(g : H_{R'} \to V\) as in (ii) vanishes on \(U_{R'}\). It suffices to prove that \(g\) vanishes on each \(U_\alpha\), \(\alpha \in R'\). Now if \(t \in T(S')\), \(X \in \mathbf{W}(\mathfrak{g}^\alpha)(S')\), one has \[ 1 = g\big(t \exp_\alpha(X)\, t^{-1} \exp_\alpha(-X)\big) = g\big(\exp_\alpha((\alpha(t) - 1)X)\big). \] Since \(\alpha : T \to \mathbf{G}_{m,S}\) is faithfully flat, one deduces at once that \(g\) vanishes on \(U_\alpha^*\); but every section of \(U_\alpha\) is locally the sum of two sections of \(U_\alpha^*\). We therefore have \[ \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(H, V) = \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(H/U_{R'}, V) \] for every \(V\) as above. Applying this result to \(V = \mathbf{G}_{m,S}\), one deduces at once (i) and (iii), then (iv) and the second assertion of (ii). It now suffices to prove the first assertion of (i); the only non-trivial fact is that every closed invariant subgroup \(U\) of \(H\), smooth over \(S\) with connected unipotent geometric fibres, is a subgroup of \(H^u\). Now we have first of all:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 5.6.10

Let \(G\) be a reductive \(S\)-group, \(T\) a maximal torus, and \(U\) a subgroup-prescheme of \(G\), smooth over \(S\), with unipotent geometric fibres, normalised by \(T\). Then \(U \cap T = e\).

Indeed, since \(T = \mathrm{Centr}_G(T)\), one has \(U \cap T = U^T\) (invariants under \(\mathrm{int}(T)\)). Applying Exp. XIX 1.4, one deduces that \(U \cap T\) is smooth over \(S\); but it is also radicial over \(S\): for every \(s \in S\), \(U(\overline{s}) \cap T(\overline{s})\) consists of elements that are at once unipotent and semi-simple.

If \(U\) is an invariant subgroup of \(H\) as above, the semi-direct product \(T \cdot U\) is therefore a subgroup of type (R) of \(G\), with solvable geometric fibres. We may thus assume it to be of the form \(H_{R''}\), with \(R'' \subset R'\). It suffices to prove that \(U = U_{R''}\), and we are therefore reduced to the case where \(H = T \cdot U\); but since the quotient \(H/U\) is commutative, \(U\) is a subsheaf of the sheaf of commutators of \(H\), which is \(H^u\). Q.E.D.
Note that we have in fact just proved:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.6.11

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, and \(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\). The maps \[ H \mapsto H^u, \qquad U \mapsto T \cdot U \] are mutually inverse isomorphisms between the set of subgroups of type (R) of \(G\) containing \(T\) and having solvable geometric fibres, and the set of closed (or retrocompact) subgroups of \(G\), smooth over \(S\), normalised by \(T\), with connected unipotent geometric fibres.

In particular, if \((G, T, M, R)\) is split, \(H_{R'}\) and \(U_{R'}\) correspond to each other.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.6.12

Let \(S\) be a prescheme and \((G, T, M, R)\) a split \(S\)-group (resp. and let \(R^+\) be a system of positive roots of \(R\) defining the Borel group \(B\)).

Every subgroup-prescheme of \(G\) which is smooth and of finite presentation, with connected unipotent geometric fibres (resp. every subgroup-prescheme of \(B^u\) which is smooth and of finite presentation), normalised by \(T\), is locally on \(S\) of the form \(U_{R'}\), where \(R'\) is a subset of \(R\) contained in a system of positive roots (resp. a subset of \(R^+\)) of type (R).
For the "resp." case, it suffices to note that the geometric fibres of the given group are unipotent and connected by BIBLE, 13-05, th. 1 d).
Proposition 5.6.9 has moreover the following corollary:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.6.13

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(H\) a subgroup of type (R) with solvable geometric fibres, and \(\mathrm{Tor}(H)\) the functor of maximal tori of \(H\): \[ \mathrm{Tor}(H)(S') = \{\text{maximal tori of } H_{S'}\}. \] Then \(\mathrm{Tor}(H)\) is representable by an affine smooth \(S\)-prescheme, which is a principal homogeneous bundle under \(H^u\) for the obvious law \(((h, T) \mapsto \mathrm{int}(h)T)\).

Indeed, if \(T\) and \(T'\) are two maximal tori of \(H_{S'}\), there exists a unique section \(h \in H^u(S')\) such that \(\mathrm{int}(h)T = T'\). The uniqueness of \(h\) follows at once from \(\mathrm{Norm}_G(T) \cap H^u = e\) (cf. for example 5.6.1); it suffices to prove the existence of \(h\) locally for the étale topology, and we may assume \(T\) and \(T'\) conjugate by a section of \(H\); but then we conclude by \(H = H^u \cdot T\). It follows that \(\mathrm{Tor}(H)\) is a principal homogeneous sheaf under \(H^u\), which is affine and smooth over \(S\), and this yields the statement at once.
5.7. Bruhat's theorem
Reminder 5.7.1.

Let \(k\) be an algebraically closed field, \(G\) a reductive \(k\)-group, \(B\) a Borel group of \(G\), \(T\) a maximal torus of \(B\), and \(N = \mathrm{Norm}_G(T)\). Then \[ G(k) = B(k)\, N(k)\, B(k); \] this is Bruhat's theorem (BIBLE, 13-11, cor. 1 to th. 3); more precisely, with the notation of 3.6, the sets \[ B(k)\, Q_w(k)\, B(k) = B^u(k)\, Q_w(k)\, B^u(k) \] form, as \(w\) runs through \((N/T)(k)\), a partition of \(G(k)\). If \(B'\) is another Borel group of \(G\) containing \(T\), the sets \(B'(k)\, Q_w(k)\, B(k)\) also form a partition of \(G(k)\). Indeed, if \(w_0 \in N(k)\) is such that \(\mathrm{int}(w_0)B = B'\), one has \[ w_0 B(k)\, Q_w(k)\, B(k) = B'(k)\, Q_{w_0 w}(k)\, B(k). \]

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 5.7.2

Let \((G, T, M, R)\) be a split \(S\)-group, \(R^-\) a system of positive roots of \(R\), and \(B' = B_{R^-}\) the Borel group it defines. For \(w \in W\), one writes (cf. 5.6.5): \[ R_-^w = R^- \cap w(R^-), \qquad B'^u_w = U_{R_-^w} = \prod_{\alpha \in R_-^w} U_\alpha. \] If \(n_w \in \mathrm{Norm}_G(T)(S)\) is a representative of \(w\) (3.8), one may also write \[ B'^u_w = B'^u \cap \mathrm{int}(n_w)B'^u. \]

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 5.7.3

Let \((G, T, M, R)\) be a split \(S\)-group, \(R^+\) a system of positive roots of \(R\), \(R^- = -R^+\), and \(B\) (resp. \(B'\)) the Borel group of \(G\) defined by \(R^+\) (resp. \(R^-\)). Let \(w \in W\), and let \(Q_w\) and \(B'^u_w\) be the corresponding subpreschemes of \(G\) (3.8 and 5.7.2).

  1. (i)

    The sheaf \(B' \cdot Q_w \cdot B\), image of the morphism \[ B' \times_S Q_w \times_S B \longrightarrow G \] induced by the product in \(G\), is representable by a subprescheme of \(G\) (and in fact by a closed subprescheme of the open set \(n_w \Omega_{R^+}\)).

  2. (ii)

    The morphism \[ B'^u_w \times_S Q_w \times_S B^u \longrightarrow G, \] induced by the product in \(G\), is an immersion whose image is the preceding subprescheme.

Let us first show that the morphism of (ii) is an immersion. By definition, \(\mathrm{int}(n_w)^{-1}\) induces a closed immersion of \(B'^u_w\) into \(B'^u\), so that the morphism \[ (u, b) \longmapsto n_w^{-1} u\, n_w b \] induces a closed immersion \[ B'^u_w \times_S B \longrightarrow \Omega_{R^+}. \] This immediately implies that the morphism of (ii) induces a closed immersion of the left-hand side into the open set \(n_w \Omega_{R^+}\). To prove (i), it suffices to see that \[ B'(S)\, Q_w(S)\, B(S) = B'^u_w(S)\, Q_w(S)\, B^u(S). \] Now, if \(\alpha \in R\), one has \(\mathrm{int}(n_w)U_\alpha(S) = U_{w(\alpha)}(S)\), so that if \(w^{-1}(\alpha) \in R^+\), \[ \begin{aligned} U_\alpha(S) Q_w(S) B(S) &= U_\alpha(S)\, n_w T(S) B^u(S) \\ &= n_w\, U_{w^{-1}(\alpha)}(S) T(S) B^u(S) \\ &= n_w B(S) = Q_w(S) B^u(S). \end{aligned} \] In view of the definition of \(R_-^w\), this yields the desired assertion at once.

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 5.7.4

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \((G, T, M, R)\) a split \(S\)-group, \(B\) the Borel group defined by the system of positive roots \(R^+\), and \(B'\) the Borel group defined by \(R^- = -R^+\).

  1. (i)

    (Bruhat's theorem) The preschemes \(B'^u_w \cdot Q_w \cdot B\) form, as \(w\) runs through \(W\), a partition of the underlying set of \(G\).

  2. (ii)

    For each \(w \in W\), let \(n_w\) be a representative of \(w\) in \(\mathrm{Norm}_G(T)(S)\) (3.8); then the open sets \(n_w \Omega = n_w B'^u \cdot T \cdot B^u\) form, as \(w\) runs through \(W\), a covering of \(G\).
Both assertions may indeed be verified on the geometric fibres, where one concludes by 5.7.1 and 5.7.3.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 5.7.5

(i) implies that if \(S\) is the spectrum of a field, \(G(S)\) is the disjoint union of the \(B'^u_w(S) \cdot T(S) \cdot B^u(S)\). The corresponding assertion for an arbitrary \(S\) (even local or artinian) is obviously false. Note however that (ii) implies that if \(S\) is local, \(G(S)\) is indeed the union of the \(n_w \Omega(S)\). In fact:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.7.6

Let \(R_0\) be a system of simple roots of the split group \(G\) over the local scheme \(S\).

  1. (i)

    Then \(G(S)\) is generated by \(T(S)\) and the \(U_\alpha(S)\), \(\alpha \in R_0 \cup -R_0\).

  2. (ii)

    If \(G\) is simply connected, \(G(S)\) is already generated by the \(U_\alpha(S)\), \(\alpha \in R_0 \cup -R_0\).

Indeed, let \(H\) be the subgroup of \(G(S)\) generated by the \(U_\alpha(S)\), \(\alpha \in R_0 \cup -R_0\). Note first that \(H\) contains a representative of each \(s_\alpha\) (\(\alpha \in R_0\)) in \(\mathrm{Norm}_G(T)(S)\) (Exp. XX 3.1), hence a representative \(n_w\) of each \(w \in W\).

Since every \(\alpha \in R\) may be written \(w(\alpha_0)\) with \(w \in W\), \(\alpha_0 \in R_0\), one has \[ U_\alpha(S) = \mathrm{int}(n_w) U_{\alpha_0}(S) \subset H. \] The subgroup generated by \(H\) and \(T(S)\) therefore contains \(\Omega(S)\) and hence is the whole of \(G(S)\), by the remark made earlier.
If now \(G\) is simply connected, let us prove that \(H \supset T(S)\). By Exp. XX 2.7, \(H\) contains \(\alpha^*(\mathbf{G}_m(S))\) for every \(\alpha \in R_0\), and it suffices to apply 4.3.8.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 5.7.6.1

Instead of taking, for each \(\alpha \in R_0\), \(U_\alpha(S)\) and \(U_{-\alpha}(S)\), one may content oneself with taking \(U_\alpha(S)\) and a representative \(w_\alpha\) of the symmetry \(s_\alpha\), or else \(U_\alpha(S)\) and a section of \(U_{-\alpha}^*\), ….

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.7.7

If \(G\) is of semi-simple rank 1, choose a \(u_\alpha \in U_\alpha^*(S)\). Then \(\Omega\) and \(u_\alpha \Omega\) form a covering of \(G\).

Indeed, if \(u_{-\alpha}\) is the section of \(U_{-\alpha}\) paired with \(u_\alpha\), one has, by 5.7.4 (ii), \[ G = \Omega \cup u_{-\alpha}^{-1} u_\alpha u_{-\alpha}^{-1} \Omega, \] whence \[ G = u_{-\alpha} G = u_{-\alpha} \Omega \cup u_\alpha u_{-\alpha}^{-1} \Omega = \Omega \cup u_\alpha \Omega. \]

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.7.8

Let \(S\) be a prescheme and \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group. Then \(G\) is essentially free over \(S\) (Exp. VIII 6.1).

Indeed, the assertion is local for the (fpqc) topology, so we may assume \(G\) split. Then \(G\) admits a covering by open sets isomorphic to \(\mathbf{G}_{a,S}^N \times_S \mathbf{G}_{m,S}^n\), hence essentially free.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 5.7.9

Under the conditions of 5.7.4, let \(\alpha\) be a simple root of \(R^+\) and \(u_\alpha \in U_\alpha^*(S)\). For every \(v \in U_{-\alpha}(S)\), one has \[ \Omega \cdot v \subset \Omega \cup u_\alpha \cdot \Omega \]

We have to compare two open sets of \(G\), and it suffices to do so when \(S\) is the spectrum of a field \(k\). We must therefore prove \[ \Omega(k) v \subset \Omega(k) \cup u_\alpha \Omega(k). \] Now \[ \begin{aligned} \Omega(k) v = B'^u(k) T(k) B^u(k) v &= U_{-\widehat{\alpha}}(k) U_{-\alpha}(k) T(k) U_\alpha(k) U_{\widehat{\alpha}}(k) v \\ &\subset U_{-\widehat{\alpha}}(k) Z_\alpha(k) U_{\widehat{\alpha}}(k) v. \end{aligned} \] (One uses the decomposition of 5.6.8). Applying now 5.6.8 (iii) and using 5.7.7 for the group \(Z_\alpha\), one obtains \[ \begin{aligned} \Omega(k) v \subset U_{-\widehat{\alpha}}(k) Z_\alpha(k) v U_{\widehat{\alpha}}(k) &\subset U_{-\widehat{\alpha}}(k) Z_\alpha(k) U_{\widehat{\alpha}}(k) \\ &\subset U_{-\widehat{\alpha}}(k) U_{-\alpha}(k) T(k) U_\alpha(k) U_{\widehat{\alpha}}(k) \cup U_{-\widehat{\alpha}}(k)\, u_\alpha U_{-\alpha}(k) T(k) U_\alpha(k) U_{\widehat{\alpha}}(k). \end{aligned} \] Using once again 5.6.8 (iii) (for \(R^-\) instead of \(R^+\)), one obtains the result.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.7.10

Under the conditions of 5.7.4, choose for each simple root \(\alpha\) a \(u_\alpha \in U_\alpha^*(S)\). Let \(U_1\) be the submonoid of \(B^u(S)\) generated by the \(u_\alpha\). The open sets \(u\, \Omega\), for \(u \in U_1\), form a covering of \(G\).

Once again, we may assume that \(S\) is the spectrum of a field \(k\); by virtue of 5.7.6, it suffices to prove that \(\bigcup_{u \in U_1} u\, \Omega(k)\) is stable under right multiplication by \(T(k)\), \(U_\alpha(k)\), \(U_{-\alpha}(k)\) (for \(\alpha\) simple). In the first two cases this is trivial. In the last, it follows from the lemma.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 5.7.11

Let us point out a special case of 5.7.2. If \(w = s_\alpha\) is the symmetry with respect to the simple root \(\alpha\), then \[ R^- \cap s_\alpha(R^-) = R^- - \{-\alpha\} \] (Exp. XXI 3.3.1), and hence, in the notation of 5.6.8, one has \[ B'^u_{s_\alpha} = U_{-\widehat{\alpha}}. \]

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 5.7.12

In fact, the proof of 5.7.10 yields at once the following statement: under the conditions of 5.7.10, let \(\Gamma\) be the submonoid of \(G(S)\); in order that the open sets \(g\, \Omega\) (\(g \in \Gamma\)) form a covering of \(G\), it is necessary and sufficient that for every \(s \in S\) and every simple root \(\alpha\), one have \[ (u_\alpha)_{\overline{s}}\, B'^u(\overline{s}) \subset \Gamma \cdot B'^u(\overline{s}) \cdot T(\overline{s}) \cdot B^u(\overline{s}). \]

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 5.7.13

By 5.5.5 (iii), arguing as in 5.7.1, one obtains at once the following variant of 5.7.4: let \((G, T, M, R)\) be a split \(S\)-group, and \(B\) and \(B'\) two Borel groups of \(G\) containing \(T\); for every \(w \in W\), the sheaf \(B' \cdot Q_w \cdot B\) is representable by a subprescheme of \(G\); these subpreschemes form, for \(w \in W\), a partition of the underlying set of \(G\). One may also give the analogue of 5.7.3 (ii): one must set \[ B'^u_w = B'^u \cap \mathrm{int}(n_w)\widetilde{B}^u, \] where \(\widetilde{B}\) is the Borel group "opposite" to \(B\) relative to \(T\) (cf. 5.9.2).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.7.14

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, and \[ \mathrm{Ad} : G \longrightarrow \mathrm{GL}_{\mathscr{O}_S}(\mathfrak{g}) \] its adjoint representation. Then \(\mathrm{Ker}(\mathrm{Ad}) = \mathrm{Centr}(G)\), (in other words, the canonical homomorphism deduced from \(\mathrm{Ad}\) by passage to the quotient: \[ \mathrm{ad}(G) = G/\mathrm{Centr}(G) \longrightarrow \mathrm{GL}_{\mathscr{O}_S}(\mathfrak{g}) \] is a monomorphism.

We may assume \(G\) split. Choose on \(\Gamma_0(R)\) a total order structure compatible with the group structure, and let \(R^+\) be the set of positive roots. By virtue of 5.7.4 (ii) and 4.1.6, it suffices to prove that if \(n_w\) is a representative of the element \(w\) of \(W\), if \(u \in U(S)\), \(t \in T(S)\), \(v \in U^-(S)\), and if \(\mathrm{Ad}(n_w v t u) = \mathrm{id}\), then \(w = e\), \(v = e\), \(u = e\). For each \(m \in R \cup \{0\}\), set \[ \mathfrak{g}^{>m} = \coprod_{n > m} \mathfrak{g}^n, \qquad \mathfrak{g}^{<m} = \coprod_{n < m} \mathfrak{g}^n. \] Let \(X \in \Gamma(S, \mathfrak{g}^m)\); let us write \(\mathrm{Ad}(tu)X = \mathrm{Ad}(v^{-1} n_w^{-1})X\). Now \[ \mathrm{Ad}(t)\, \mathrm{Ad}(u)X - m(t)X \in \Gamma(S, \mathfrak{g}^{>m}), \] \[ \mathrm{Ad}(v^{-1} n_w^{-1})X - \mathrm{Ad}(n_w^{-1})X \in \Gamma(S, \mathfrak{g}^{< w^{-1}(m)}). \] If \(w \ne e\), there exists an \(\alpha \in R\) such that \(w^{-1}(\alpha) < \alpha\), and taking \(m = \alpha\), one derives a contradiction, since \[ \mathrm{Ad}(tu)X \in \Gamma(S, \mathfrak{g}^m + \mathfrak{g}^{>m}) \cap (\mathfrak{g}^{w^{-1}(m)} + \mathfrak{g}^{< w^{-1}(m)}) = 0. \] We therefore have \(w = e\), and we may choose \(n_w = e\); one then has \[ \mathrm{Ad}(v^{-1})X - X \in \Gamma(S, \mathfrak{g}^{<m} \cap (\mathfrak{g}^m + \mathfrak{g}^{>m})) = 0, \] whence \(\mathrm{Ad}(v)X = X\) and hence \(\mathrm{Ad}(v) = \mathrm{id}\). Likewise \(\mathrm{Ad}(u) = \mathrm{id}\). One then concludes by 5.6.2 bis.
5.8. Schemes associated with a reductive group

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 5.8.1

Let \(S\) be a prescheme and \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group. Let \(\mathscr{H}\) be the functor of subgroups of type (R) of \(G\): for every \(S' \to S\), \(\mathscr{H}(S')\) is the set of subgroups of type (R) of \(G_{S'}\) (cf. 5.2.1). Then \(\mathscr{H}\) is representable by a quasi-projective \(S\)-prescheme, of finite presentation over \(S\).

By virtue of Exp. XII 7.12, we may assume that \(G\) is adjoint. Consider then the morphism \[ u : \mathscr{H} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Grass}(\mathfrak{g}) \] which associates with each subgroup of type (R) its Lie Algebra (which is a locally direct-factor sub-Module of \(\mathfrak{g}\). It is a monomorphism by 5.3.3. It suffices to prove that it is representable by an immersion of finite presentation, in other words to prove the following assertion: given a locally direct-factor sub-Module \(\mathfrak{h}\) of \(\mathfrak{g}\), the \(S' \to S\) such that \(\mathfrak{h}_{S'}\) is the Lie Algebra of a subgroup of type (R) of \(G_{S'}\) are exactly those which factor through a certain subprescheme (of finite presentation) of \(S\). We may obviously assume \(S\) noetherian and \(\mathfrak{h}\) of constant rank \(r\). We must first express that \(\mathfrak{h}_{S'}\) is a Lie sub-Algebra of \(G_{S'}\), i.e. that if one considers the fibre product of the diagram \[ \xymatrix{ \mathfrak{h} \otimes \mathfrak{h} \ar[r]^-{[\;,\;]} & \mathfrak{g} \\ \mathfrak{h}' \ar[u] \ar[r]_-{v} & \mathfrak{h} \ar[u] } \] \(v_{S'}\) is an isomorphism. Since \(\mathfrak{h}\) is locally free, this condition is expressed by the fact that \(S' \to S\) factors through a certain open subprescheme of \(S\). We therefore replace \(S\) by this subprescheme, and we must now express (5.3.1) that if we write \(H = \mathrm{Norm}_G(\mathfrak{h})\) (which is a closed subgroup-prescheme of \(G\)), \(H_{S'}\) is smooth along the unit section. Introducing the inverse image \(\mathfrak{n}_{H/G}\) of the conormal sheaf \(\mathscr{N}_{H/G}\) under the morphism \(e_H : S \to H\), we must express (SGA 1, II 4.10) that the canonical morphism \[ w : \mathfrak{n}_{H/G} \longrightarrow \omega^1_{G/S} \] is universally injective on \(S'\) (i.e. that \(w_{S'}\) is universally injective) and that \(\omega^1_{H/S} \otimes_{\mathscr{O}_S} \mathscr{O}_{S'}\) is locally free of rank \(r = \mathrm{rang}(\mathfrak{h})\).

The first condition is again equivalent to the fact that \(S' \to S\) factors through a certain open subprescheme of \(S\); let us replace \(S\) by this subprescheme. The second condition is expressed by the fact that \(S' \to S\) factors through a subprescheme \(Z\) of \(S\) (TDTE IV 3.6). Replacing \(S\) by \(Z\), it only remains for us to express that \((\mathrm{Norm}_G(\mathfrak{h})^0)_{s'}\) has the same reductive rank as \(G_{s'}\) at every point \(s' \in S'\), or, what amounts to the same, that \(H_s\) has the same reductive rank as \(G_s\) at every point \(s\) of the (set-theoretic) image of \(S'\) in \(S\). Now this condition defines an open subset of \(S\) (Exp. XIX 6.2).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark

In general, it is not smooth over \(S\). It is so, however, if \(6\) is invertible on \(S\), or if there exists \(p \in \mathrm{Spec}\, \mathbf{Z}\) such that \(p \cdot 1_S = 0\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.8.2

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, and \(H\) a subgroup of type (R) of \(G\). (Recall (5.3.10) that \(\mathrm{Norm}_G(H)\) is representable by a closed subgroup-prescheme of \(G\), smooth over \(S\)).

Then the quotient sheaf \(G/\mathrm{Norm}_G(H)\) is representable by a quasi-projective \(S\)-prescheme, smooth and of finite presentation over \(S\) (which is in fact an open subset of \(\mathscr{H}\)).

Indeed, consider the morphism \[ f : G \longrightarrow \mathscr{H}, \] defined set-theoretically by \(f(g) = \mathrm{int}(g)H\). By virtue of 5.3.9, this morphism is smooth and of finite presentation, hence open. Let \(V = f(G)\), endowed with its structure of open subprescheme of \(\mathscr{H}\). The morphism \(f : G \to V\) is covering with kernel \(\mathrm{Norm}_G(H)\), which proves that \(G/\mathrm{Norm}_G(H)\) is representable by \(V\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.8.3

Let \(S\) be a prescheme and \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group. Consider the functors \(\mathrm{Tor}(G)\), \(\mathrm{Bor}(G)\), \(\mathrm{Kil}(G)\) defined by \[ \begin{aligned} \mathrm{Tor}(G)(S') &= \{\text{Maximal tori of } G_{S'}\}, \\ \mathrm{Bor}(G)(S') &= \{\text{Borel groups of } G_{S'}\}, \\ \mathrm{Kil}(G)(S') &= \{\text{Killing couples of } G_{S'}\ (\text{cf. 5.3.13})\}. \end{aligned} \]

  1. (i)

    \(\mathrm{Tor}(G)\), \(\mathrm{Bor}(G)\), \(\mathrm{Kil}(G)\) are representable by smooth \(S\)-preschemes of finite presentation, with integral geometric fibres, and respectively affine, projective, affine over \(S\).

  2. (ii)

    The canonical morphism \(\mathrm{Kil}(G) \to \mathrm{Tor}(G)\) (resp. \(\mathrm{Kil}(G) \to \mathrm{Bor}(G)\)) is finite étale surjective (resp. affine smooth surjective).

  3. (iii)

    Let \(T\) be a maximal torus of \(G\) (resp. \(B\) a Borel group of \(G\), resp. \(B \supset T\) a Killing couple of \(G\)). The morphism \[ G \longrightarrow \mathrm{Tor}(G), \qquad \text{resp.}\ \ G \longrightarrow \mathrm{Bor}(G), \qquad \text{resp.}\ \ G \longrightarrow \mathrm{Kil}(G) \] defined by \[ g \mapsto \mathrm{int}(g)T, \qquad \text{resp.}\ \ g \mapsto \mathrm{int}(g)B, \qquad \text{resp.}\ \ g \mapsto (\mathrm{int}(g)B, \mathrm{int}(g)T) \] induces an isomorphism \[ G/\mathrm{Norm}_G(T) \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \mathrm{Tor}(G), \qquad \text{resp.}\ \ G/B \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \mathrm{Bor}(G), \qquad \text{resp.}\ \ G/T \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \mathrm{Kil}(G). \]

One sees first that (iii) follows from the conjugacy theorem for maximal tori (resp. Borels, resp. Killing couples) and from the fact that \[ \mathrm{Norm}_G(B) = B, \qquad \mathrm{Norm}_G(B) \cap \mathrm{Norm}_G(T) = T, \] all results established earlier (5.1.2, 5.3.12, 5.3.14, 5.6.1).

It follows first that the canonical morphisms \[ \mathrm{Tor}(G) \longrightarrow \mathscr{H}, \qquad \mathrm{Bor}(G) \longrightarrow \mathscr{H} \] are representable, locally for the étale topology, by open immersions (5.8.2 and 5.12 resp. 5.5.5), hence, by descent, that \(\mathrm{Tor}(G)\) and \(\mathrm{Bor}(G)\) are representable by open subsets of \(\mathscr{H}\). Likewise \(\mathrm{Kil}(G)\) is locally (for (ét)) representable by a prescheme affine over the base (Exp. IX 2.3), hence representable by an affine \(S\)-prescheme, by descent of affine schemes.

The assertions of (ii) follow at once from 5.5.5 (ii) and 5.6.13. It already follows that \(\mathrm{Tor}(G)\) is affine over \(S\) (EGA II 6.7.1). It therefore only remains to prove the fact that \(\mathrm{Bor}(G)\) is projective over \(S\). We already know that it is quasi-projective; it remains to prove that it is proper; now it has connected fibres, so by EGA IV\(_3\) 15.7.10 we are reduced to proving this on the geometric fibres; if \(S\) is the spectrum of an algebraically closed field, one has \(\mathrm{Bor}(G) = G/B\) by (iii), and one concludes by BIBLE, 6-09, th. 4.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 5.8.4

Under the conditions of 5.8.3, let \(Q\) be a central subgroup of multiplicative type of \(G\). The obvious morphisms define isomorphisms \[ \mathrm{Tor}(G) \simeq \mathrm{Tor}(G/Q), \qquad \mathrm{Bor}(G) \simeq \mathrm{Bor}(G/Q), \qquad \mathrm{Kil}(G) \simeq \mathrm{Kil}(G/Q). \]

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.8.5

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, and \(P\) a subgroup-prescheme of \(G\), smooth and of finite presentation over \(S\). The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    For each \(s \in S\), \(P_{\overline{s}}\) is a parabolic subgroup of \(G_{\overline{s}}\) (i.e. the quotient prescheme \(G_{\overline{s}}/P_{\overline{s}}\) is proper over \(\overline{s}\), or again \(P_{\overline{s}}\) contains a Borel group of \(G_{\overline{s}}\), cf. BIBLE, 6-09, th. 4).

  2. (ii)

    The quotient sheaf \(G/P\) is representable by an \(S\)-prescheme smooth and projective over \(S\).

Moreover, under these conditions, \(P\) is closed in \(G\), with connected fibres, and one has \(P = \mathrm{Norm}_G(P)\).

Obviously (ii) \(\Rightarrow\) (i). If (i) holds, \(P_{\overline{s}}\) is connected and \(\mathrm{Norm}_{G(\overline{s})}(P_{\overline{s}}) = P(\overline{s})\), as follows at once from the conjugacy of the Borel groups (for the second point, cf. BIBLE, 12-06, lemma 4); it follows that \(P\) is of type (R), and that \(P = \mathrm{Norm}_G(P)\), hence is closed in \(G\). By 5.8.2, \(G/P = G/\mathrm{Norm}_G(P)\) is representable by a quasi-projective \(S\)-prescheme. Its fibres are connected and proper, hence it is projective by the reasoning of 5.8.3.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 5.8.6

The statements 5.8.1, 5.8.2, 5.8.5 are obviously valid for an \(S\)-group of type (RA), or for an \(S\)-group of type (RR) satisfying 5.1.8.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 5.8.7

Through the inner automorphisms of \(G\), one has canonical operations: \[ \begin{aligned} G &\longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_S(\mathrm{Tor}(G)), \\ G &\longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_S(\mathrm{Bor}(G)), \\ G &\longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_S(\mathrm{Kil}(G)), \end{aligned} \] which, in the situation of 5.8.3 (iii), are identified with the canonical operations \[ \begin{aligned} G &\longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_S(G/\mathrm{Norm}_G(T)), \\ G &\longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_S(G/B), \\ G &\longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_S(G/T). \end{aligned} \] In particular one concludes that \[ \begin{aligned} \mathrm{Ker}\big(G \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_S(\mathrm{Tor}(G))\big) &= \mathrm{Ker}\big(G \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_S(\mathrm{Bor}(G))\big) \\ &= \mathrm{Ker}\big(G \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_S(\mathrm{Kil}(G))\big) \\ &= \mathrm{Centr}(G). \end{aligned} \]

It is indeed clear that \(\mathrm{Centr}(G)\) operates trivially on each of the three schemes. Conversely, the kernel of \(G \to \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_S(\mathrm{Kil}(G))\) is "the intersection of the maximal tori of \(G\)" in the sense of 4.1.7, hence \(\mathrm{Centr}(G)\) (loc. cit.). For \(\mathrm{Bor}(G)\), one notes that "the intersection of the Borel groups of \(G\)" is also "the intersection of its maximal tori" (see the following no.). For \(\mathrm{Tor}(G)\), one uses Exp. XII 4.11.
5.9. Properties special to Borel groups
Most of these properties will be generalized in Exp. XXVI to parabolic groups.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 5.9.1

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(B\) and \(B'\) two Borel groups of \(G\). One says that \(B\) and \(B'\) are in general position (or that \(B'\) is in general position relative to \(B\)) if \(B \cap B'\) is a (maximal) torus of \(G\).

If \(T\) is a maximal torus of \(G\) contained in \(B\) and \(B'\), one says that \(B\) and \(B'\) are opposite (relative to \(T\)) if \(B \cap B' = T\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.9.2

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(B\) a Borel group of \(G\), \(T\) a maximal torus of \(B\). There exists a unique Borel group \(B'\) of \(G\) opposite to \(B\) relative to \(T\).

If \((G, T, M, R)\) is a splitting of \(G\) with respect to \(T\) and if \(B = B_{R^+}\) (5.5.1), then \(B' = B_{-R^+}\).

By faithfully flat descent, it suffices to prove the proposition in the split case, \(B = B_{R^+}\) (5.5.5 (iv)). Then \(B_{-R^+}\) is indeed opposite to \(B\) (4.1.2); let us show that it is the only Borel group of \(G\) containing \(T\) which is opposite to \(B\). If \(B'\) is a Borel group of \(G\) containing \(T\), then \(B'\) is locally on \(S\) of the form \(B_{R'^+}\), where \(R'^+\) is a second system of positive roots of \(R\) (5.5.5 (iii)). If \(R'^+ \ne -R^+\), there exists \(\alpha \in R'^+ \cap R^+\), hence such that \(U_\alpha \subset B_{R^+} \cap B_{R'^+}\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.9.3

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(B\) a Borel group of \(G\).

  1. (i)

    If \(B'\) is a Borel group of \(G\), the following conditions are equivalent:

    1. (a)

      \(B'\) is in general position with respect to \(B\) (5.9.1).

    2. (b)

      \(B'^u \cap B^u = e\).

    3. (b′)

      \(B'^u \cap B = e\).

    4. (c)

      The product in \(G\) induces an open immersion \(B'^u \times_S B \to G\).

    5. (c′)

      The canonical morphism \(B'^u \to G/B\) is an open immersion.

  2. (ii)

    The functor \(\mathrm{Opp}(B)\): \[ S' \longmapsto \left\{ \begin{array}{l} \text{Borel groups of } G_{S'} \text{ in} \\ \text{general position with respect to } B_{S'} \end{array} \right\} \] is representable by an open subprescheme of \(\mathrm{Bor}(G)\) (5.8.3). The morphism \[ \mathrm{Opp}(B) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Tor}(B) \] defined by \(B' \mapsto B \cap B'\) is an isomorphism. In particular (5.6.13) the inner automorphisms of \(B^u\) endow \(\mathrm{Opp}(B)\) with the structure of a principal homogeneous bundle under \(B^u\).

Let us first examine (i). We have (a) \(\Rightarrow\) (c); indeed, (c) is local for the étale topology; by 5.5.5 (iv), we are reduced to the case where \(G\) is split with respect to \(B \cap B'\) and \(B\) is of the form \(B_{R^+}\); by 5.9.2, we then have \(B'^u = U_{-R^+}\) and we are reduced to 4.1.2.

We have trivially (c′) \(\Leftrightarrow\) (c) \(\Rightarrow\) (b′) \(\Rightarrow\) (b). It thus remains to prove (b) \(\Rightarrow\) (a). Let us first prove (ii); the second assertion is a formal consequence of 5.9.2, the third follows from it at once by 5.6.13; let us then prove the first; it is local for the étale topology and we may therefore assume that \(B\) possesses a maximal torus \(T\); let \(B'_0\) be the group opposite to \(B\) relative to \(T\) (5.9.2).

By what precedes, the morphism \(B^u \to \mathrm{Bor}(G)\) induced by the canonical morphism \(G \to G/B'_0 \to \mathrm{Bor}(G)\) (5.8.3) induces an isomorphism \(B^u \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \mathrm{Opp}(G)\). We thus have a commutative diagram \[ \xymatrix{ B^u \ar[r] \ar[d]_{\wr} & G/B'_0 \ar[d]^{\wr} \\ \mathrm{Opp}(B) \ar[r] & \mathrm{Bor}(G). } \] Now the morphism \(B^u \to G/B'_0\) is an open immersion (by (i) (a) \(\Rightarrow\) (c′)), which completes the proof of (ii). Let us note at once the corollary

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.9.4

Let \(G\) be a reductive \(S\)-group and \(B\) and \(B'\) two Borel groups of \(G\). If \(s \in S\) is such that \(B_{\overline{s}}\) and \(B'_{\overline{s}}\) are in general position, there exists an open set \(V\) of \(S\) containing \(s\) such that \(B_V\) and \(B'_V\) are in general position.

It thus only remains for us to prove (b) \(\Rightarrow\) (a). By virtue of the preceding corollary, it suffices to do so when \(S\) is the spectrum of an algebraically closed field \(k\). We may assume \(G\) split with respect to a maximal torus \(T\) of \(B\). Let \(B'_0\) be the Borel group opposite to \(B\). The Borel groups of \(G\) are conjugate, hence there exists \(g \in G(k)\) with \(\mathrm{int}(g)B'_0 = B'\). By Bruhat's theorem, one may write \(g = bnb'\), with \(b \in B(k)\), \(b' \in B'_0(k)\), \(n \in \mathrm{Norm}_G(T)(k)\). We thus have \[ B' = \mathrm{int}(b)\, \mathrm{int}(n)\, B'_0 \] and \(B' \cap B = \mathrm{int}(b)\big(\mathrm{int}(n)B'_0 \cap B\big)\). If \(n \notin T(k)\), then \(\mathrm{int}(n)B'^u_0 \cap B^u \ne e\) (cf. the proof of 5.9.2); it follows that (b) implies \(B' \cap B = \mathrm{int}(b)(B'_0 \cap B) = \mathrm{int}(b)T\). Q.E.D.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.9.5

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(B\) a Borel group of \(G\), \(B^u\) its unipotent part. There exists a sequence of subgroups of \(B\): \[ U_0 = B^u \supset U_1 \supset \cdots \supset U_n \supset \cdots \] possessing the following properties:

  1. (i)

    Each \(U_i\) is smooth, with connected fibres, characteristic in \(B\); the inner automorphisms of \(B^u\) operate trivially on the quotient (sheaves) \(U_i/U_{i+1}\), \(i \geqslant 0\).

  2. (ii)

    For each \(i \geqslant 0\), there exist a locally free \(\mathscr{O}_S\)-Module \(\mathscr{E}_i\) and an isomorphism of \(S\)-sheaves of groups \[ U_i/U_{i+1} \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \mathbf{W}(\mathscr{E}_i). \]

  3. (iii)

    For every \(s \in S\), \((U_n)_s = e\) for \(n \geqslant \dim(B^u_s)\).

Let us first suppose that there exist a splitting \((G, T, M, R)\) of \(G\) and a system of positive roots \(R^+\) of \(R\) such that \(B = B_{R^+}\). We denote by \(R_0\) the set of simple roots of \(R^+\); for each \(\alpha \in R^+\), we denote by \(\mathrm{ord}(\alpha)\) the sum of the coefficients of \(\alpha\) over the basis \(R_0\) of \(\Gamma_0(R)\); it is the order of \(\alpha\) relative to \(R^+\). One has \(\mathrm{ord}(\alpha) \leqslant \mathrm{Card}(R^+)\). For every \(i > 0\), let \(R^{(i)}\) be the set of roots of order \(> i\); it is a closed set of positive roots, so one may construct (5.6.5) \[ U_i = U_{R^{(i)}}. \] If \(\alpha \in R^+\) and \(\beta \in R^{(i)}\), then \(\alpha + \beta \in R^{(i+1)}\). It follows, by 5.5.2, that each \(U_i\) is an invariant subgroup of \(B\) and that the inner automorphisms of \(B^u\) operate trivially on \(U_i/U_{i+1}\). This group is moreover identified with \[ \prod_{\mathrm{ord}(\alpha) = i+1} U_\alpha \] and is therefore endowed with a vector structure.

If \(B\) is of the form \(B_{R'^+}\) for another splitting \((G, T', M', R')\) of \(G\), let us show that the groups \(U'_i\) constructed as above by means of the new splitting coincide with the \(U_i\), and that the vector structures on the successive quotients likewise coincide. By 5.6.13, there exists \(b \in B^u(S)\) with \(T' = \mathrm{int}(b)T\); the assertion to be proved is local on \(S\) and one may therefore suppose that the isomorphism \(T \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} T'\) induced by \(\mathrm{int}(b)\) comes by duality from an isomorphism of root data \[ h : (M', M'^*, R', R'^*) \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} (M, M^*, R, R^*). \] It is clear that the roots of \(R'^+\) are the \(\alpha \circ \mathrm{int}(b) = h(\alpha)\), \(\alpha \in R^+\); that the simple roots of \(R'^+\) are the \(\alpha \circ \mathrm{int}(b) = h(\alpha)\), \(\alpha \in R_0\), and hence that \(\mathrm{ord}(h(\alpha)) = \mathrm{ord}(\alpha)\) for \(\alpha \in R^+\). On the other hand, it is clear by transport of structure that the vector groups \(U'_{h(\alpha)}\) are none other than the \(\mathrm{int}(b)U_\alpha\). One thus has \(\mathrm{int}(b)U_i = U'_i\); but as \(U_i\) is invariant, this gives \(U_i = U'_i\).
Likewise the isomorphism of vector groups \[ \mathrm{int}(b) : U_i/U_{i+1} \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} U'_i/U'_{i+1} \] is the identity, by virtue of what has already been proved.

Let us now treat the general case. There exist a covering family (ét) \(\{S_i \to S\}\) and, for each \(i\), a splitting \((G_i, T_i, M_i, R_i)\) and a system of positive roots \(R_i^+\) of \(R_i\) such that \(B \times_S S_i = B_{R_i^+}\) (5.5.5 (iii)). For each \(i\), one thus has a family \[ B_{S_i} = U_{i,0} \supset U_{i,1} \supset \cdots \supset U_{i,j} \supset \cdots \] and vector structures on the \(U_{i,j}/U_{i,j+1}\). By descent, it suffices to prove that for every pair \((i, i')\) and every \(j\), one has \[ U_{i,j} \times_{S_i} S_{ii'} = U_{i',j} \times_{S_{i'}} S_{ii'} \] (one writes \(S_{ii'} = S_i \times_S S_{i'}\)) and that the vector structures on the quotients \[ (U_{i,j}/U_{i,j+1}) \times_{S_i} S_{ii'} \qquad \text{and} \qquad (U_{i',j}/U_{i',j+1}) \times_{S_{i'}} S_{ii'} \] coincide. Now if \(S_{ii'} = \varnothing\), this is trivial; if \(S_{ii'} \ne \varnothing\), then one is in the situation studied above: \(B \times_S S_{ii'}\) is defined by the system of positive roots \(R_i^+\) (resp. \(R_{i'}^+\)) in the splitting \((G_{S_{ii'}}, T_i \times_{S_i} S_{ii'}, M_i, R_i)\) (resp. in the splitting \((G_{S_{ii'}}, T_{i'} \times_{S_{i'}} S_{ii'}, M_{i'}, R_{i'})\)).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.9.6

If \(S\) is affine, \(\mathrm{H}^1(S, B^u) = e\): every principal bundle under \(B^u\) possesses a section.

Indeed, \(S\) decomposes into a direct sum of subpreschemes on each of which \(B^u\) is of constant relative dimension. By (iii), one may therefore suppose that there exists an \(n\) such that \(U_n = e\). Since, by TDTE I, B.1.1, \[ \mathrm{H}^1(S, U_i/U_{i+1}) = \mathrm{H}^1(S, \mathbf{W}(\mathscr{E}_i)) = 0, \] one has \(\mathrm{H}^1(S, B^u) = 0\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.9.7

If \(S\) is affine, \(B\) possesses maximal tori. If \(T\) is a maximal torus of \(B\), \(\mathrm{H}^1(S, T) = \mathrm{H}^1(S, B)\).
The first assertion follows at once from 5.9.6 and 5.6.13; the second is deduced from it in the standard way.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.9.8

If \(G\) is a reductive \(S\)-group, the canonical morphism (cf. 5.8.3) \[ \mathrm{Kil}(G) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Bor}(G) \] possesses sections over every affine open set.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.9.9

Under the conditions of 5.9.5, suppose \(S\) affine; then there exists a locally free \(\mathscr{O}_S\)-Module \(\mathscr{E}\) such that \(B^u\) is, as a prescheme, \(S\)-isomorphic to \(\mathbf{W}(\mathscr{E})\).

Indeed, let us prove by induction on \(i\) that \(B^u/U_i\) is \(S\)-isomorphic to \(\mathbf{W}(\mathscr{E}_0 \oplus \cdots \oplus \mathscr{E}_{i-1})\). This is clear for \(i = 0\); suppose \(i \geqslant 1\). Then \(B^u/U_i\) is a principal homogeneous bundle with base \(B^u/U_{i-1}\) under the group \((U_{i-1}/U_i)_{B^u/U_{i-1}}\). Since \(B^u/U_{i-1}\) is affine, by the induction hypothesis, and \(U_{i-1}/U_i = \mathbf{W}(\mathscr{E}_{i-1})\), this bundle is trivial. One thus has (at least) an isomorphism of \(S\)-preschemes \[ B^u/U_i \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} (B^u/U_{i-1}) \times_S \mathbf{W}(\mathscr{E}_{i-1}) = \mathbf{W}(\mathscr{E}_0 \oplus \cdots \oplus \mathscr{E}_{i-1}). \] One concludes at once by condition (iii) of 5.9.5.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.9.10

Let \(S\) be a semi-local scheme, \(\{s_i\}\) its closed points, \(B\) a Borel group of the reductive \(S\)-group \(G\). The canonical map \[ B^u(S) \longrightarrow \prod_i B^u(\mathrm{Spec}\, k(s_i)) \] is surjective.

Indeed, if \(S = \mathrm{Spec}(A)\), \(k(s_i) = A/\mathfrak{p}_i\), and if \(\mathscr{E}\) is given by the \(A\)-Module \(E\), one has \[ B^u(S) = E \otimes A, \qquad B^u(\mathrm{Spec}\, k(s_i)) = E \otimes_A (A/\mathfrak{p}_i). \] The assertion then follows at once from the fact that \(A \to \prod_i A/\mathfrak{p}_i\) is surjective.
5.10. Subgroups of type (R) with reductive fibres

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.10.1

Let \((G, T, M, R)\) be a split \(S\)-group, \(R'\) a part of \(R\) of type (R) (5.4.2), \(H_{R'}\) the corresponding subgroup of \(G\). The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    \(H_{R'}\) is reductive (i.e. with reductive geometric fibres).

  2. (ii)

    One has \(R' = -R'\), i.e. \(R'\) is symmetric.

Moreover, under these conditions, \((H_{R'}, T, M, R')\) is a splitting of \(H_{R'}\); for every system of positive roots \(R^+\) of \(R\), \(R'^+ = R' \cap R^+\) is a system of positive roots of \(R'\) and \[ B_{R^+} \cap H_{R'} = H_{R'^+} \] is a Borel group of \(H_{R'}\), whose unipotent part is \[ U_{R^+} \cap H_{R'} = U_{R'^+}. \]

Obviously (i) \(\Rightarrow\) (ii) (it suffices to check it fibre by fibre, and \(R'\) is a root system of \(H_{R'}\) with respect to \(T\)). To prove (ii) \(\Rightarrow\) (i), one notes, by 5.4.3, that \[ H_{R'} \cap Z_\alpha = \mathrm{Centr}_{H_{R'}}(T_\alpha) = Z_\alpha \] for every \(\alpha \in R'\), and one applies the criterion of Exp. XIX 1.12.

If \(R^+\) is a system of positive roots of \(R\), then \(R^+ \cap R'\) is obviously a closed part of \(R'\) such that \(R'^+ \cup -R'^+ = R'\) and \(R'^+ \cap -R'^+ = \varnothing\), hence a system of positive roots of \(R'\). The two other assertions follow respectively from 5.6.1 (vi) and 5.6.7 (i).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.10.2

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(H\) a reductive sub-\(S\)-group such that for every \(s \in S\), \(G_{\overline{s}}\) and \(H_{\overline{s}}\) have the same reductive rank. Then \(H\) is closed in \(G\), \(\mathrm{Norm}_G(H)\) is smooth over \(S\), and \(\mathrm{Norm}_G(H)/H\) is representable by a finite étale \(S\)-prescheme.

If \(T\) is a maximal torus of \(H\) and \(B\) a Borel group of \(G\) containing \(T\), then \(B \cap H\) is a Borel group of \(H\), whose unipotent part is \((B \cap H)^u = B^u \cap H\).

The first assertions follow at once from 5.3.10 and 5.3.18, via the fact that the Weyl groups of \(G\) and of \(H\) are finite (Exp. XIX 2.5). The other assertions are local for the étale topology and reduce to the case studied in 5.10.1.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.10.3

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group.

  1. a)

    If \(Q\) is a torus of \(G\), \(\mathrm{Centr}_G(Q)\) is a subgroup of type (R) of \(G\) with reductive fibres. If \(Q \subset Q'\) are two tori of \(G\), then \(\mathrm{Centr}_G(Q) \supset \mathrm{Centr}_G(Q')\).

  2. b)

    If \(H\) is a subgroup of type (R) of \(G\) with reductive fibres, \(\mathrm{rad}(H)\) (4.3.6) is a torus of \(G\). If \(H \subset H'\) are two subgroups of type (R) of \(G\) with reductive fibres, then \(\mathrm{rad}(H) \supset \mathrm{rad}(H')\).

  3. c)

    If \(Q\) is a torus of \(G\), one has \[ \mathrm{rad}(\mathrm{Centr}_G(Q)) \supset Q \quad \text{and} \quad \mathrm{Centr}_G(\mathrm{rad}(\mathrm{Centr}_G(Q))) = \mathrm{Centr}_G(Q). \]

  4. d)

    If \(H\) is a subgroup of type (R) of \(G\) with reductive fibres, \[ \mathrm{Centr}_G(\mathrm{rad}(H)) \supset H \quad \text{and} \quad \mathrm{rad}(\mathrm{Centr}_G(\mathrm{rad}(H))) = \mathrm{rad}(H). \]

Indeed, a) follows at once from Exp. XIX 2.8. To prove b), it suffices to note that \(\mathrm{rad}(H') \subset H\), since \(H\) contains (locally for (fpqc)) a maximal torus of \(G\), hence of \(H'\). The first assertion of c) (resp. d)) is trivial, the second follows by the usual reasoning.
This proposition leads to the following definition:

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 5.10.4

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group. One says that the subtorus \(Q\) of \(G\) is a critical torus if it is the radical of its centralizer. One says that the reductive subgroup of type (R) \(H\) of \(G\) is critical if it is the centralizer of its radical.
One then has:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.10.5

For every subtorus \(Q\) of \(G\), \(\mathrm{Centr}_G(Q)\) is critical. For every subgroup of type (R) with reductive fibres \(H\) of \(G\), \(\mathrm{rad}(H)\) is a critical torus of \(G\). The maps \[ Q \mapsto \mathrm{Centr}_G(Q), \qquad H \mapsto \mathrm{rad}(H) \] are mutually inverse isomorphisms between the set of critical tori of \(G\) and that of its critical reductive subgroups of type (R).

If \(Q\) is a torus of \(G\), \(\mathrm{rad}(\mathrm{Centr}_G(Q))\) is the smallest critical torus of \(G\) containing \(Q\). If \(H\) is a reductive subgroup of type (R) of \(G\), \(\mathrm{Centr}_G(\mathrm{rad}(H))\) is the smallest critical reductive subgroup of type (R) of \(G\) containing \(H\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.10.6

Let \((G, T, M, R)\) be a split \(S\)-group, \(R'\) a part of \(R\). The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    \(R'\) is of type (R), \(H_{R'}\) is reductive and critical.

  2. (ii)

    There exist a system of simple roots \(R_0\) of \(R\) and a part \(R'_0\) of \(R_0\) such that \(R'\) is the set of elements of \(R\) which are linear combinations of the elements of \(R'_0\).

  3. (iii)

    \(R'\) is closed, symmetric, and every system of simple roots of \(R'\) is the intersection with \(R'\) of a system of simple roots of \(R\).

Indeed, by Exp. XXI 3.4.8, (ii) and (iii) are equivalent, and are also equivalent to the fact that \(R'\) is the intersection of \(R\) with a \(\mathbf{Q}\)-vector subspace of \(M \otimes \mathbf{Q}\). Now this last condition is implied by (i): if \(H_{R'} = \mathrm{Centr}_G(Q)\), then \(R'\) is the set of elements of \((R)\) which vanish on \(Q\) (Exp. II 5.2.3 (ii)). Finally, this condition implies (i), for \((H_{R'})\) is the maximal torus of \(\bigcap_{\alpha \in R'} \mathrm{Ker}(\alpha)\), hence \(\mathrm{Centr}_G(\mathrm{rad}(H_{R'}))\) is none other than \(H_{R''}\), where \(R''\) is the intersection of \(R\) with the vector subspace generated by \(R'\).

Let us summarize some of the preceding results: let \((G, T, M, R)\) be a split \(S\)-group, and let \(R_0\) be a system of simple roots of \(R\) and \(R^+\) the corresponding system of positive roots; let us choose a part \(R'_0\) of \(R_0\), denote by \(R'\) the set of elements of \(R\) which are linear combinations of the elements of \(R'_0\), and put \(R'^+ = R' \cap R^+\). Let \(T_{R'_0}\) be the maximal torus of \(\bigcap_{\alpha \in R'_0} \mathrm{Ker}(\alpha)\) and \(Z_{R'_0} = \mathrm{Centr}_G(T_{R'_0})\).

Then \(Z_{R'_0}\) is a reductive subgroup of \(G\), with radical \(T_{R'_0}\); \((Z_{R'_0}, T, M, R')\) is a split \(S\)-group; \(B_{R^+} \cap Z_{R'_0}\) is the Borel group of \(Z_{R'_0}\) defined by the system of positive roots \(R'^+\) (or else by the system of simple roots \(R'_0\)), and its unipotent part is \(U_{R^+} \cap Z_{R'_0} = U_{R'^+}\).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 5.10.8

Under the conditions of 5.10.4, let \(Q\) be a critical torus of \(G\), \(L = \mathrm{Centr}_G(Q)\) its centralizer. Since \(Q = \mathrm{rad}(L)\), \(Q\) is a characteristic subgroup of \(L\); it follows at once that \[ \mathrm{Norm}_G(L) = \mathrm{Norm}_G(Q), \] hence also \[ \mathrm{Norm}_G(L)/L = \mathrm{Norm}_G(Q)/\mathrm{Centr}_G(Q) = W_G(Q). \]
By 5.10.2, one deduces from this

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.10.9

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(Q\) a critical torus of \(G\). The Weyl group \(W_G(Q)\) is (étale) finite over \(S\).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 5.10.10

Under the conditions of 5.10.7, one can make explicit \[ W_G(T_{R'_0}) = \mathrm{Norm}_G(Z_{R'_0})/Z_{R'_0}. \] It is the constant group associated with the quotient \(W_1/W_2\), where \(W_1\) is the subgroup of \(W\) consisting of the elements which normalize the subgroup of \(M\) generated by \(R'_0\), and \(W_2\) the subgroup of \(W\) generated by the \(s_\alpha\), \(\alpha \in R'_0\).
5.11. Subgroups of type (RC)

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 5.11.1

Let \(S\) be a prescheme and \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group. A group subprescheme \(H\) of \(G\) is said to be of type (RC) if it is of type (R), i.e. (5.2.1) satisfies the following two conditions:

  1. (i)

    \(H\) is smooth and of finite presentation over \(S\), with connected fibres;

  2. (ii)

    for every \(s \in S\), \(H_{\overline{s}}\) contains a maximal torus of \(G_{\overline{s}}\);

and if it satisfies moreover the following condition:

  1. (iii)

    for every \(s \in S\) and every maximal torus \(T\) of \(H_{\overline{s}}\), the set of roots of \(H_{\overline{s}}\) relative to \(T\) is a closed subset of the set of all roots of \(G_{\overline{s}}\) relative to \(T\).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 5.11.2

As we have already pointed out in 5.4.8, condition (iii) is a consequence of the others when \(6\) is invertible on \(S\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 5.11.3

Let \((G, T, M, R)\) be a split \(S\)-group and \(R'\) a closed part of \(R\). Let \[ R_1 = \{\alpha \in R',\ -\alpha \in R'\} \qquad \text{and} \qquad R_2 = \{\alpha \in R',\ -\alpha \notin R'\}. \] Then \(R_1\) and \(R_2\) are closed. Consider the groups \(H_{R'}\), \(H_{R_1}\) and \(U_{R_2}\) (5.4.7 and 5.6.5), which are smooth and have connected fibres.

  1. (i)

    The group \(U_{R_2}\) is normal in \(H_{R'}\) and \(H_{R'}\) is the semi-direct product of \(U_{R_2}\) by \(H_{R_1}\).

  2. (ii)

    \(H_{R_1}\) is reductive, \(U_{R_2}\) has unipotent geometric fibres; every normal subgroup of \(H_{R'}\) which is smooth and of finite presentation over \(S\), with connected unipotent geometric fibres, is contained in \(U_{R_2}\), and every reductive subgroup of \(H_{R'}\) containing \(T\) is contained in \(H_{R_1}\).

  3. (iii)

    One has \(U_{R_2} \cap \mathrm{Norm}_G(H_{R_1}) = e\).

We have (iii) first of all by 5.6.7 (i). The first assertion of (i) follows from 5.6.7 (ii). Since \(U_{R_2} \cap H_{R_1} = e\) by (iii), the semi-direct product \(H_{R_1} \cdot U_{R_2}\) is a subgroup of \(H_{R'}\); but these are two subgroups of \(G\) of type (R), containing \(T\), and they have the same Lie algebra \(\mathfrak{g}_{R'}\); they therefore coincide by 5.3.5, which completes the proof of (i).

Let us now prove (ii); the first two assertions are nothing but 5.10.1 and 5.6.5. Let \(U\) be a group subprescheme of \(H_{R'}\), smooth and of finite presentation, normal (hence normalised by \(T\)), with connected unipotent geometric fibres; by 5.6.12, one has, locally on \(S\), \(U = U_{R''}\), where \(R''\) is a part of \(R'\) such that \(R'' \cap -R'' = \varnothing\). If \(U \not\subset U_{R_2}\), then \(R'' \not\subset R_2\), hence there exists \(\alpha \in R''\) with \(-\alpha \in R'\). Then \(Z_\alpha \subset H_{R'}\) (5.4.3), hence \(Z_\alpha\) normalises \(U\). But \(U\) contains \(U_\alpha\) and \(Z_\alpha\) possesses a section \(w\) such that \(\mathrm{int}(w)U_\alpha = U_{-\alpha}\); this implies \(-\alpha \in R''\), contradicting the hypothesis \(R'' \cap -R'' = \varnothing\).
Finally, if \(L\) is a reductive subgroup of \(H_{R'}\) containing \(T\), one has locally on \(S\), \(L = H_{R'''}\), with \(R'''\) symmetric, hence contained in \(R_1\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.11.4

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(H\) a group subprescheme of \(G\) of type (RC).

  1. (i)

    \(H\) is closed in \(G\), and \(\mathrm{Norm}_G(H)/H\) is representable by a finite étale group \(S\)-prescheme.

  2. (ii)

    \(H\) possesses a largest normal group subprescheme which is smooth and of finite presentation over \(S\), with connected unipotent geometric fibres; it is called the unipotent radical of \(H\) and is denoted \(\mathrm{rad}^u(H)\). The quotient sheaf \(H/\mathrm{rad}^u(H)\) is representable by a reductive \(S\)-group.

  3. (iii)

    If \(T\) is a maximal torus of \(H\), then \(H\) possesses a reductive subgroup \(L\) containing \(T\), of type (RC), possessing the following two properties:

    1. (a)

      Every reductive subgroup of \(H\) containing \(T\) is contained in \(L\).

    2. (b)

      \(H\) is the semi-direct product \(H = L \cdot \mathrm{rad}^u(H)\), i.e. the canonical morphism \(L \to H/\mathrm{rad}^u(H)\) is an isomorphism.

Moreover, \(L\) is the unique reductive subgroup of \(H\) containing \(T\) and satisfying either one of the two preceding conditions. Finally, one has the following relations: \[ \mathrm{Norm}_H(L) = L, \qquad \mathrm{Norm}_H(T) = \mathrm{Norm}_L(T), \qquad W_H(T) = W_L(T), \] in particular \(W_H(T)\) is finite over \(S\).
Proof. By virtue of 5.3.18, (i), which is local for the étale topology, is a consequence of the last assertion of (iii).
The assertions of (ii) are local for the étale topology. One may therefore assume oneself to be in the situation of 5.11.3, where one concludes at once by (i) and (ii).

By virtue of the uniqueness assertions contained therein, (iii) is likewise local for the étale topology and one may again reduce to the situation of 5.11.3, where properties (a) and (b) have been verified. The uniqueness of an \(L\) satisfying (a) is trivial; the uniqueness of an \(L\) satisfying (b) is evident, in view of (a). The relation \(\mathrm{Norm}_H(L) = L\) is nothing but 5.11.3 (iii); if a section of \(H\) normalises \(T\), then it normalises \(L\), by uniqueness of \(L\), hence is a section of \(L\) by what has just been proved, which proves the second relation; the third is then trivial.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.11.5

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(\mathscr{H}_c\) the functor of subgroups of type (RC) of \(G\), which is a subfunctor of the functor \(\mathscr{H}\) of 5.8.1.

  1. (i)

    \(\mathscr{H}_c\) is representable by an open subprescheme of \(\mathscr{H}\), smooth, quasi-projective and of finite presentation over \(S\).

  2. (ii)

    There exist a finite étale \(S\)-prescheme \(\mathcal{C}\ell_c\) and a morphism \[ c\ell : \mathscr{H}_c \longrightarrow \mathcal{C}\ell_c, \] smooth, quasi-projective, of finite presentation, surjective and with connected geometric fibres, having the following property:

    For every \(S' \to S\) and all \(H, H' \in \mathscr{H}_c(S')\), \(c\ell(H) = c\ell(H')\) if and only if \(H\) and \(H'\) are conjugate in \(G\) locally for the étale topology (or, what amounts to the same by 5.3.11, if for every \(s \in S\), \(H_{\overline{s}}\) and \(H'_{\overline{s}}\) are conjugate by an element of \(G(\overline{s})\)).

  3. (iii)

    \(\mathcal{C}\ell_c\) and \(c\ell\) are determined (up to a unique isomorphism) by the preceding conditions.

  4. (iv)
