    If \((G, T, M, R)\) is a splitting of \(G\), there exists an isomorphism \(\mathcal{C}\ell_c \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} E_S\) (where \(E_S\) is the constant scheme defined by the set \(E\) of conjugacy classes modulo \(W\) of closed parts of \(R\)) such that, for every closed part \(R'\) of \(R\), \(c\ell(H_{R'})\) corresponds to the canonical image of \(R'\) in \(E_S(S) = \mathrm{Hom}_{\text{loc.const.}}(S, E)\).

It is clear first of all that \(\mathscr{H}_c\) is an (ét) sheaf and that (ii) implies that \(\mathcal{C}\ell_c\) is nothing but the quotient sheaf of \(\mathscr{H}_c\) by the equivalence relation defined by conjugation.

This implies first of all (iii), as well as the fact that it suffices to verify (i) and (ii) locally for the étale topology. We therefore reduce to the situation of (iv); let us first construct a morphism \[ f : \mathscr{H}_c \longrightarrow E_S. \] It suffices to construct a map \(\mathscr{H}_c(S) \to E_S(S)\) functorial in \(S\); let then \(H\) be a subgroup of \(G\) of type (RC); since \(H\) possesses maximal tori locally for the étale topology, and since the maximal tori of \(G\) are conjugate locally for the étale topology, there exist a covering family \(\{S_i \to S\}\) and for each \(i\) a \(g_i \in G(S_i)\) and a closed part \(R_i\) of \(R\) such that \(\mathrm{int}(g_i)(H \times_S S_i) = H_{R_i} \times_S S_i\); each \(R_i\) defines a section \(\eta_i\) of \(E_S\), i.e. an element of \(E_S(S_i)\); it now suffices to prove that the family \((\eta_i)\) comes from a section \(\eta = f(H)\) of \(E_S\) over \(S\), and that this section depends only on \(H\).

To do this, we are reduced to proving that \(H_{R'}\) and \(H_{R''}\) are conjugate locally for the étale topology if and only if \(R'\) and \(R''\) are conjugate by an element of the Weyl group \(W\), which is trivial.

For every \(\eta \in E\), there exists an \(H_0 \in \mathscr{H}_c(S)\) such that \(f(H_0) = \eta\): it suffices to take \(H_0 = H_{R'}\) where \(R'\) is a closed part of \(R\) whose image in \(E\) is \(\eta\). If \(H \in \mathscr{H}_0(S')\), \(S' \to S\), then \(H\) is conjugate to \(H_0\) locally for the étale topology if and only if \(f(H) = \eta\) (as one sees at once by the preceding argument), which shows that \(f^{-1}(\eta)\) is identified with the quotient \(G/\mathrm{Norm}_G(H_0)\), which by 5.8.2 is an open subset of \(\mathscr{H}\), smooth, quasi-projective of finite presentation over \(S\), with connected non-empty fibres. Since \(E_S\) is the sum of the open subpreschemes images of the sections corresponding to the \(\eta \in E\), \(\mathscr{H}_c\) is identified with the sum of the \(f^{-1}(\eta)\), \(\eta \in E\), which proves (i) and (ii). Finally (iv) is verified by construction.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.11.6

If \(u \in \mathcal{C}\ell_c(S')\), \(S' \to S\), then \(c\ell^{-1}(u)\) is a smooth quasi- projective \(S'\)-prescheme of finite presentation with connected non-empty fibres; it is an open subset of \(\mathscr{H}_c\) and a "homogeneous" prescheme under \(G_{S'}\) (by inner automorphisms). In particular, if \(H \in c\ell^{-1}(u)(S')\), the morphism \(G_{S'} \to (\mathscr{H}_c)_{S'}\) defined by \(g \mapsto \mathrm{int}(g)H\) identifies \(G_{S'}/\mathrm{Norm}_{G_{S'}}(H)\) with \(c\ell^{-1}(u)\).

blocks.title: Examples
blocks.html:
Examples 5.11.7

In particular, one has two canonical sections \(u_t\), \(u_b\) of \(\mathcal{C}\ell_c\) corresponding respectively to the maximal tori (\(R' = \varnothing\)) and to the Borel groups (\(R' =\) system of positive roots). The \(S\)-preschemes \(c\ell^{-1}(u_t)\) and \(c\ell^{-1}(u_b)\) are nothing but the \(S\)-preschemes \(\mathrm{Tor}(G)\) and \(\mathrm{Bor}(G)\) introduced in 5.8.3. We shall see other examples in Exp. XXVI.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 5.11.8

One can construct an \(S\)-prescheme \(\mathcal{C}\ell\), of finite presentation and unramified, and a smooth surjective morphism \(\mathscr{H} \to \mathcal{C}\ell\), with connected geometric fibres, enjoying properties analogous to 5.11.5 (ii) and (iii).
6. The derived group
6.1. Preliminaries

In this no., we fix a prescheme \(S\), a split \(S\)-group \((G, T, M, R)\), a system of positive roots \(R^+\) of \(R\), and we write \[ B = B_{R^+}, \qquad B^- = B_{R^-}, \qquad U = B^u, \qquad U^- = (B^-)^u, \] \[ \Omega = \Omega_{R^+} = U^- \cdot T \cdot U. \]

We denote by \(T'\) the subtorus of \(T\) "image of the family \(\alpha^*\), \(\alpha \in R\)"; in other words \(T'\) is the image of the group morphism \[ \mathbf{G}_{m,S}^R \longrightarrow T \] defined by \((z_\alpha)_{\alpha \in R} \mapsto \prod_{\alpha \in R} \alpha^*(z_\alpha)\). One sees at once that if \(R_0\) denotes the set of simple roots of \(R^+\), the morphism \[ \mathbf{G}_{m,S}^{R_0} \longrightarrow T' \] defined in the same way is surjective with finite kernel. If one identifies \(T\) with \(\mathrm{D}_S(M)\), then \(T'\) is identified with \(\mathrm{D}_S(M/N)\), where \[ N = M \cap \mathscr{V}(R^*)^\perp \] (we write \(\mathscr{V}(R^*)^\perp\) for the orthogonal of \(\mathscr{V}(R^*)\) in the duality between \(V\) and \(V^*\)).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 6.1.2

The morphism defined by the product in \(T\) \[ \mathrm{rad}(G) \times_S T' \longrightarrow T \] is an isogeny (cf. 4.2.9).

Indeed, the canonical morphism \(\mathrm{rad}(T) \to T/T'\) comes by duality from the morphism of commutative groups \[ M \cap \mathscr{V}(R^*)^\perp \longrightarrow M/M \cap \mathscr{V}(R), \] which one sees at once to be injective with finite cokernel (cf. Exp. XXI 6.3).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 6.1.3

We set \(\Omega' = U^- \cdot T' \cdot U\); it is a closed subprescheme of \(\Omega = U^- \cdot T \cdot U\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 6.1.4

Let \(\alpha\) be a simple root and \(w_\alpha \in \mathrm{Norm}_G(T)(S)\) a lifting of \(s_\alpha\). One has \[ \mathrm{int}(w_\alpha)\Omega' \cap \Omega \subset \Omega'. \]

It suffices for us to prove that if \(g \in \Omega'(S)\) and if \(\mathrm{int}(w_\alpha)g \in \Omega(S)\), then \(\mathrm{int}(w_\alpha)g \in \Omega'(S)\). By 5.6.8, let us write \[ g = a \exp_{-\alpha}(Y)\, t \exp_\alpha(X)\, b, \] with \(a \in U_{-\widehat{\alpha}}(S)\), \(Y \in \Gamma(S, \mathfrak{g}^{-\alpha})\), \(t \in T'(S)\), \(X \in \Gamma(S, \mathfrak{g}^\alpha)\), \(b \in U_{\widehat{\alpha}}(S)\). One then has \[ \mathrm{int}(w_\alpha)g = \mathrm{int}(w_\alpha)a \cdot \mathrm{int}(w_\alpha)\big(\exp_{-\alpha}(Y) t \exp_\alpha(X)\big) \cdot \mathrm{int}(w_\alpha)b. \] By virtue of 5.6.8 (iv), one has \[ \mathrm{int}(w_\alpha)a \in U_{-\widehat{\alpha}}(S), \qquad \mathrm{int}(w_\alpha)b \in U_{\widehat{\alpha}}(S). \] There result the equivalences (on setting \(h = \exp_{-\alpha}(Y)\, t \exp_\alpha(X)\)): \[ \mathrm{int}(w_\alpha)g \in \Omega(S) \iff \mathrm{int}(w_\alpha)h \in \Omega(S) \] \[ \mathrm{int}(w_\alpha)g \in \Omega'(S) \iff \mathrm{int}(w_\alpha)h \in \Omega'(S). \] We are therefore reduced to the case where \(g = h\). Since one has (4.1.12) \[ Z_\alpha \cap \Omega = U_{-\alpha} \cdot T \cdot U_\alpha, \qquad Z_\alpha \cap \Omega' = U_{-\alpha} \cdot T' \cdot U_\alpha, \] we are reduced to proving the following assertion: \[ \mathrm{int}(w_\alpha)h \in (U_{-\alpha} \cdot T \cdot U_\alpha)(S) \Longrightarrow \mathrm{int}(w_\alpha)h \in (U_{-\alpha} \cdot T' \cdot U_\alpha)(S). \] But this last follows at once from Exp. XX 3.12, which shows that the component on \(T\) of \(\mathrm{int}(w_\alpha)h\) is of the form \(t \cdot \alpha^*(z) \in T'(S)\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 6.1.5

For every \(w \in \mathrm{Norm}_G(T)(S)\), there exists an open subset \(V_w\) of \(G\), containing the unit section, such that \[ \mathrm{int}(w)\Omega' \cap V_w \subset \Omega'. \]

Let us choose for each simple root \(\alpha\) an \(n_\alpha \in \mathrm{Norm}_G(T)(S)\) lifting \(s_\alpha\). For every point \(s \in S\), there exist an open subset \(V\) of \(S\) containing \(s\), a \(t \in T(V)\) and, on \(V\), a relation \[ w = n_{\alpha_1} \cdots n_{\alpha_p} t, \qquad \text{with the } \alpha_i \text{ simple}. \] We may obviously content ourselves with giving the proof for \(V = S\); it is done by induction on \(p\). If \(p = 0\), then \(w \in T(S)\) and one takes \(V_w = G\); suppose then \(w = n_\alpha \cdot w'\), with \(w'\) satisfying the conclusion of the lemma; there exists therefore an open subset \(V_{w'}\) of \(G\), containing the unit section, such that \(\mathrm{int}(w')\Omega' \cap V_{w'} \subset \Omega'\). One may then write \[ \begin{aligned} \mathrm{int}(w)\Omega' \cap \mathrm{int}(n_\alpha)V_{w'} \cap \Omega &= \mathrm{int}(n_\alpha)\big(\mathrm{int}(w')\Omega' \cap V_{w'}\big) \cap \Omega \\ &= \mathrm{int}(n_\alpha)\Omega' \cap \Omega \subset \Omega', \end{aligned} \] by 6.1.4. One then takes \(V_w = \mathrm{int}(n_\alpha)V_{w'} \cap \Omega\) and we are done.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 6.1.6

There exists an open subset \(V_0\) of \(G\), containing the unit section, such that for every \(S' \to S\), one has \[ U(S')\, U^-(S') \cap V_0(S') \subset \Omega'(S'). \]

Let indeed \(w_0\) be an element of \(\mathrm{Norm}_G(T)(S)\) lifting the symmetry of the Weyl group with \(w_0^2 \in T(S)\), that is to say such that \(\mathrm{int}(w_0)U = U^-\), (Exp. XXI 3.6.14). Let us show that the open subset \(V_0 = V_{w_0}\) of 6.1.5 answers the question. Indeed \[ \begin{aligned} U(S')\, U^-(S') &= \mathrm{int}(w_0)\big(\mathrm{int}(w_0)^{-1} U(S') \cdot \mathrm{int}(w_0)^{-1} U^-(S')\big) \\ &= \mathrm{int}(w_0)\big(U^-(S') \cdot U(S')\big) \subset \mathrm{int}(w_0)\Omega'(S'). \end{aligned} \] Whence \[ U(S')\, U^-(S') \cap V_0(S') \subset \mathrm{int}(w_0)\Omega'(S') \cap V_0(S') \subset \Omega'(S'). \]

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 6.1.7

Consider the morphism \[ f : \quad \Omega = U^- \cdot T \cdot U \longrightarrow T/T' \] composed of the second projection and the canonical morphism from \(T\) to \(T/T'\). Then \(f\) is "generically multiplicative": there exists an open subset \(V\) of \(\Omega \times_S \Omega\), containing the unit section (and therefore relatively schematically dense, Exp. XVIII 1.3) such that for every \(S' \to S\) and every \((x, y) \in V(S')\), one has \(xy \in \Omega(S')\) and \(f(xy) = f(x)f(y)\).

Let indeed \(x\) and \(y\) be two sections of \(\Omega\) over \(S'\). Let us write \[ \begin{cases} x = utv \\ y = u't'v' \end{cases} \qquad \begin{cases} u, u' \in U^-(S'), \quad t, t' \in T(S'), \\ v, v' \in U(S'). \end{cases} \] Let \(V_0\) be the open subset of 6.1.6 and \(V\) the open subset of \(\Omega \times_S \Omega\) defined by "\(vu' \in V_0(S')\)" (it is the inverse image of \(V_0\) under the morphism \(\Omega \times_S \Omega\) which is written set-theoretically \((x, y) \mapsto vu'\)). Then \(V\) answers the question. Indeed, for \((x, y) \in V(S')\), one has \[ xy = (utv)(u't'v') = (ut)(vu')(t'v'). \] But \(vu' \in \Omega'(S')\), whence \[ xy \in U^-(S')\, t\, \Omega'(S')\, t'\, U(S') \subset U^-(S')\, tt'\, T'(S')\, U(S'), \] which shows that \(xy \in \Omega(S')\) and that \[ f(xy) = f(tt') = f(t)f(t') = f(x)f(y). \]

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.1.8

There exists a group morphism \[ f : G \longrightarrow T/T' \] inducing on \(T\) the canonical projection. The kernel \(\mathrm{Ker}(f)\) of \(f\) is a closed group subprescheme of \(G\), smooth over \(S\) and with connected fibres. Every group morphism from \(G\) into a presheaf in commutative groups over \(S\), separated for (fppf), vanishes on \(\mathrm{Ker}(f)\).

The first assertion follows at once from 4.1.11. One has immediately \(\mathrm{Ker}(f) \cap \Omega = \Omega'\), which proves that \(\mathrm{Ker}(f)\) is smooth over \(S\). Every morphism \(g\) from \(G\) into a separated commutative group prescheme vanishes on \(U\) and \(U^-\), by 5.6.9 (ii). It therefore vanishes also on \(T'\) by Exp. XX 2.7, hence on \(\Omega'\). Taking the notations of 5.7.10, one sees that \(U_1 \subset \mathrm{Ker}(f)(S)\), which shows that \[ \mathrm{Ker}(f) = \bigcup_{u \in U_1} u\, \Omega', \] hence that \(\mathrm{Ker}(f)\) has connected fibres and that every \(g\) as above vanishes on \(\mathrm{Ker}(f)\).
6.2. Derived group of a reductive group

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 6.2.1

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group.

  1. (i)

    \(\mathrm{D}_S(G) = \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, \mathbf{G}_{m,S})\) is representable by a twisted constant \(S\)-group, whose type at \(s \in S\) is \(\mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{rgred}(G_s) - \mathrm{rgss}(G_s)}\).

  2. (ii)

    Let us write \(\mathrm{corad}(G) = \mathrm{D}_S(\mathrm{D}_S(G))\), which is therefore an \(S\)-torus. The biduality morphism (cf. Exp. VIII § 1) \[ f_0 : G \longrightarrow \mathrm{corad}(G) \] is smooth and surjective.

  3. (iii)

    The composed morphism \[ \mathrm{rad}(G) \longrightarrow G \longrightarrow \mathrm{corad}(G) \] is an isogeny (cf. 4.2.9).

  4. (iv)

    The kernel of \(f_0\), denoted \[ \text{dér}(G) = \mathrm{Ker}(f_0) \] is a closed group subprescheme of \(G\), semi-simple over \(S\), which is called the derived group of \(G\). If \(G\) is semi-simple, \(\text{dér}(G) = G\).

  5. (v)

    Every group morphism from \(G\) into a presheaf in commutative \(S\)-groups, separated for (fppf), vanishes on \(\text{dér}(G)\) and therefore factors through \(f_0\).

Proof. All the assertions of the theorem are local for the étale topology; one may therefore reduce to the case where \(G\) is split over \(S\). Consider then the morphism \(f\) of 6.1.8. By the last assertion of 6.1.8, one has at once an isomorphism \[ \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, \mathbf{G}_{m,S}) \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(T/T', \mathbf{G}_{m,S}), \] which proves (i), then (ii), and gives a commutative diagram \[ \xymatrix{ G \ar[r]^-{f_0} \ar[dr]_{f} & \mathrm{corad}(G) \ar[d]^{\wr} \\ & T/T'. } \] One then has (v) by 6.1.8, and (iii) by 6.1.2. One also has \(\mathrm{Ker}(f) = \mathrm{Ker}(f_0)\), which by 6.1.8 implies that \(\text{dér}(G)\) is smooth over \(S\) and has connected fibres; it remains to check that its fibres are semi-simple; now they are reductive by Exp. XIX 1.7, being normal subgroups of reductive groups. By (iii), \(\mathrm{rad}(G) \cap \text{dér}(G)\) is finite, which does indeed imply that the fibres of \(\text{dér}(G)\) are semi-simple.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 6.2.2
  1. a)

    By construction, in the case where \(G\) is split, \(\text{dér}(G)\) is the (fppf) subsheaf of \(G\) generated by the \(U_\alpha\), \(\alpha \in R\). (It even suffices to take the \(U_\alpha\), \(\alpha \in R_0 \cup (-R_0)\)).

  2. b)

    By (v), \(\text{dér}(G)\) is indeed the (fppf) sheaf of commutators of \(G\) (and even the separated (fppf) presheaf…).

  3. c)

    When \(S\) is the spectrum of the algebraically closed field \(k\), \(\text{dér}(G)(k)\) is the group of commutators of \(G(k)\) (Exp. VIB).

Let us now consider the two exact sequences \[ 1 \longrightarrow \mathrm{rad}(G) \longrightarrow G \longrightarrow \mathrm{ss}(G) \longrightarrow 1, \] \[ 1 \longrightarrow \text{dér}(G) \longrightarrow G \longrightarrow \mathrm{corad}(G) \longrightarrow 1. \] Since \(\mathrm{rad}(G)\) is central in \(G\), the product in \(G\) defines a group morphism \[ u : \quad \mathrm{rad}(G) \times_S \text{dér}(G) \longrightarrow G \] which is covering by virtue of 6.2.1 (iii), hence surjective, hence flat (Exp. VI). Its kernel is isomorphic to \(\mathrm{rad}(G) \cap \text{dér}(G)\), which is also the kernel of \(\mathrm{rad}(G) \to \mathrm{corad}(G)\), hence is a finite subgroup of multiplicative type of \(\mathrm{rad}(G)\).
One reasons in the same way for the morphism \[ G \longrightarrow \mathrm{corad}(G) \times_S \mathrm{ss}(G), \] whose kernel is \(\text{dér}(G) \cap \mathrm{rad}(G)\). We therefore have the

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.2.4

Let \(G\) be a reductive \(S\)-group. The morphisms \[ \mathrm{rad}(G) \times_S \text{dér}(G) \longrightarrow G, \qquad G \longrightarrow \mathrm{corad}(G) \times_S \mathrm{ss}(G), \qquad \mathrm{rad}(G) \longrightarrow \mathrm{corad}(G) \] are central isogenies, and their kernels are isomorphic.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 6.2.5

The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    \(G\) is the product of a semi-simple group and a torus.

  2. (ii)

    \(\mathrm{rad}(G) \times_S \text{dér}(G) \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} G\).

  3. (iii)

    \(G \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \mathrm{corad}(G) \times_S \mathrm{ss}(G)\).

  4. (iv)

    \(\mathrm{rad}(G) \cap \text{dér}(G) = e\).

Let us return provisionally to the case of a split group. Let us keep the notations of 6.1. Set \(N = M \cap \mathscr{V}(R^*)^\perp\). One therefore has \(T' = \mathrm{D}_S(M/N)\). We have seen that \(U^- \cdot T' \cdot U\) was an open neighbourhood of the unit section of \(\text{dér}(G)\). One therefore has \[ \mathscr{L}ie(\text{dér}(G)/S) = \mathfrak{t}' \oplus \coprod_{\alpha \in R} \mathfrak{g}^\alpha. \] Since the characters induced on \(T'\) by the \(\alpha \in R\) are non-zero and distinct (cf. Exp. XXI 1.2.5 – we have moreover already used this fact in 6.1.2), \(R\) is a root system of \(G\) relative to \(T\). It is then immediate (by \(U_\alpha \subset \text{dér}(G)\)) that the morphisms \(\exp\) of \(\text{dér}(G)\) "are" those of \(G\), and likewise for the coroots.
Hence:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.2.7

In the preceding notations, \((\text{dér}(G), T', M/N, R)\) is a split group with root datum \(\text{dér}(\mathscr{R}(G))\). The canonical morphism \(\text{dér}(G) \to G\) gives by functoriality the canonical morphism of root data \(\mathscr{R}(G) \to \text{dér}(\mathscr{R}(G))\) of Exp. XXI 6.5.
N.B. The reader may, by way of exercise, construct the diagram of split groups corresponding to the three left-hand columns of the diagram of root data of Exp. XXI 6.5.7.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.2.8

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(\text{dér}(G)\) its derived group.

  1. (i)

    For every maximal torus \(T\) of \(G\), \(T \cap \text{dér}(G)\) is a maximal torus of \(\text{dér}(G)\). For every maximal torus \(T'\) of \(\text{dér}(G)\), \(\mathrm{Centr}_G(T') = \mathrm{rad}(G) \cdot T'\) is a maximal torus of \(G\). The two preceding constructions are inverse to one another and establish a bijective correspondence between the maximal tori of \(G\) and those of \(\text{dér}(G)\).

  2. (ii)

    For every Borel group \(B\) of \(G\), \(B \cap \text{dér}(G)\) is a Borel group \(B'\) of \(\text{dér}(G)\). One has \(B'^u = B^u\). For every Borel group \(B'\) of \(\text{dér}(G)\), \(\mathrm{Norm}_G(B') = \mathrm{rad}(G) \cdot B'\) is a Borel group of \(G\). The preceding maps are inverse to one another and establish a bijective correspondence between the Borel groups of \(G\) and those of \(\text{dér}(G)\).

By the theorem of local conjugacy of maximal tori and the construction of the derived group, the only assertion remaining to be proved in (i) is the following: if \(T\) is a maximal torus of \(G\), then \[ T = (T \cap \text{dér}(G)) \cdot \mathrm{rad}(G) = \mathrm{Centr}_G(T \cap \text{dér}(G)). \] The first assertion is trivial (since one reduces to the split case); the second follows from it at once, since \(\mathrm{rad}(G)\) is central in \(G\), hence \(T = \mathrm{Centr}_G(T) = \mathrm{Centr}_G(T \cap \text{dér}(G))\). One reasons in the same way for (ii).
6.3. Subgroups with commutative quotients
Let \(G\) be a reductive \(S\)-group. If \(H\) is a subsheaf in groups of \(G\), the following conditions are equivalent:

1. –

    \(H\) contains \(\text{dér}(G)\).

  2. –

    \(H\) is normal; \(G/H\) is commutative.

Then the canonical morphism \(f_0 : G \to \mathrm{corad}(G)\) sends \(H\) onto a subsheaf \(f_0(H)\) of \(\mathrm{corad}(G)\); one has \[ G/H \simeq \mathrm{corad}(G)/f_0(H), \qquad H/\text{dér}(H) \simeq f_0(H), \] \[ \text{dér}(G) = \text{dér}(H), \qquad H = f_0^{-1}(f_0(H)). \] Since \(\text{dér}(G)\) is smooth over \(S\) and has connected fibres, \(H \mapsto f_0(H)\) establishes a one-to-one correspondence between the closed (resp. retrocompact) group subpreschemes of \(G\) containing \(\text{dér}(G)\), smooth over \(S\) and with connected fibres, and the closed (resp. retrocompact) group subpreschemes of \(\mathrm{corad}(G)\), smooth over \(S\) and with connected fibres. Now \(\mathrm{corad}(G)\) is a torus, hence a smooth group subprescheme of \(\mathrm{corad}(G)\) with connected fibres and retrocompact is a subtorus of it (Exp. X 8.2), hence is closed in \(\mathrm{corad}(G)\).

If \(H\) is a closed group subprescheme of \(G\), smooth over \(S\), with connected fibres and normal in \(G\), then \(H\) is reductive. If moreover \(H \supset \text{dér}(G)\), then \(\text{dér}(H) = \text{dér}(G)\) and \(f_0(H)\) is identified with \(\mathrm{corad}(H)\). We have thus proved the

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.3.3

Let \(G\) be a reductive \(S\)-group. Every group subprescheme \(H\) of \(G\) which is normal in \(G\), with commutative quotient (i.e. containing \(\text{dér}(G)\)), smooth over \(S\), with connected fibres and retrocompact in \(G\), is closed and reductive. One has \(\text{dér}(H) = \text{dér}(G)\), \(f_0(H)\) is identified with \(\mathrm{corad}(H)\); one has \[ G/H \simeq \mathrm{corad}(G)/\mathrm{corad}(H), \qquad H = (H \cap \mathrm{rad}(G)) \cdot \text{dér}(G). \] Moreover, \(H \mapsto f_0(H)\) defines an isomorphism between the set of subgroups \(H\) of \(G\) possessing the preceding properties and the set of subtori of \(\mathrm{corad}(H)\).
By a new application of Noether's theorem, one deduces from this the

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.3.4

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\). For every subgroup \(H\) of \(G\) as above, \(T \cap H\) is a maximal torus of \(G\) and one has \[ G/H \simeq T/T \cap H, \qquad H = (T \cap H) \cdot \text{dér}(G). \] Moreover, \(H \mapsto T \cap H\) is an isomorphism between the set of subgroups \(H\) of \(G\) as above and the set of subtori of \(T\) containing \(T \cap \text{dér}(G)\).
